1.

AT THE TWENTY-FIFTH HOUR

Private Building, Astrobe
+

Cosmos Kingmaker, Peter Proctor, and Fabian Foreman choose a candidate for World President while mechanical Killers demolish Foreman's building around them. Kingmaker calls Astrobe mankind's third chance; Foreman argues that previous worlds died without wholly failing. The Killers hunt Foreman because he wants Astrobe to die and be reborn. After rejecting living candidates and considering men from Earth's past, the three agree to send for Thomas More. Kingmaker and Proctor leave. Foreman remains as the building collapses, having said that he knows a way out.

“He had one completely honest moment right at the end. I can't think of anyone else who ever had one.”

Characters
Cosmos KingmakerPeter ProctorFabian ForemanCaptain John Chezem IIIThe Colonel
Themes
The Three MastersDeath and RenewalPolitical SymbolsThe Mustard Seed
Outline
I. The Masters under siege +
  • Kingmaker is the Heraldic Lion, Proctor the Sleek Fox, and Foreman the Worried Hawk.
  • Each believes that he controls the other two; each is partly right.
  • The Killers demand Foreman's life. Captain Chezem takes command after the colonel dies.
II. Death and failure +
  • Kingmaker names the Old World, America, and Astrobe as mankind's three chances.
  • Foreman disputes the count and distinguishes a world's death from its failure.
  • Foreman wants a death and resurrection of Astrobe; the Killers sense his intention.
III. Choosing More +
  • Proctor wants a manageable public symbol; Kingmaker wants a good man; Foreman wants a great man.
  • Living candidates, a manufactured candidate, and historical candidates are considered.
  • Kingmaker proposes using Chronometanastasis. Foreman's list contains only Thomas More.
IV. The building falls +
  • The three approve More's selection.
  • Kingmaker and Proctor escape through the shattered wall.
  • Foreman stands inside as the building collapses; the final sentence recalls his escape route.
› Notes and sources (12)
1. The twenty-fifth hour

Kingmaker imagines a crisis continuing beyond the last possible hour. The title also invites comparison with C. Virgil Gheorghiu’s novel about a person trapped in the classifications and machinery of modern society. The resemblance is especially apt while Astrobe’s mechanical Killers batter down the building.

C. Virgil Gheorghiu, The Twenty-Fifth Hour (1949; English translation, 1950).

2. The lion, the fox, and the hawk

Kingmaker’s lion and Proctor’s fox recall Machiavelli’s advice that a prince needs both strength and cunning. Foreman’s hawk adds a third figure to the pair. Their competing claims to control one another make government a contest among these different kinds of power.

Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chap. 18.

3. Kingmaker and Fabian

Kingmaker’s name recalls Warwick, the magnate who made and unmade English kings. Fabian can suggest Fabius Cunctator, the Roman commander famous for delay, and the society named after him. Foreman’s waiting and carefully timed intervention suit that association, although the novel does not explain his name.

Shakespeare, 3 Henry VI, 3.3; the historical epithets Warwick the Kingmaker and Fabius Cunctator.

4. The crack of doom

The phrase belongs to Macbeth’s vision of a seemingly endless succession of kings. Here the Masters argue over postponing judgment while the Killers provide the thunder outside. A familiar expression becomes a physical event in the scene.

Shakespeare, Macbeth, 4.1.

5. The doom clock

Foreman’s mechanical man belongs to the clock that threatens Astrobe. The image recalls the Doomsday Clock of Cold War public life. A manufactured president cannot save the world if he is another part of the machinery bringing about its end.

The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ Doomsday Clock, introduced in 1947.

6. Deaths and failures

Foreman distinguishes the death of a historical world from its failure. His account develops into the five-hundred-year sequence in Chapter 13. Toynbee offers a useful comparison for the language of civilizational breakdown, especially the later phrase Time of Troubles; Foreman’s particular chronology is his own.

Arnold J. Toynbee, A Study of History; Past Master, chap. 13.

7. Byerly and the manufactured candidate

Byerly’s name appears amid doubts about whether a candidate is human and a proposal to manufacture the ideal president. This makes Asimov’s Stephen Byerley, the politician suspected of being a robot, a plausible allusion. The spelling differs, and Lafferty leaves the connection unstated.

Isaac Asimov, “Evidence” (1946) and “The Evitable Conflict” (1950).

8. Chronometanastasis

The name combines Greek words for time and migration. It makes travel into the past sound like a change of dwelling. The embedded resemblance to anastasis, resurrection, also suits the project of bringing a long-dead man back into public life.

Greek chronos, time; metanastasis, migration; anastasis, rising or resurrection.

9. Why Plato is rejected

Foreman objects to Plato’s claim that justice makes a man happy. He wants someone who can be unhappy over an unjust situation. The discussion tests the difference between designing an ideal commonwealth and suffering with the people who inhabit an actual one.

Plato, Republic 1.354a; Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

10. A great man from the past

The candidates include rulers, counselors, a jurist, and an architect. Foreman reduces his own list to More and to one decisive act of honesty. This resembles the great-man theory of history, but the choice also makes the supposedly exemplary man dependent on those who recruit him.

Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841).

11. The honest moment and the lost head

The exchange anticipates More’s execution on Tower Hill in 1535 and his second execution on Astrobe. Roper records More speaking plainly against the statute after his conviction. That episode helps illuminate Foreman’s interest in a final honest act; Lafferty’s More is a fictional reworking of the historical martyr.

William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, account of the trial and execution.

12. The mustard seed

Foreman needs only a very small beginning. The Gospel seed that grows into a great plant gives his political experiment a religious scale. Chapter 13 returns to the image when he explains what he expects More’s death to accomplish.

Matthew 13:31–32; Mark 4:30–32; Luke 13:18–19.

2.

MY GRAVE, AND I IN IT

Cathead → Spaceport → Hopp-Equation Space → Earth (London/Chelsea) → Return
+

Paul, a hunted pilot deprived of his surname and citizenship, agrees to bring Thomas More to Astrobe. With help from Rimrock and other allies, he escapes the spaceport and travels to Earth through Hopp-Equation Space. His ninety-second sleeps contain elaborate passage dreams. In London, Brooks provides the time machine; Paul travels into the past and walks to More's home in Chelsea. More has already heard of Astrobe's future from other time travelers. He agrees to go when he recognizes himself as the mysterious Past Master. Back in the future, he visits his own grave before departing for Astrobe with Paul.

“We built it too small, Paul, we built it too small.”

Characters
PaulFabian ForemanThomas MoreBrooksRimrockBatterseaShantyWalter CopperheadSliderAdam
Themes
Time TravelIdentityPassage DreamsUtopia
Outline
I. Paul's mission +
  • Paul has survived a year of pursuit by the Killers.
  • Rimrock brings him into contact with Foreman.
  • Paul steals Foreman's grasshopper; a clash between spaceport guards and pursuing Killers helps him reach the spacecraft.
  • Rimrock, Copperhead, Battersea, Shanty, and Slider take part in the confusion.
II. Passage dreams +
  • The flight takes about seven hundred standard hours.
  • Hopp travel reverses polarity, including handedness and sexual characteristics.
  • Paul estimates twenty thousand dreams, each contained within no more than ninety seconds of sleep.
  • Dreams include Adam, his sister, Ouden, Sour John's kidney, and the destruction of Rhium and Antirhium.
III. More in Chelsea +
  • Paul uses Brooks's machine in London, then walks to Chelsea.
  • More already knows of time travelers and of Astrobe.
  • More describes Utopia as a bitter satire misunderstood as an ideal.
  • The name Past Master persuades him that he may be the man who saves Astrobe.
IV. The grave and the return +
  • More and Paul go to confession before leaving the sixteenth century.
  • In future London, More visits the grave that still contains his bones.
  • He discovers modern books and tobacco, then leaves for Astrobe.
  • His passage dreams anticipate the Masters and other figures he will meet.
› Notes and sources (17)
1. Paul the traveler

More explicitly connects the pilot with his name-saint, the apostle whose journeys fill Acts. The comparison gives Paul’s mission a spiritual possibility that its organizers do not explain to him. His confession before his own birth adds a comic reversal to that connection.

Acts 13–28.

2. The guards and the hounds

Paul’s escape depends on bringing the mechanical guards and Killers together like bears and hounds in a baiting. The image anticipates the journey to More’s England, where bear-baiting was a familiar public spectacle. Paul and his allies arrange the encounter and exploit the confusion.

The English bear-baiting tradition.

3. Reversal in Hopp-Equation space

Paul’s change of handedness recalls the mirror-reversed traveler in Wells’s “The Plattner Story.” Lafferty extends the joke to sex and voice. This bodily reversal also begins the novel’s larger pattern of left-handed actions and unexpected means of rescue.

H. G. Wells, “The Plattner Story” (1896).

4. Dreams and the human unconscious

The statement that ansels existed in the human unconscious before people discovered them on Astrobe invites comparison with Jung’s archetypes. The novel lets an image encountered in dreams become a creature met in waking life. It does not require that every passage dream be decoded into a single fixed meaning.

C. G. Jung, writings on the collective unconscious and archetypes.

5. Adam

The first man’s name belongs to a boy who repeatedly appears in scenes of battle and death. His insistence that each death belongs to another bearer of the name complicates any simple account of resurrection. The biblical association brings the deaths of individual men into the story of mankind.

Genesis 2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45.

6. Sour John and the stolen emerald

Sour John is also a storyteller in Lafferty’s “The Ugly Sea.” His theft of an idol’s green eye recalls J. Milton Hayes’s music-hall monologue, but the replacement kidney turns the adventure into a joke about mistaken value. Paul’s objection to the port’s geography is overruled by the teller.

R. A. Lafferty, “The Ugly Sea” (1960); J. Milton Hayes, “The Green Eye of the Little Yellow God” (1911).

7. Rhium and Antirhium

The paired stars borrow the names of the opposing headlands at the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth. Their linked rotation resembles a centrifugal governor regulating a machine. When the chain breaks, the dream makes a cosmic catastrophe out of a mechanical failure.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.86; Strabo, Geography 8.2.3.

8. More’s Utopia

More calls his book a bitter joke that later readers have mistaken for a blueprint. This is the fictional More’s account of his intention. It establishes the central predicament: the author must live in, and eventually govern, a world that has taken his imagined commonwealth seriously.

Thomas More, Utopia (1516).

9. The sickest possible world

More’s description of Utopia reverses the familiar formula of the best of all possible worlds. The later history of that formula, especially Voltaire’s Pangloss, makes the line another deliberate-looking anachronism in the speech of a man who already knows several futures.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Theodicy (1710); Voltaire, Candide (1759).

10. The meeting at Chelsea

Paul finds More free in his garden before the decision that will lead to his death. Historically, More refused the oath in April 1534 and was imprisoned until his execution in July 1535. The novel combines that situation with a journey about a thousand years back from 2535; its calendar does not resolve into an exact historical date.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More; More’s imprisonment, 1534–35.

11. Holbein’s portrait

Paul recognizes More partly from Holbein’s portrait. The contrast between the short, familiar-looking man and the tall Astrobian pilot makes the historical figure physically unheroic before the narrative tests what kind of hero he can become.

Hans Holbein the Younger, Sir Thomas More (1527), Frick Collection.

12. Past Master

The title joins a master from the past with the ordinary meaning of an expert. It also recalls an office formerly held in a guild or lodge. The later language of masters, a station, and an inner circle extends those institutional associations.

The guild and Masonic office of past master; Past Master, chap. 4.

13. Mercy and the old things

More’s Latin plea for mercy belongs to the language of prayer. The publican’s farewell and lament for the old things likewise draw on scriptural idiom. In this scene the promise of things made new is heard by someone who fears what the religious changes will destroy.

Miserere mihi, Domine, Roman Missal, Introit for the Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Colossians 2:6; Revelation 21:4–5.

14. Looking into his own grave

The chapter title comes from More’s visit to the grave that already contains his bones. The historical More prepared a tomb and epitaph at Chelsea, but his body was buried at St. Peter ad Vincula in the Tower. Lafferty’s scene makes the traveler confront the fact of his first death before he goes to meet a second.

More’s Chelsea epitaph (1532); Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More.

15. The head and the signet ring

The burial tradition separates More’s body in the Tower from his head at Canterbury. The future priest’s discovery of identifiable bones and a signet ring belongs to Lafferty’s fiction. Its purpose is to make More’s presence and his completed death equally tangible.

Thomas Stapleton, Tres Thomae (1588), account of Margaret Roper and More’s head.

16. Enskied and sainted

The rare verb enskied recalls Lucio’s description of Isabella in Measure for Measure. Paul has just reminded More of his canonization; the flight then sends the sainted man literally into the sky. More’s enthusiasm for a newly discovered cigar keeps the ascent comic.

Shakespeare, Measure for Measure, 1.4.

17. The woman in More’s dream

Succubus, Eve, Lilith, Judith, Mary, and Valkyrie bring demonic, maternal, holy, and martial figures into one image. Judith’s beheading of Holofernes is especially pointed in a novel about More’s head. The composite anticipates Evita without reducing her to one of its names.

Genesis 2–3; Judith 13; the traditions of Lilith and the Valkyries.

3.

AT THE NAKED SAILOR

Astrobe Orbit → Landing → Cathead → The Naked Sailor Inn
+

A false ansel impersonates Rimrock and draws Paul and Thomas into an ambush after their arrival on Astrobe. The real Rimrock warns them too late, but Cathead allies rescue them. At the Naked Sailor, Thomas sees severe poverty and learns that the inhabitants chose to leave the Golden Cities. He asks what makes a being human, recognizing intellect and spirit in Rimrock. Ouden confronts Paul, Thomas, and the ansel in an encounter described as a leftover passage dream. Battersea and the others then escort Thomas's party to Cosmopolis.

“I have one juice left that you do not know.”

Characters
PaulThomas MoreRimrockBatterseaShantyWalter CopperheadOudenEvita
Themes
Golden vs. RottingTelepathy/EutheopathyNothingness (Ouden)Refuge in Hell
Outline
I. The false warning +
  • An ansel voice directs Paul towards the edging trees.
  • Rimrock announces that another being spoke in his place.
  • Paul and Thomas fight the attackers; Cathead men carry them to safety.
II. The Naked Sailor +
  • Paul wakes injured; Thomas's broken jaw has been wired.
  • Thomas encounters the misery of Cathead and the Barrio.
  • Paul says that the inhabitants can return to comfortable lives but refuse to do so.
  • The Killers murder a demented man; hungry people seize his goats.
III. Rimrock and Ouden +
  • Thomas recognizes Rimrock as human in the sense of possessing body, spirit, and intellect.
  • Rimrock has dealt with the false ansel.
  • Ouden threatens to extinguish life and imagination.
  • The narrator calls the speaking human presence Paul-Thomas, leaving the individual speaker uncertain.
IV. The escort +
  • Battersea, Shanty, Copperhead, and others form an armed convoy.
  • The party leaves the slums, skirts Wu Town, and enters Cosmopolis.
  • The three Masters and Pottscamp await Thomas.
› Notes and sources (7)
1. The Naked Sailor and the seven hells

More places the inn in a numbered division of Hell and consoles Paul that three worse divisions remain. The Qur’an supplies seven gates, while later commentaries arrange the inhabitants differently. The joke’s exact assignment of Christians to a fourth division should be read as More’s statement within the scene.

Qur’an 15:44; George Sale, Preliminary Discourse to The Koran (1734).

2. Poverty and Utopia

More’s outrage at starvation and punishing labor recalls Hythloday’s indictment of England in Utopia. Cathead confronts him with a further difficulty: its inhabitants have chosen to leave material abundance. His familiar political explanations cannot yet account for that choice.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

3. Holy poverty

More accepts voluntary religious poverty but recoils from deprivation that degrades its sufferers. The distinction matters throughout the Cathead chapters. His admiration for a modest life does not make him an advocate of the conditions he sees here.

The Franciscan tradition of holy poverty; More’s account of common life in Utopia.

4. The oceanic man

Rimrock’s seal-like body and ability to move on land recall the seal-people of northern folklore. His shifting between no legs, four, and two can also suggest the Sphinx’s riddle about man. More’s decisive test, however, is intellect and spirit rather than an animal’s outward shape.

The selkie tradition; Apollodorus, Library 3.5.8.

5. Ouden and the Greek joke-names

Ouden means nothing. The name extends the learned naming games of Utopia, whose island, city, and river carry teasing Greek meanings. Here the word becomes a speaker who describes his nothingness as active, hungry, and destructive.

Greek ouden, nothing; More, Utopia.

6. Nothingness and evil

More’s denial that Ouden has being can be read alongside Augustine and Aquinas on evil as a privation of good. Ouden answers that his nothingness is a vortex. The exchange tests what that destructive claim means; it does not by itself settle the novel’s metaphysics in Ouden’s favor.

Augustine, Confessions 7.12; Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 48.

7. The one kindling

Ouden remembers a single kindling that overcame him and claims that he is extinguishing it. John’s light shining in darkness supplies a strong biblical comparison. Paul-Thomas answers with the possibility of rekindling and with a resource that Ouden does not know.

John 1:4–5.

4.

ON HAPPY ASTROBE

Cosmopolis, Astrobe
+

Rimrock and Copperhead arrange a triumphal reception that Thomas has imagined without consciously ordering. The Exultation Trumpets sound, the assembled leaders rise, and Thomas accepts the burden before it has formally been offered. He then speaks with Kingmaker, Proctor, Foreman, and Pottscamp. Recalled dreams show Kingmaker as a spider, Proctor as a fox above the void, and Foreman as a hawk counting shells. Pottscamp promises a later meeting with the real Circle of Masters. Thomas is dazzled by Astrobe's achievements but resists being treated merely as a public figurehead.

“I accept the great burden that has been given me to bear.”

Characters
Thomas MoreCosmos KingmakerPeter ProctorFabian ForemanPottscampPaulEvitaRimrockWalter Copperhead
Themes
Whited SepulcherThe Astrobe DreamPolitical TheaterPast Master Prophecy
Outline
I. The triumph +
  • Evita calls the golden city a whited sepulcher.
  • Rimrock and Copperhead transmit Thomas's unspoken intentions.
  • Battles secure the twelve trumpet towers; the Exultation Trumpets sound.
  • The leaders stand and acclaim Thomas at Convocation Hall.
II. Kingmaker +
  • Thomas blocks a verbal mind-probe by thinking in Latin.
  • Kingmaker describes Hopp and Horwitz travel and the six Proven Reserve Worlds.
  • Thomas insists that an elected president must govern.
  • The spider dream shows Kingmaker defending a world of webs.
III. Proctor and Foreman +
  • Proctor praises easy termination and threatens to break Thomas if he becomes more than a toy.
  • The fox dream places Proctor at home in the void.
  • Foreman says that Thomas's death will be needed.
  • The hawk's thirty shells suggest betrayal.
IV. Pottscamp +
  • The dream of a boy and his toy ends with the toy eating its maker.
  • Thomas cannot tell which figure represents Pottscamp.
  • Pottscamp promises to introduce eight other entities and reveal the back of Astrobe's tapestry.
› Notes and sources (12)
1. Every man a king

The golden inhabitants appear to fulfill the promise associated with Huey Long’s slogan. Their magnificence makes More eager to join them. Later encounters ask whether this universal royalty has left its beneficiaries capable of thought, refusal, or spiritual life.

Huey P. Long, Every Man a King (1933) and the Share Our Wealth slogan.

2. A catalogue of paradises

More praises Astrobe through a mixture of Gospel language, classical myth, and Irish otherworld geography. The pearl of great price stands beside Iris, Great Brasil, and the Hesperides. This abundance of names reveals how much hope he brings to what he is seeing.

Matthew 13:45–46; the myths of Iris and the Hesperides; the Irish Hy-Brasil tradition.

3. The whited sepulcher

Evita’s answer comes from Christ’s denunciation of tombs beautiful outside and full of death within. She supplies the diagnosis while More is still admiring the surface. The contrast governs both this chapter and the later discovery of Astrobe’s deformed reverse.

Matthew 23:27.

4. Fawney men and false gold

A fawney man practices a ring swindle, passing a worthless ring off as valuable. More’s compliment to Rimrock therefore associates enchantment with deceptive gold. It belongs beside the repeated question of what Golden Astrobe’s apparent wealth is worth.

The thieves’ cant terms fawney and fawney rig.

5. The Greek and Jewish mechanical man

More explicitly recalls older dreams of artificial servants. Greek examples include Hephaestus’s golden attendants and the bronze Talos; the Jewish tradition supplies the golem. Pottscamp’s dream of the toy that consumes its maker gives that admiration a frightening sequel.

Homer, Iliad 18.417–20; Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 4; the golem tradition.

6. The president as a masked performer

The former presidents’ extravagant names sound to More like gladiators or American wrestlers. His sponsors likewise plan to present a recognizable persona to the public. The joke makes political office resemble a staged performance whose billing matters more than its holder’s freedom to act.

The novel’s explicit comparison with gladiators and masked professional wrestlers.

7. Washing one’s hands

Proctor’s description of Kingmaker and Foreman’s refusal to wash his hands recall Pilate. The gesture concerns responsibility for a death already being planned. Foreman’s willingness to own his part does not remove the moral question of what he is doing to his friend.

Matthew 27:24.

8. Termination and the satisfied guest

Proctor compares the man ready to die with a guest who has eaten enough. Lucretius and Horace use the satisfied guest as an image of leaving life without complaint. Astrobe turns that consolation into an argument for readily available termination.

Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 3.938; Horace, Satires 1.1.117–19.

9. Termination and More’s own book

Utopia allows priests and magistrates to urge a voluntary death upon someone suffering from incurable, painful illness. Astrobe makes termination a common response to weariness. The altered conditions are essential to the comparison: Lafferty’s institution is much broader than the practice described by More.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Slaves, and of Their Marriages.”

10. False dawn

Foreman spoils the consoling proverb about darkness before dawn by inserting a false dawn. He later claims responsibility for making a particular sun rise, borrowing language ordinarily applied to God. His confidence invites scrutiny as the cost of his promised renewal becomes clear.

Matthew 5:45; the proverb about darkness before dawn.

11. The thirty shells

Foreman’s counting and weeping make the shells a strong counterpart to Judas’s thirty pieces of silver. The scene anticipates the betrayal named openly in Chapter 13. The warning about Mother Carey’s chicken adds the storm petrel’s maritime associations to the threatened victim.

Matthew 26:15; 27:3–5; the sailors’ name Mother Carey’s chicken.

12. Camiroi and Puca

The school assignments in Pottscamp’s dream contain names from Lafferty’s other fiction. Treating those peoples and languages as ordinary school subjects gives the invented worlds a shared background while the toy’s effortless learning exposes the child’s dependence on it.

Lafferty, “Primary Education of the Camiroi” (1966), “Polity and Custom of the Camiroi” (1967), and The Reefs of Earth (1968).

5.

THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO COME

Cosmopolis → the edge of the Feral Lands
+

A precis machine explains the Astrobe Dream: individual people must merge into one city and finally into Holy Nothingness. Thomas recognizes his own satire in this program, yet increasingly admires Astrobe. He and Paul watch a grotesque mechanical replica of the Mass. The chapter then introduces the conflicting views of Thomas's companions and Rimrock's account of the ansels’ ascent from the ocean. Though he has become an advocate of Golden Astrobe, Thomas feels drawn to the mountains and decides to walk through the Feral Lands.

“Well, I have sampled Golden Astrobe and it is wonderful. But I am still hungry.”

Characters
Thomas MorePaulEvitaRimrockWalter CopperheadScrivenerSliderMaxwell
Themes
The Astrobe DreamThe Replica MassThe AnselsThe Mountain
Outline
I. The precis machine +
  • The machine makes the city superior to its individual inhabitants.
  • It describes perfection as the loss of private identity and consciousness.
  • Thomas recognizes the program as his own bitter joke in Utopia.
II. The replica Mass +
  • Paul takes Thomas to a preserved church in Cosmopolis.
  • A coin starts a mechanical religious performance.
  • Paul distinguishes this burlesque from living worship in Cathead and the Feral Lands.
  • Thomas dismisses the Church; Paul defends the faith he found in Cathead.
III. The companions +
  • Rimrock describes his people's ascent through the ocean's surface, their sky.
  • Evita chooses to accompany Thomas and proposes seducing a saint.
  • Slider doubts whether the Christian promise extends to Astrobe; Scrivener endorses the Astrobe Dream.
  • Maxwell describes his loose attachment to bodies; Copperhead predicts that Thomas will save the world but not himself.
IV. Towards the mountain +
  • Thomas's fascination with the mountain disturbs the group.
  • The Feral Lands have no transportation booths.
  • Copperhead estimates seven or nine days for the circuit to Cathead.
  • Thomas insists on going despite the threat of the Killers.
› Notes and sources (14)
1. The Shape of Things to Come

The title names Wells’s future history, in which a world administration reorganizes civilization and suppresses religion. Astrobe’s managed happiness and its treatment of worship as an antiquity give the allusion particular force. Chapter 10 answers this title with The Deformity of Things to Come.

H. G. Wells, The Shape of Things to Come (1933), especially book 4.

2. The same everywhere

Kingmaker’s praise of Astrobe’s uniformity recalls Utopia’s closely similar towns. More’s wish to travel puts the author in opposition to the commonwealth associated with his name. He insists on seeing what an account of the whole planet leaves out.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Towns, Particularly of Amaurot.”

3. The Dream as a version of Utopia

The precis machine describes common access to goods, freedom from poverty, and a simplified legal order. These recall institutions in Utopia, although the golden world gives them a different purpose. More’s recognition is also a crisis of authorship: his joke has become a place people must inhabit.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2.

4. The Big O and the Omega Point

Astrobe’s account of humanity converging into a single organism invites comparison with Teilhard de Chardin’s Omega Point. The novel’s Omega becomes Ouden and the Big O, a destination described as nothingness. This is a satirical resemblance; Teilhard’s own account gives convergence a transcendent and Christian end.

Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, The Phenomenon of Man (1955; English translation, 1959).

5. Holy Nothingness

The Dream’s religious vocabulary makes the abolition of transcendence sound like an act of worship. It can be read against the death-of-God debates contemporary with the novel. The phrase also occurs in Richard Rubenstein’s theology, but the shared wording alone does not establish a direct source.

Richard L. Rubenstein, After Auschwitz (1966); Thomas J. J. Altizer, The Gospel of Christian Atheism (1966).

6. Travel beyond the booths

Utopia regulates travel with official permission; Astrobe’s instantaneous transport serves the civilized regions. The comparison helps explain why a walk matters here. Leaving the convenient network lets More encounter places and people that the official description does not adequately explain.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of the Travelling of the Utopians.”

7. Hunting and the author of Utopia

More’s delight in either end of a hunt contrasts with the Utopians’ contempt for hunting. The contrast separates the character’s appetites from the rules of the society in his book. His attraction to the wild draws him further from Astrobe’s claim that civilized life is complete.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, discussion of pleasure and hunting.

8. The tree and its fruit

More imagines his joke as a tree unexpectedly bearing fruit, then judges a failing religious institution by the image of a barren tree. The Gospel language makes him apply to the Church a test that also bears on his own political invention.

Matthew 7:17–20; Luke 13:6–9.

9. The replica Mass

The museum rite combines guitar, drugs, theatrical dress, and commercial sponsorship. Its details turn a religious service into a degraded exhibit. The scene can be read in relation to the liturgical and popular culture of the 1960s, but its grotesque composite is Lafferty’s fictional projection.

The novel’s account of the museumized Mass; mid-twentieth-century liturgical and popular culture.

10. Dante’s infernal instruments

More himself invokes Dante when he hears the instruments. Relevant passages include Barbariccia’s obscene trumpet, Master Adam’s lute-shaped body and drum-like belly, and Nimrod’s horn. The reference is comic and composite: Dante does not describe an orchestra of guitars in the lowest circle.

Dante, Inferno 21.139; 30.49–54, 103; 31.12–18.

11. What he will be given to see

Pottscamp’s assurance about what will be given in the hour recalls Christ’s promise of words to disciples brought before hostile authorities. The change from speaking to seeing suits More’s journey. The question is whether he can recognize what the encounters disclose.

Matthew 10:19–20.

12. Rimrock’s sky

The ansels’ ancestors climbed through what they had taken for the sky and found land above the sea. Plato imagines a sea-dweller making a similar discovery in the Phaedo. The parallel makes Rimrock’s account a challenge to the belief that one’s familiar world exhausts reality.

Plato, Phaedo 109c–110a.

13. Evita, Eve, and Lilith

More calls Evita Lilith rather than Eve; she claims both names. The exchange brings the first mother and the rebellious first wife of later Jewish legend into the same woman. It continues the composite female figure of More’s passage dream.

Genesis 2–3; Alphabet of Ben Sira, the Lilith story.

14. All nations and the end of the world

Slider questions whether Christ’s commission and promise apply beyond Earth. His argument depends on taking nations and world in a narrowly terrestrial sense. Chapter 8 gives the Metropolitan’s direct answer, making this a dispute within the novel rather than an established limit on the Promise.

Matthew 28:19–20; Past Master, chap. 8.

6.

STING IN THE TAIL

Feral Lands → Goslar, City of the Salic Emperors
+

Thomas's party enters a wilderness of interwoven vegetation, water, and formidable animals. Father Oddopter joins them. He, Paul, and Evita kill a hydra that he identifies as the Devil; Thomas eats its cooked brains while disputing the meaning of the hunt. At Goslar, Charles the Six Hundred and Twelfth receives the travelers but lodges Scrivener in the machinery shed. Evita recounts her longevity and her search for Hell. Father Oddopter describes spirits and bodies produced through imagination. Drinking, stories, and the joke of Goslar's occupied privy loosen Thomas's attachment to perfection.

“The Devil has his several forms, but we must kill him every day to limn his limits.”

Characters
Thomas MorePaulEvitaFather OddopterRimrockWalter CopperheadMaxwellScrivenerSliderEmperor Charles the 612th
Themes
The Feral LandsThe Devil-killThe Salic EmperorsEmbodied Belief
Outline
I. The Feral Lands +
  • Rimrock and Copperhead take separate routes and protect the travelers.
  • Paul describes the food animals and the predators that feed on them.
  • Thomas thinks wild life could supply what civilized Astrobe lacks.
II. Killing the hydra +
  • Father Oddopter catches a large fish to use as bait.
  • The monk, Paul, and Evita attack the hydra's eye and brain.
  • Oddopter identifies the hunt as the daily killing of the Devil; Thomas calls it sport and illusion.
  • The brains are roasted in a mud casing. Copperhead later examines the entrails.
III. Natural and transformed ansels +
  • The travelers meet hunters killing natural ansels.
  • Thomas distinguishes these animals from the intelligent Rimrock.
  • Oddopter admits that the apparent acquisition of soul and intellect poses a theological problem.
IV. The Salic court +
  • Goslar grew from a fraternity at the university in Wu Town.
  • The Killers murder successive emperors; the fraternity immediately chooses replacements.
  • Charles excludes Scrivener from the common room as a machine.
  • The skulls of former emperors preserve the dynasty's oral history.
V. Evita and the evening's tales +
  • Evita recognizes emperors to whom she was consort and describes an experiment that prolonged her life.
  • She identifies Golden Astrobe as the Hell she sought.
  • Oddopter describes wandering spirits, contingent bodies, and the Feral Lands’ psychic powers.
  • Thomas pays to use the public privy, drinks green lightning, and joins the storytelling.
› Notes and sources (17)
1. The sting in the tail

The closing image of a fair face and a dangerous tail recalls Dante’s Geryon, the embodiment of fraud. It also belongs to the proverbial poison reserved for the tail or end. Astrobe’s pleasing appearance has concealed what More discovers behind it.

Dante, Inferno 17.1–27; the proverb in cauda venenum.

2. Old animal names on a new planet

Kastroides recalls the extinct giant beaver Castoroides, and the direwolves likewise borrow a prehistoric name. Paul warns that the resemblance lies in the names. The earthly vocabulary helps the travelers begin to describe creatures whose behavior and proportions remain unfamiliar.

The names Castoroides and dire wolf; the novel’s explanation of borrowed animal names.

3. Rouks and the roc

The enormous predatory bird recalls the roc of travel legend. Its habit of displaying human bodies on thorns also resembles a shrike’s impaled prey, enlarged to a human scale. More’s comparison with men hanging dead wolves reverses the ordinary relation between hunter and hunted.

The roc in the Sindbad voyages and Marco Polo; the natural history of shrikes.

4. Sextus and the sprite

More names Sextus Empiricus in support of a being suited to every environment. Father Oddopter then appears as an answer to the speculation. Sextus reports arguments about living beings in different cosmic regions; the scene turns that philosophical material into a joke about the observers themselves.

Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists, book 1; compare Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.42.

5. Babes in the woods

Oddopter’s grand title for a familiar story mocks the travelers’ innocence. Like the abandoned children of the ballad, they do not fully understand the danger surrounding them. His greeting is protective advice delivered as teasing.

The ballad “The Babes in the Wood” and its later theatrical versions.

6. Doubting Thomas

The apostle asks for evidence before believing; More sees the Devil-kill and then tries to exclude what he has seen from his account of reality. Oddopter challenges the rule by which More has decided in advance that only one order of things can exist.

John 20:24–29.

7. Fishing for the Devil

The bait and hook invite comparison with the Christian interpretation of Leviathan: the Devil takes what he desires and is caught through it. Gregory the Great reads the hook as Christ’s humanity concealing divinity. Evita’s bait and Oddopter’s fishing give that theological image a violent comic form.

Job 41:1, or 40:20 in the Douay-Rheims numbering; Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job, book 33.

8. The hydra and the daily killing

The name recalls the monster whose severed heads grow again in Heracles’ labor. Oddopter makes the repeated killing a daily necessity. He also says the Devil can take other forms, so the significance belongs to this encounter and its recurrence, rather than to every animal called a hydra.

The Lernaean Hydra; Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2.

9. Copperhead’s divination

Reading entrails belongs to the ancient haruspex; interpreting birds belongs to the augur. Copperhead draws on this vocabulary and practice here and on the mountain. More’s uneasiness recalls the biblical prohibition on divination and consultation with the dead.

Deuteronomy 18:10–11; the Roman traditions of haruspicy and augury.

10. A wandering monk

Oddopter vows never to sleep twice in the same place. This can be set beside both Christ’s homelessness and Benedict’s criticism of wandering monks. Lafferty gives a positive discipline to a form of life that monastic rules often treated with suspicion.

Luke 9:58; Rule of St. Benedict, chap. 1.

11. Goslar and the Salic Emperors

The name recalls the German imperial city associated with the Salian dynasty. Lafferty transfers imperial ceremony to a precarious settlement with an oral history preserved through the skulls of its rulers. More treats its authority seriously even when the surrounding circumstances are comic.

The imperial palace and Salian history of Goslar.

12. The emperor’s journey

The newly chosen ruler travels without provisions, money, or spare clothing. The instructions echo the sending of the apostles. That vulnerable arrival also makes the emperor’s office a small-scale counterpart to More’s dangerous appointment.

Luke 9:3; Matthew 10:9–10.

13. The privy and royal names

More’s henry and proposed charles treat the familiar john as though a privy ought to bear the reigning monarch’s name. The joke brings Henry VIII into the petty frustrations of the visit. More’s caution about crossing royalty recalls how much a confrontation with a king can cost.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Norfolk’s warning about striving with princes and More’s advice to Cromwell.

14. Evita’s bargain

Evita calls herself Faustina when she describes the longevity experiment as a bargain with the Devil. The Evil Scientist gives the Faust story a laboratory setting. Her return home after seeking Hell makes the discovery of Golden Astrobe’s nature the bitter result of the bargain.

The Faust tradition, especially the rejuvenation in Goethe’s Faust, part 1.

15. Coming home and recognizing it

Evita’s journey around the world to recognize her own home can be compared with Chesterton’s returning yachtsman and Eliot’s end of exploration. Her discovery reverses their welcome: the home she finally recognizes is Hell.

G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy, chap. 1; T. S. Eliot, “Little Gidding,” section 5.

16. Superstition and over-belief

Oddopter’s over-belief has bodily consequences: it leaves marks and makes the feral regions powerful. William James’s term offers a useful comparison for belief that reaches beyond what evidence establishes. Lafferty gives that surplus of belief a creaturely presence.

William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), concluding discussion of over-beliefs.

17. Green lightning and the electrode

Slider proposes electrically produced pleasure as a superior alternative to drinking. The contrast sets the ease of a manufactured sensation beside a physical, communal activity he cannot manage. It belongs to the novel’s larger dispute over whether discomfort can be removed without losing forms of life.

The chapter’s comparison of green lightning with electrical stimulation.

7.

ON THUNDER MOUNTAIN

Goslar → Electric Mountain → Cathead
+

Father Oddopter celebrates Mass at Goslar. Thomas then defends the Astrobe Dream so fiercely that Charles expels him, though his companions continue with him. During the climb of Electric Mountain, Scrivener recounts the sleeping kings and declares his rejection of Ouden. Copperhead has already examined a rouk's entrails at the summit and left. A lightning storm accompanies the Killers’ assault. Scrivener, Adam, Oddopter, and Maxwell's current body are killed. Slider is disregarded as no threat. Evita leads Thomas and Paul down the mountain; the three reach Cathead profoundly changed.

“They had been transfigured on the mountain.”

Characters
Thomas MorePaulEvitaFather OddopterRimrockWalter CopperheadAdamScrivenerSliderMaxwellEmperor Charles the 612th
Themes
Scrivener’s ChoiceThe Sleeping KingsDeath on the MountainTransfiguration
Outline
I. Mass and expulsion +
  • The consecration briefly revives Thomas's faith.
  • Charles warns that Scrivener's sender enables the Killers to track the party.
  • Thomas refuses to sacrifice Scrivener, but then accepts the killing of companions who oppose the Dream.
  • Charles expels Thomas; Paul, Evita, and Oddopter stay with him.
II. Scrivener's change +
  • Scrivener criticizes Thomas for valuing machinery above humanity.
  • He recounts human legends of sleeping kings and the machines’ attempt to adopt an ancient gear train.
  • Ouden displaced that mechanical king.
  • Scrivener declares that he has rejected Ouden.
III. The summit +
  • Adam joins the climbers.
  • Oddopter describes apparitions shaped by electricity and the observer's mind.
  • The summit holds the entrails of a rouk examined by Copperhead, who has departed.
  • The view reveals the cities, wilderness, and other Thunder Mountains.
IV. The assault and escape +
  • The Killers attack during the lightning storm.
  • Scrivener fights and dies; Slider is ignored.
  • Adam and Oddopter die; Maxwell loses his present body.
  • Evita times a descent to the lightning. She, Thomas, and Paul escape to Cathead.
› Notes and sources (11)
1. Sinai and the Transfiguration

Trumpets, cloud, thunder, and lightning recall Sinai. The changed, shining survivors also invite the Gospel comparison that the narrator names as transfiguration. What they encounter includes the faces of Ouden, so the resemblance does not make their vision a simple repetition of a biblical revelation.

Exodus 19:16–19; 34:29–30; Matthew 17:1–9.

2. Lifting the eyes to the mountains

More’s criticism of the golden inhabitants borrows the upward movement of the psalm. He immediately imagines abandoning such impulses once he governs. His own attraction to the mountain is therefore already in conflict with the settled life he wants to administer.

Psalm 121:1, numbered 120:1 in the Douay-Rheims and Vulgate.

3. The sleeping kings

Scrivener gathers rulers expected to return when their people need them. The recurring legend gives More’s recruitment a wider pattern. Historical deaths, folk traditions, and invented futures mingle in the list; the list should not be treated as a set of accurate biographies.

The return-of-the-king traditions of Arthur and Frederick Barbarossa.

4. Alaric under the river

The diverted river and secret burial come from the account of Alaric’s death in Jordanes. The promise that he will rise and lead again belongs to the sleeping-king pattern added here. The distinction shows how historical material becomes a usable legend.

Jordanes, Getica 30.158.

5. Kennedy and Roadstorm

Kennedy’s open automobile enters the same company as ancient and medieval kings. Roadstorm extends the catalogue into Lafferty’s own fiction and recalls Roadstrum of Space Chantey. The sequence treats very recent history and invented history as material from which legends of return are made.

John F. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963; Lafferty, Space Chantey (1968).

6. The ram with the double sign

Oddopter says the marked ram belongs to Scripture. Abraham’s substitute sacrifice and Daniel’s two-horned ram are possible points of comparison. The scene does not choose between them or explain the double sign completely; More’s repeated appointment to death gives the image its immediate force.

Genesis 22:13; Daniel 8:3.

7. A priest forever

Paul’s words over Oddopter identify the dead man with the priesthood of Melchisedech. The verse belongs to the biblical and liturgical language of enduring priesthood. It follows a morning Mass offered for members of the party who would die that day.

Psalm 110:4, numbered 109:4 in the Douay-Rheims and Vulgate; Hebrews 5:6; 7:17.

8. The lightning and the paradox of motion

The single point of light seems to occupy several places at once. Zeno’s arrow offers a plausible comparison for the old paradox named in the passage. Lafferty makes the apparent solution an overwhelming event through which the travelers must find a still narrower instant of escape.

Aristotle, Physics 6.9, 239b, on Zeno’s arrow.

9. Literally astonished

The narrator explicitly connects astonishment with being thunderstruck. The event revives the history inside the word. The same habit of making a familiar phrase happen bodily governs many of the novel’s jokes and horrors.

The history of astonish through Old French estoner and the Latin vocabulary of thunder and stupefaction.

10. The false sky and the empyrean

The possibility of light outside a false sky recalls the empyrean of medieval cosmology and Dante. The narrator poses it as a question. The view into a pit then makes the distinction between apparent height and genuine transcendence more difficult.

Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 66, a. 3; Dante, Paradiso 30.

11. Scrivener, Slider, and humanity

Scrivener’s choice and Slider’s reversal make personhood a matter of allegiance and action as well as origin. Scrivener dies resisting the Killers. The scene prepares the question, asked later by the Programmed Persons themselves, of whether creatures made from other materials can receive spiritual life.

Past Master, chaps. 7, 10, and 13.

8.

BLACK CATHEAD

Cathead, Astrobe
+

Thomas studies Cathead's deadly industries, rat-infested buildings, plague, and widespread mental illness. Copperhead, Battersea, Shanty, and Rimrock explain why people refuse the Golden Life, but he still proposes destroying the city. A woman predicts his nine-day reign. He visits the dying Metropolitan, who recognizes him, recites the collect for John Fisher and Thomas More, and says that Christ has renewed the promise to the Church on Astrobe. Thomas leaves unconvinced. The final scene shows dead sea-gleaners being sold with fish for grinding into meal.

“We have the promise. We last till the end of the world.”

Characters
Thomas MorePaulEvitaThe MetropolitanRimrockWalter CopperheadBatterseaShanty
Themes
The Horrors of CatheadThe Remnant ChurchThe PromiseChrist on Astrobe
Outline
I. The industries and the rats +
  • Cathead's processes kill workers while duplicating products cheaply available elsewhere.
  • Oxypyrites extraction has neither market nor pay.
  • The Rat Castle houses a billion rats; the district's rats kill thousands daily.
  • Plague and the immense Bethelem district deepen the account of suffering.
II. The refusal of comfort +
  • Copperhead calls misery preferable to having no life.
  • Battersea and Shanty call Thomas blind and foolish.
  • Rimrock says he too gave up a comfortable life that submerged his identity.
  • Thomas still thinks Cathead must be destroyed.
III. The Metropolitan +
  • A woman predicts that Thomas will be king for nine days.
  • The Metropolitan recognizes Thomas through the collect of his feast with John Fisher.
  • He predicts his own death thirty hours before Thomas's.
  • He says Christ walked on Astrobe with Saint Klingensmith and renewed the Promise.
IV. The sea-gleaners +
  • Three workers have died on plague day.
  • The scow-master removes their boots and rolls their bodies into the fish.
  • The buyer accepts the bodies but deducts a coin for each because they are inferior material for the grinders.
› Notes and sources (13)
1. Twenty hours of work

Utopia limits the working day to six hours. Cathead’s twenty-hour labor makes the comparison brutal, especially because efficient machines already exist elsewhere. More must confront people who prefer this destructive work to the comfortable life offered by the golden cities.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Trades, and Manner of Life.”

2. Choosing servitude

Utopia includes outsiders who voluntarily enter service because its conditions are better than those at home. Cathead reverses the movement: people choose bondage and deprivation to escape the perfected society. The parallel places freedom of choice inside conditions that More finds intolerable.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Slaves, and of Their Marriages.”

3. Dostoevsky and chosen unhappiness

The Underground Man challenges a rationally perfected society by defending the capacity to choose what is painful or disadvantageous. Cathead raises a related question: whether suffering can become proof that one is alive and capable of refusal. The comparison explains the argument without making Cathead’s misery desirable in itself.

Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground, part 1, sections 7–9.

4. Escape from the golden cities

Barricades and gunfire give the migration a recognizable modern political setting. The Berlin Wall offers a historical comparison, but Lafferty reverses the expected economic destination: these refugees run from abundance into poverty. Their behavior exposes something that Astrobe’s measures of well-being cannot register.

The border barriers and shootings of the Cold War; the novel’s account of the exodus into Cathead.

5. The yellow flag and the lungers

The flag uses the traditional maritime signal of contagion. Lunger is an older American word for a consumptive. Both terms make bodily disease a constant feature of the city’s life; the weekly plague and lethal work are concrete conditions, not merely symbols of spiritual suffering.

The quarantine flag tradition; the American slang term lunger.

6. Bethlehem and Bedlam

The district’s name recalls the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem, whose name became Bedlam. Lafferty enlarges a madhouse into a large part of a city. The movement from institution to district makes the question of madness political as well as medical.

Bethlem Hospital, London; the development of the word bedlam.

7. Holbein’s skeletons

More’s Dutchman is most naturally read as Holbein, his portraitist and the designer of the Dance of Death woodcuts. Older English could use Dutch broadly for German. The remark places the skeletal Metropolitan among images in which death confronts people of every social rank.

Hans Holbein the Younger, Dance of Death, published 1538; Sir Thomas More, 1527.

8. The fisherman’s ring

The ring associates the Metropolitan with Saint Peter and papal office. The novel also calls him the Pope of Astrobe. These signs give the nearly abandoned church an authority that its physical poverty and small congregation do not measure.

The papal Ring of the Fisherman; the chapter’s description of the Metropolitan.

9. More hears his own collect

The Metropolitan recites the prayer honoring John Fisher and Thomas More as martyrs. More recognizes Fisher and hears himself placed within a liturgical commemoration that followed his earthly life. The prayer confronts his uncertainty with the Church’s judgment about the man he became.

The collect for Saints John Fisher and Thomas More in the English proper of the Roman Missal after their canonization in 1935.

10. The Promise on Astrobe

The Metropolitan applies Christ’s promise to this world and answers Slider’s attempt to exclude it. His account of Christ walking on Astrobe gives the answer a local history. The scene asks whether a new planet can be outside the reach of an apparently earthly promise.

Matthew 16:18; 28:20; Past Master, chap. 5.

11. The blind man who sees

The physically blind Metropolitan calls More blind because he fails to recognize what is before him. John’s account of the man born blind supplies the comparison: sight and spiritual understanding can move in opposite directions. More’s confidence in his diagnosis of Cathead is the object of the rebuke.

John 9:39–41.

12. The response More remembers

The blessing and More’s answering line come from the psalm used in the prayers at the foot of the altar. His ready response shows religious memory operating beneath his professed uncertainty. The words ask for renewed life at the very moment he is confronting a church thought to be dying.

Psalm 85, numbered 84 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims; the Roman Mass, Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos.

13. Stones, clods, and the woman’s touch

The promise that the planet itself will testify recalls the stones that cry out in Luke. The woman who touches More likewise recalls a Gospel encounter, although here she gives him a prophecy rather than receives a cure. Both episodes place knowledge outside the institutions and explanations he trusts.

Luke 19:40; Mark 5:25–34.

9.

KING-MAKER

Cosmopolis, Astrobe
+

Kingmaker discovers that Thomas's voice transmits on Replica while his image does not. The chapter explains Astrobe's successive voting systems and its many parties. The Crank defends personal freedom, but Thomas rejects him and has him expelled. Thomas campaigns for the Astrobe Dream and threatens Cathead. He notices that someone else is thinking and speaking through him, yet accepts those imposed ideas. The Pandomation and Open Mind Act abolish privacy. By the chapter's end the Killers still watch him, but no longer threaten him.

“Somebody else spoke some of those words out of my mouth.”

Characters
Thomas MoreCosmos KingmakerPaulEvitaRimrockThe Crank
Themes
Invisible to ReplicaWeighted VotePolitical MachineryPublic Appeal
Outline
I. The public image +
  • Thomas is visually absent from Replica but remains audible.
  • Kingmaker says about one person in a hundred has this peculiarity.
  • Rimrock and Evita have already won broad audiences for Thomas.
II. Voting and parties +
  • One person, one vote gave way to weighted voting.
  • Sensing machines now assess opinion directly.
  • The unexpected strength of Cathead and the Barrio prompts plans to exclude dissenting judgments.
  • Those modifications will not be ready for this election.
III. The Crank +
  • The sole member of a certified party receives his legally required hearing.
  • He attacks coercion in education, marriage, reproduction, work, and mental life.
  • Thomas rejects every point and orders machines to remove him.
IV. The campaign and the invaded mind +
  • Thomas preaches merger between humans and the Programmed.
  • Paul urges him to expel the intruders from his mind.
  • Pandomation exposes private activities; the Open Mind Act authorizes mental intrusion.
  • Thomas threatens Cathead, promises the Merging Singularity, and ceases to appear dangerous to the Killers.
› Notes and sources (11)
1. King-making

The title recalls the historical Kingmaker, Warwick, and brings the name Cosmos Kingmaker into the account of how a ruler is manufactured. Acclamation, publicity, party arrangements, and effective phrasing do the work once associated with a vote. The final ease of the process is part of its menace.

Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick; Shakespeare, 3 Henry VI, 3.3.

2. Cecily and the adopted daughter

More compares Evita with his youngest daughter. Historically that daughter was Cecily, educated with her sisters in More’s household. His paternal comparison sits uneasily with Evita’s age, experience, and refusal to be treated as a child.

More’s family: Cecily More Heron; Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More.

3. The wrong apostle

The Crank combines doubting Thomas with Judas. More corrects him, but the confusion reveals what Astrobe admires: it has turned the supposed betrayer of Christ into a hero. The error belongs to the characters’ damaged religious memory and should not be repeated as a description of either apostle.

John 20:24–29; the Gospel accounts of Judas’s betrayal.

4. From one person, one vote to no vote

The account starts with an egalitarian formula, passes through unequal voting weights, and ends by abolishing voting. Mill’s plural voting and Shute’s fictional multiple-vote scheme offer comparisons for the middle stage. The succession makes the removal of political choice appear to be one more modernization.

John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government, chap. 8; Nevil Shute, In the Wet (1953).

5. Demos, Ochlos, and the anesthetics

Demos names the people as a political body; ochlos names a crowd or mob. The Esthetics, Anesthetics, and Local Anesthetics turn disputes about taste and sensation into party labels. The catalogue mixes learned political names with jokes about feeling and its suppression.

Greek demos, people; ochlos, crowd; aisthesis, perception or sensation.

6. The Crank and the right to unhappiness

The Crank’s defense of choosing one’s occupation and unhappiness recalls John the Savage’s demand in Brave New World. More answers from the side of the administered society. The encounter therefore exposes the distance between the candidate’s public confidence and the liberty a dissenter wants.

Aldous Huxley, Brave New World, chap. 17.

7. Moving mountains

More turns the Gospel image of mountain-moving faith into a political joke. The promise to move the world ahead follows his own unsettling mountain experience. Biblical words now help him sell the program whose deeper claims he has begun to forget.

Matthew 17:20; 1 Corinthians 13:2.

8. Green pastures

The speech approaches the language of Psalm 23 and then corrects itself into a more acceptable statement of progress. The interrupted phrase briefly introduces rest under a shepherd into a speech about collective advancement. It also raises the question of who is supplying More’s words.

Psalm 23:2, numbered 22:2 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims.

9. All things to all men

More’s happy new phrase belongs to Saint Paul. In its biblical setting it concerns winning others for the gospel; in the campaign it promises universal political appeal. The narrator’s doubt about who speaks through More turns the apparent improvisation into evidence of manipulation.

1 Corinthians 9:22.

10. The total good

The speech replaces a good calculated for many persons with the good of a merged singularity. Bentham’s familiar formula supplies the point of departure. The crucial change is the disappearance of distinct persons from the account of what their common good should be.

Jeremy Bentham, A Fragment on Government (1776), preface; the utilitarian formula of the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

11. Pandomation and the Open Mind Act

Rooms exposed to spectators invite comparison with the glass houses of We and the telescreens of Nineteen Eighty-Four. Astrobe also extends access into thought. The Open Mind Act’s subtitle turns an expression of tolerance into a claim to enter another person’s mind.

Yevgeny Zamyatin, We (1924); George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).

10.

THE DEFORMITY OF THINGS TO COME

A settlement between Cathead and Wu Town
+

Thomas begins to resist the thoughts imposed on him. The Killers pursue him through a settlement between Cathead and Wu Town, and he is drawn into a room with nine Programmed Persons. Their three groups identify themselves as Jackals, Dogs, and Wolves. Pottscamp describes their manufacture, demonic occupants, and extensions in Thomas's mind. They intend to extinguish humanity, themselves, and ultimately all existence. Thomas finally understands Cathead's refusal of the Dream. The Nine suppress his memory of the meeting. Outside, Northprophet and Pottscamp ask what they must do to be saved; Thomas dismisses them as mocking him.

“The Vision is the Golden Premise of Nothing Beyond; and the Conclusion is Holy Ouden, Nothing Here Either, Nothing Ever.”

Characters
Thomas MorePottscampNorthprophetBoggleSkybolSwampersKnobnosterBeebonnetHolygeeGandy
Themes
The Nine DevilsPhilosophy of AnnihilationProgrammed PersonsBeing vs. Nothingness
Outline
I. The trap +
  • Thomas recognizes the thoughts in his head as intrusions.
  • The Killers turn dangerous as he resists.
  • He enters a door in a blind alley and finds the Nine in darkness.
  • He takes the seat reserved for Ouden.
II. The three groups +
  • Boggle, Skybol, and Swampers: Jackals, specializing in retrogression.
  • Northprophet, Knobnoster, and Beebonnet: Dogs, specializing in rechabitism.
  • Pottscamp, Holygee, and Gandy: Wolves, specializing in extrapolation.
  • Each has an extension in Thomas's brain.
III. Their account of themselves +
  • Pottscamp says ancient devils inhabit the manufactured bodies.
  • He describes the use of twelve criminals as material for the first devices.
  • The Nine deny consciousness and purpose and plan total extinction.
  • Thomas learns that Proctor is Programmed and that Foreman still resists them.
IV. Resistance and forgetting +
  • Thomas recognizes why Cathead refuses the surrogate life.
  • Swampers and Gandy raise the possibility of the Spirit or God's hand reaching mechanical beings.
  • The Nine suppress Thomas's memory through retrogression.
  • Northprophet and Pottscamp then ask to be saved, a plea Thomas cannot take seriously.
› Notes and sources (13)
1. The deformation of Wells’s future

The title answers Chapter 5 and Wells’s The Shape of Things to Come. More now sees the claim to perfected humanity from its reverse side. The Programmed Persons explain what their completion of human history would remove.

H. G. Wells, The Shape of Things to Come (1933); Past Master, chap. 5.

2. The door in the wall

The door appears where there should be none and leaves no opening afterward. Wells’s disappearing door offers a close comparison, particularly under this chapter title. Lafferty changes the destination from an alluring garden to the Nine’s room of coercion and disclosure.

H. G. Wells, “The Door in the Wall” (1906).

3. Below the salt

More invokes the seating order of a great household when he takes Ouden’s reserved place. His refusal of a lower seat becomes a refusal to acknowledge Nothing as his superior. A social expression gives his resistance a physical and ceremonial form.

The traditional distinction between seating above and below the salt.

4. The reverse of the tapestry

The Nine present themselves as mankind seen from behind. Cervantes compares translation with the reverse of a tapestry, where the figures remain visible through knots and threads. The analogy helps describe a recognizable human pattern made rough or deformed, while the Nine insist that their reverse is the true side.

Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, part 2, chap. 62.

5. Rechabitism

The Rechabites in Jeremiah obey an ancestral command to abstain from wine and settled possessions. Northprophet names rechabitism as his trio’s specialty without defining the process. In this conversation its association with abstinence can be set beside the Programmed Persons’ desire to eliminate their appetite for life.

Jeremiah 35.

6. Houses swept and garnished

Pottscamp explicitly describes the bodies as houses entered by devils. His language comes from Christ’s account of an expelled spirit returning to an empty, ordered house with worse companions. The account distinguishes the constructed bodies from the beings that occupy them.

Matthew 12:43–45; Luke 11:24–26.

7. The machine that succeeds mankind

Butler’s evolving machines and Čapek’s artificial workers provide earlier versions of humanity being superseded by its creations. Lafferty joins that prospect to the language of possession. The question therefore concerns both the material construction of the Programmed Persons and what has come to live in them.

Samuel Butler, Erewhon, “The Book of the Machines”; Karel Čapek, R.U.R. (1920).

8. Opening the box

The warning about taking the lid off a box invites the comparison with Pandora. Jack-in-the-box language makes the released powers sound like unruly toys. The image grows until the box is Astrobe itself, and the dispute turns to whether hope has survived inside it.

Hesiod, Works and Days 90–105; the later Pandora’s-box tradition.

9. Hell and nonbeing

More’s preference for existence even in Hell can be compared with Milton’s Satan, while his preference for the lunger’s life over kingship recalls Achilles in the underworld. The differences matter: More is resisting annihilation, and his chosen comparison is the life of an actual suffering person.

Milton, Paradise Lost 1.263; Homer, Odyssey 11.489–91.

10. Water, clay, and artificial bodies

Swampers asks whether the spirit that came to water and clay could come to the materials of a Programmed Person. Genesis supplies the language of creation and animated earth. The question leaves open a possibility that the Nine’s general account of themselves tries to close.

Genesis 1:2; 2:7.

11. What must we do to be saved?

Northprophet and Pottscamp echo the jailer’s question to Paul and Silas. More dismisses their appeal as mockery. Pottscamp’s later penitence makes it difficult to assume that this moment has only one tone or purpose.

Acts 16:30; Past Master, chap. 13.

12. The second death

Revelation uses the phrase for the final condition of the condemned. More also faces the literal prospect of being beheaded twice. The overlap places his personal ordeal inside the novel’s larger questions about resurrection, extinction, and the death of a world.

Revelation 20:6, 14; 21:8.

13. Writer, lawyer, and chancellor

More’s soliloquy turns three achievements of his earlier life into traps: he must inhabit his fiction, find its legality, and administer it. His political competence has helped make his captivity possible. The question of what he will refuse now becomes more urgent than what he can manage.

More’s authorship of Utopia and his legal and governmental career; the chapter’s closing soliloquy.

11.

NINE DAY KING

Cosmopolis, Astrobe
+

Thomas enjoys his presidency while the Nine's influence persists. He signs legislation, tries to remove harmful riders, and struggles to remember the meeting he has forgotten. A clause outlawing belief in the Beyond appears inside the Earth Severance Act; he cuts it out. It returns in the Botch Bill, which he vetoes. Presented independently a third time, the measure confronts him with the penalty for repeated veto: death. He defends the remaining religious communities but nearly gives way. Proctor's threats and Foreman's deliberate provocation bring him to the final refusal.

“Whether there be Things Beyond I do not know. Ye'd forbid the mind to consider them. I forbid the forbidding.”

Characters
Thomas MoreCosmos KingmakerPeter ProctorFabian ForemanPottscampNorthprophet
Themes
Conscience vs. PowerThree VetoesBan the BeyondMartyrdom
Outline
I. The nine-day presidency +
  • The year is Astrobe 535, corresponding to Earth 2535 by the old count.
  • Lawmasters submit bills; machines recommend approval.
  • Thomas's amendments are circumvented by provisions in other bills.
II. The first two refusals +
  • Thomas removes the clause from the Earth Severance Act.
  • It returns as a rider to the Botch Bill.
  • He vetoes the entire Botch Bill and asks why the proposal matters so much.
III. The third presentation +
  • The measure is presented as a separate bill.
  • Kingmaker reports the Metropolitan's death.
  • Thomas defends the synagogue, mosque, remaining sects, and green-robed monks.
  • The penalty concerns three vetoes of the same proposal, however it is presented.
IV. The final refusal +
  • Thomas says he will sign.
  • Proctor threatens him again, while Foreman appeals to his pride and courage.
  • Thomas writes his veto across the bill.
  • The assembled rulers sentence him to death.
› Notes and sources (10)
1. The Nine Day King

The title invites comparison with Lady Jane Grey, the Nine Days’ Queen, who was deposed and later executed. More also recalls the young Salic ruler as a One Day Emperor. The comparison gives his presidency the shape of a brief elevation already overshadowed by the block.

Lady Jane Grey’s reign in July 1553; the proverb of a nine days’ wonder.

2. The philosopher king

More explicitly thinks of Plato’s ideal ruler. Utopia had already debated whether a philosopher could serve usefully in a prince’s council. Astrobe gives More the supreme office, but the bills and their hidden provisions reveal how little final authority that office guarantees.

Plato, Republic 5.473c–d; Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

3. Astrobe’s calendar

The year 535 A.S. corresponds to 2535 by the old count. The omitted Free Years complicate the colony’s elapsed time. The dates place More roughly a thousand years beyond his earthly death while exposing another way the official account orders and compresses history.

The chapter’s account of anno scientiae and the Free Year.

4. The sun as a hole

The words spoken through More recall Anaximander’s account of the sun as an opening through which fire is seen. In Astrobe’s argument the opening becomes an emblem of emptiness. The comparison is useful, but no philosopher is named in the scene.

Ancient accounts of Anaximander’s cosmology, including Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies 1.6.

5. Ban the Beyond

More’s name for the measure recalls the modern slogan Ban the Bomb. The resemblance gives the abolition of transcendence the familiar language of a public campaign. The provision would prohibit considering things beyond the Dream, including the possibility that the Dream is incomplete.

The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament slogan; the chapter’s description of the bill.

6. The remnants

The legal heading reduces surviving religious communities to leftovers. Isaiah and Romans give remnant a different significance: a people preserved through apparent defeat. The small numbers therefore do not settle the value or future of the communities the bill would abolish.

Isaiah 10:20–22; Romans 11:5.

7. Kingmaker’s Fall

Kingmaker tells of creatures who leave perfection in search of something beyond and fall into the void. The account reverses the value of escape: faith in a beyond becomes the original error. More’s suspicion that the labels have been switched opens the possibility that Golden Astrobe is itself the emptiness.

Compare Genesis 3 and Revelation 12:7–9; Kingmaker’s allegory in this chapter.

8. Veto: I forbid

More writes the Latin formula across the bill. His prohibition defends the freedom to consider what the measure would prohibit. The constitutional penalty follows three refusals of the proposal in its successive forms, so his third veto makes the act of reading and rejecting legislation a decision about his life.

Latin veto, I forbid; the chapter’s law concerning repeated vetoes.

9. More’s first refusal

The novel explicitly compares this refusal with the act that led to More’s first death. Historically he refused the oath in 1534 and was later convicted of treason. Lafferty changes the issue and the character’s stated certainty, while retaining the demand for assent and the fatal cost of withholding it.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, accounts of the oath and trial.

10. The friend who requires the head

More asks who pushed him into the corner before. Roper records his judgment that Henry’s friendship would not save his head if the king could gain by taking it. Foreman’s friendship and manipulation repeat that disturbing proximity between affection and political use.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, More’s conversation with Roper after Henry’s visit to Chelsea.

12.

THE ULTIMATE PEOPLE

George's Shop / Cosmopolis
+

The Eagles gather at George the Syrian's Cosmopolis shop. Maxwell returns in an old woman's manufactured body, and Adam appears again. Battersea outlines a noon rescue, though Copperhead and Adam predict Thomas's death. The group drinks and tells stories that the surveillance machines cannot interpret. Foreman joins them and reports a carnival in the square. A new Metropolitan has already proclaimed an interdict. As the city revives its forgotten feasts and passions, bells ring from churches long destroyed. Evita tells Thomas that the rescue will save him.

“And one more, high and powerful and clear, the July Bell.”

Characters
PaulGeorge the SyrianEvitaRimrockWalter CopperheadBatterseaShantyMaxwellAdamFabian Foreman
Themes
Fools’ CarnivalThe Five Hundred BellsWakeLast Night
Outline
I. The gathering +
  • Shanty, Battersea, Paul, Copperhead, Maxwell, Evita, Rimrock, and Adam assemble.
  • Maxwell's borrowed body is Programmed; his surviving identity troubles the distinction between person and machine.
  • Battersea plans the rescue for noon and returns to Cathead to prepare.
II. The wake +
  • The others hold a wake for Thomas before his death.
  • Adam recounts Saint Brandon's voyage to Astrobe.
  • George tells of a Syrian and a dromedary restarting the world.
  • The monitors mistake the tales for a code and fail to interpret them.
III. The carnival +
  • Foreman arrives by a private entrance.
  • Cosmopolis erupts in revelry, fighting, penitence, and hope.
  • A new Metropolitan places the world under interdict.
  • The Wooly Ram feast returns; Programmed Persons hide in fear.
IV. The bells +
  • Five hundred bells sound, many from churches long razed.
  • The people recognize their old names and voices.
  • The July Bell joins them.
  • Evita returns from reassuring Thomas, but the predictions of death remain.
› Notes and sources (10)
1. The gathering eagles

The opening recalls the Gospel saying that eagles gather where the body is. Its setting in discourse about the last things fits a night described as the world’s last. The companions gather around a man whose death is expected, while their name also carries the force of a chosen company.

Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37; compare Job 39:30.

2. Principalities and powers

The account of Evita’s long battle draws directly on Paul’s description of spiritual warfare. Her apparent youth and accumulated experience give that struggle an unusual embodiment. Her enemies exercise political control as well as the spiritual hostility named by the phrase.

Ephesians 6:12.

3. Saint Brandon’s voyage

Adam retells the voyage of Saint Brendan as an early visit to Astrobe. His nineteen monks and ninety-nine days differ from the medieval Navigatio, with its smaller chosen company and seven-year voyage. Moving the Land of Promise into space gives Astrobe a sacred past earlier than its official settlement.

Navigatio Sancti Brendani; Past Master’s name for the saint is Brandon.

4. The wake before death

The companions hold the wake while More is alive. Stories, drink, and argument become forms of attendance on a death they hope to prevent. Their conversation defeats the machines’ attempt to reduce it to useful instructions or a discoverable plan.

The wake tradition; the chapter’s account of the machines listening to the stories.

5. The fools’ carnival

Masks, mock factions, irreverence, and mingled joy and violence recall the Feast of Fools and carnival traditions. Cosmopolis begins behaving unpredictably on the night before its ceremonial execution. Its recovery of feeling is dangerous as well as hopeful.

The medieval Feast of Fools; Carnival, Halloween, and St. John’s Eve customs.

6. Candy heads and skulls

The confections invite comparison with the sugar skulls of the Mexican Day of the Dead. Here they honor an execution that has not yet happened. Death becomes something sold, eaten, mocked, and anticipated throughout the city.

The calavera tradition of the Day of the Dead.

7. Sackcloth and ashes

The carnival faction turns an act of penance into a public costume and joke. Chapter 13 gives the gesture a different weight when Pottscamp pours ashes over his head. The repetition asks whether an apparently empty imitation can become an actual act of remorse.

Matthew 11:21; Job 2:12; 42:6.

8. The interdict

The new Metropolitan invokes the Church’s power to place a territory under religious censure pending repentance. Applying it to a planet gives an old ecclesiastical action an enormous scale. His appearance also answers the earlier assumption that the dying Metropolitan would have no successor.

The historical practice of a general interdict, notably the interdict on England, 1208–14.

9. The serpent’s tooth

The narrator’s phrase for remorse recalls Lear’s pain at an ungrateful child. Cosmopolis has raised More to power and is preparing to kill him. The borrowed image makes its new emotion resemble a child’s recognition of injury done to a parent.

Shakespeare, King Lear, 1.4.

10. The funeral toll and the July Bell

The old bells recover names and a shared purpose as they toll for More. The July Bell can suggest his execution on 6 July 1535, although the novel does not explain the name. Sound carries a religious memory that the museumized churches seemed to have lost.

The Christian passing-bell and funeral-toll traditions; More’s death in July 1535.

13.

APOCEPHALON

Centrality Square, Cosmopolis
+

Unregulated rain falls on Cosmopolis. Foreman explains his theory that worlds periodically die and require a small immaterial addition to be reborn. He has advanced Thomas's execution from noon to eight o'clock, defeating Battersea's timetable. A smaller rescue rush is destroyed. Evita attacks Foreman; George, Maxwell, and Rimrock join in killing him and are then themselves killed. An unidentified stranger speaks privately with Thomas. The blade falls, and the worlds end.
