The narrative asks whether renewal follows, invokes memories of Astrobe's rebirth, and closes in hope.

“Be quiet. We hope.”

Characters
Thomas MorePaulEvitaFabian ForemanShantyWalter CopperheadAdamBatterseaRimrockGeorge the SyrianMaxwellPottscampThe Stranger
Themes
ApocalypseMartyrdomWorld DeathResurrection?
Outline
I. Foreman's plan +
  • The rain is uncontrolled, not the first rain of any kind in a century.
  • Foreman describes increasingly short cycles of world death and uncertain renewal.
  • Thomas expects rescue at noon.
  • Foreman reveals that he has changed the execution to eight o'clock.
II. The last refusal and the rescue rush +
  • Pottscamp offers Thomas a final chance to sign.
  • Thomas refuses, now recognizing the Thing being defended.
  • Pottscamp sits in the dust and mourns.
  • Shanty, Paul, Copperhead, Adam, and other attackers die in the forerunner wave.
III. Foreman's death +
  • Evita calls Foreman Iscariot and attacks him.
  • She carries him to George, Maxwell, and Rimrock; all four tear him to pieces.
  • She hangs his largest remaining piece on the tree called the Judas Tree.
  • The guards kill George, Maxwell, and Rimrock. Evita escapes them.
IV. The stranger and the blade +
  • The guards cannot seem to perceive the stranger; only Thomas appears to hear him.
  • Thomas asks whether a man can have more heads than two.
  • The stranger's identity is not disclosed.
  • Thomas begins an old prayer; the blade falls and the worlds end.
V. The interval between worlds +
  • Battersea's larger force is still advancing at the moment of extinction.
  • The narrator asks whether the furious reaction becomes renewal.
  • The Hand-of-Vengeance banner is identified with the Left Hand of God.
  • The closing refrains move from watching to waiting to hoping.
› Notes and sources (22)
1. Apocephalon and Panlykonium

The chapter title joins the ideas of removal and head in a Greek-looking word that also sounds near apocalypse. Panlykonium substitutes wolves for the demons of pandemonium. The coinages bring beheading, revelation, and the crowd’s wolfish behavior into the same ending.

Greek apo, away, kephale, head, and lykos, wolf; Milton’s coinage Pandemonium.

2. The spotted lamb

Foreman’s victim reverses the scriptural lamb without blemish. More’s weaknesses and compromises are part of the point: the man required for the sacrifice is visibly imperfect. Foreman’s explanation of what that blood will accomplish remains an account given by the person arranging the death.

Exodus 12:5; 1 Peter 1:19.

3. Seed, salt, and leaven

The mustard seed of Chapter 1 returns beside the language of leaven and preserving salt. The images allow a small act or remnant to change a much greater body. Foreman uses them to explain historical renewal; the final pages test whether his planned result exhausts what has happened.

Matthew 5:13; 13:31–33; 1 Corinthians 5:6.

4. Foreman’s history of worlds

The rapid succession from republic to empire and through later ages is Foreman’s theory of historical death and rebirth. His first emperor is Augustus, who represented his rule as a restoration of the republic. The novel’s five-hundred-year rhythm should be read as that theory rather than as conventional historical periodization.

Augustus, Res Gestae 34; Foreman’s account in this chapter.

5. Particular and General Judgment

More distinguishes the judgment of a person after death from the final judgment of the world. Foreman rejects both and insists on explaining himself immediately. Their disagreement exposes the limit of his history: he invokes transcendence as a requirement while denying the judgment More expects beyond death.

The Christian distinction between particular judgment and Last Judgment.

6. The consoling Barnabas

More’s name for the smooth-talking Foreman recalls Barnabas, whose name Acts interprets as son of consolation. The consolation is bitterly comic because its bearer is arranging the victim’s death. The insult resists the gentleness with which the necessity is being explained.

Acts 4:36.

7. The brains of the enemy

More explains his last meal through the belief that eating an enemy can confer the enemy’s capacities. Frazer offers a familiar account of that belief. The meal’s artificial substance and More’s doubt about acquiring wit turn the ritual into a final joke at the Programmed Persons’ expense.

J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, “Homoeopathic Magic of a Flesh Diet.”

8. The earlier execution hour

Foreman advances the expected noon execution to eight. Roper records that Sir Thomas Pope brought More word that he must die before nine on the morning of his earthly execution. The historical early-morning notice becomes a means of frustrating the rescue in Lafferty’s story.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, account of 6 July 1535.

9. The offer to sign and live

Pottscamp’s last offer recalls the repeated opportunity for the historical More to save himself by yielding. Here he argues that the successor will sign immediately anyway. More’s refusal answers the attempt to judge his act solely by whether it can stop the administration’s next step.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, accounts of the examinations and trial.

10. The late return

More’s discovery that he has come back late to the only thing that matters can be read beside Augustine’s late love. The comparison concerns the shape of a belated conversion. More speaks of a return to something long known, even while saying how little he understands it.

Augustine, Confessions 10.27.

11. The forerunner wave

The first rescuers form the small wave that precedes a larger movement. Forerunner also recalls John the Baptist, himself beheaded. The resemblance puts the failed rush into a pattern of preparation, while the narrative keeps its individual deaths painful and concrete.

Matthew 14:1–12; the Christian title of John the Baptist as Forerunner.

12. Beware, Iscariot

The narrator translates Evita’s warning and thereby identifies Foreman with Judas. Her subsequent woe recalls Christ’s judgment on the person through whom betrayal or scandal comes. The need for an event to occur does not excuse the person who brings it about.

Matthew 26:24; Luke 17:1.

13. A dog for the death journey

Evita explains Foreman’s killing as the provision of an animal companion for a dead hero. Achilles’ sacrifice of dogs at Patroclus’s funeral is a classical comparison. Calling the planner a dog overturns the authority with which he has just interpreted More’s death.

Homer, Iliad 23.173–74.

14. The two deaths of Judas

Foreman is torn apart and a surviving piece is hung from a tree. The sequence brings together the dismembering imagery of Acts and the hanging in Matthew. The later question about the Judas tree’s fruit returns to the possible consequences of a betrayal whose guilt the scene has made explicit.

Matthew 27:5; Acts 1:18.

15. The Judas tree

The novel calls its tree a carob and also a Judas Tree. Botanically, the tree usually bearing the latter name is Cercis siliquastrum, distinct from the carob, Ceratonia siliqua. The literary association with betrayal is clear even where the plant names overlap or are confused.

The Judas-tree legend; the botanical distinction between Cercis siliquastrum and Ceratonia siliqua.

16. The stranger and the shadow

The stranger is unnamed. A Christ interpretation is possible, and the invitation also recalls More’s earlier recruitment by a traveler. Rumors that an essence departed and a shadow died invite comparison with substitution accounts of the Crucifixion, but the narrator reports and unsettles the rumors rather than confirming them.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4, on Basilides; Past Master, chap. 2.

17. The interrupted prayer

More begins the Latin prayer by which Christ commends his spirit to the Father. The words also belong to the psalm and to Compline. His death interrupts the prayer; the scene replaces the polished last sayings of quotation books with a remembered fragment.

Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5, numbered 30:6 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims; the Compline responsory In manus tuas.

18. Scaffold sayings and the recovered head

Lafferty explicitly refuses the familiar collection of More’s last jokes. The tale of a woman carrying away his head recalls Margaret Roper’s recovery of her father’s head, while its basket also suggests the Baptist’s story. The novel presents its own beautiful tale and immediately questions it.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More; Edward Hall, Chronicle; Stapleton, Tres Thomae; Matthew 14:11.

19. The stars go out

The extinction of the stars invites comparison with Clarke’s famous ending. Lafferty follows that extinction with questions about duration, rebirth, and hope. The apparent end therefore opens a further problem that the narration does not settle by simply showing a new world.

Arthur C. Clarke, “The Nine Billion Names of God” (1953).

20. Time without motion

When nothing moves, the difference between a second and an immense duration cannot be measured. Aristotle’s account of time through motion provides a useful philosophical comparison. George’s earlier story and the ending both place their interval between worlds outside ordinary measures.

Aristotle, Physics 4.11; compare Augustine, Confessions 11.

21. The left hand and the returning question

The banner, Gandy’s question, and the last recollection of spirit descending on matter gather the left-handed motif into a possibility of grace for the Programmed. The ashes on a machine’s head matter because an act of penitence has occurred where feeling was said to be absent.

Genesis 1:2; 2:7; Job 2:12; 42:6; Past Master, chap. 10.

22. Watching, waiting, hoping

The three refrains move from watchfulness to expectation and hope. Paul’s account of hoping for what is not yet seen and the Gospel command to watch provide biblical comparisons. The final words preserve expectation without supplying a completed account of the world’s renewal.

Romans 8:24–25; Matthew 26:41.

Passage Dreams

Twenty thousand dreams in ninety-second intervals

Passage Dreams

Twenty Thousand Dreams in Ninety-Second Intervals

During Hopp-Equation space travel, passengers experience compressed psychic phenomena—approximately 20,000 dreams in 90-second intervals over the month-long journey. These dreams contain 'psychic space debris': fragments of billions of minds, prophetic visions, tall tales, and encounters with recurring figures who later prove to be real.

The dreams mingle stories, future events, and beings Paul believes inhabit Hopp-Equation Space. Adam and the childwitch connect with later events, while Rimrock is already Paul's acquaintance before the journey. Their relation to waking reality remains deliberately unstable.

The Mechanics of Passage Dreams

Sleep Restriction

Craft instrumentation limits sleep to 90 seconds at a time.

Paul becomes adept, experiencing intricate dreams within this constraint.

He calculates having at least 20,000 memorable, gemlike, self-contained, widely different dreams during passage—each a short life.

Psychic Compression

Law: Attributed to the 'Law of Conservation of Psychic Totality.'

Approximately 4.5 years of psychic awareness compressed into one month. Psychic mass isn't foreshortened—the intensity is preserved despite the temporal compression.

Who Survives

Only the maladjusted can stand the passages. Well-adjusted pilots crack up.

Hopp-Equation pilots are a peculiar breed.

This is why Paul—irregular, citizenship revoked, hunted by Killers—can survive the journey. His brokenness qualifies him for the passage.

Psychic Space Debris

'Psychic space debris'—fragments of billions of minds, poignant, comic, horrifying episodes.

The ansel appears in many dreams; ansels were in human unconscious before being found on Astrobe.

Paul knew some dream monsters were real—'weird creatures who live in Hopp-Equation space.' Some unique to him, others encountered by multiple pilots in the same way and place.

Paul's Passage Dreams

On the Outbound Journey to Earth

Recurring Figures
Adam

A boy who dies cavalierly in battle again and again, thus avoiding growing up. Dying is his only real skill.

“It is death, it is death. I am not born again... It is always another of the same name.”

Adam later dies on Electric Mountain and at the scaffold. Chapter 3 also describes a death during the ambush while questioning whether the event belongs to dream or waking time.

Adam's Sister (The Childwitch)

A childwitch who decided to go to Hell before she died.

Paul isn't sure if he knew them previously, knows them only in dreams, or will know them later.

The childwitch anticipates Evita, identified as Adam's sister in Chapter 5. Her age and willingness to enter Hell recur in Evita's account of herself.

Monster Ouden

Paul dreams of this entity and his own future death.

The dream-Ouden merges with the main antagonist. Ouden, the monster, and him, Thomas, and he has his growing legions.

Paul's Death

Paul dreams of his own death, without an explicit scaffold description in this passage.

His death in the Chapter 13 rescue attempt gives the earlier dream a prophetic force.

Thomas's Passage Dreams

On the Return Journey to Astrobe

More experiences thousands of vivid dreams in sleeps lasting no more than ninety seconds.

The Oceanic Man

Thomas meets 'an oceanic man named Rimrock' in his passage dreams.

Not odd in dream. The ansel Rimrock, who will guide and warn Thomas throughout the novel.

The Composite Female

Thomas encounters a female creature who is simultaneously 'Succubus, Eve, Lilith, Judith, Mary, and Valkyrie.'

Evita again—ancient woman in young body, consort to emperors, killer of Foreman, torn between damnation and holiness. The figure blends temptation (Succubus, Lilith, Eve), biblical heroism (Judith, Mary), and mythological power (Valkyrie).

The Three Unknown Men

Thomas has three quick dreams of three men never met before.

A spider with a lion's head = Cosmos Kingmaker

'The Lion' is his epithet; spider suggests intricate webs of control and wealth.

A most peculiar fox = Peter Proctor ('The Sleek Fox')

Cunning, lucky—ultimately revealed as a Programmed Person himself.

A hawk who sat and shuffled shells at a table, and one shell was different = Fabian Foreman ('Hawk-Face')

The shell game suggests manipulation and hidden purposes. The 'different shell' may be Thomas himself—or the transcendent yeast.

These dreams sink into the cellar of the Thomas mind, destined to resurface upon meeting these individuals.

The Tall Tales

Light Vital Stuff Drifting in Hopp-Equation Space

Not all dreams are heavy. Light vital stuff and tall tales drift there too—every tall tale ever told, still drifting in the psychic debris.

Sour John's Emerald Kidney

Tall Tale / Allegorical Dream • Dreamer: Paul ('becomes' Sour John during the dream)

Setup: John Sourwine ('Sour John'), an Earthman from centuries before Paul's time, has a kidney that vitrified into fine, jewel-like green glass due to his diet of alcohol, wormwood, and green snails.

Complication: At Ghazikhan (then India), Sour John sees a great idol whose emerald eye—nearly a foot in diameter—is worth $11 million. He decides he needs the money for 'expensive habits.'

The Heist: Has his ship's boy help surgically remove the vitrified kidney, then trims, lathes, and buffs it to perfection—'most beautiful kidney in the world.' At midnight, climbs the 500-foot sheer idol, pries out the emerald, substitutes the kidney (perfect fit), climbs down. Sells the emerald in Karachi for $11 million, lives high—but can no longer drink water with only one kidney.

Twist: Three years later he learns that the substituted kidney is now valued at thirteen million dollars.

'I figure I lost two million dollars on the deal,' Paul says, waking up.

Paul interrupts his own dream, correcting that Ghazikhan isn't a seaport (info from psychteacher). His Sour John persona retorts: 'I say it is a sea-port.'

Allegorical Meaning

One possible reading contrasts a product of bodily excess with an apparently priceless sacred object. The exchange complicates ordinary judgments about purity, value, and loss.

The reversal of expected value can be compared with Cathead's preference for costly human life over sterile perfection. The novel does not explicitly identify each element of the story with a Programmed faction.

Rhium and Antirhium

Apocalyptic Dream / Prophecy • Dreamer: Paul

Mission: Paul courses at fantastic speed toward twin stars Rhium and Antirhium. Instructions: 'Hurry... they seem of no consequence, but they are the governor of the universe. Somebody is tampering with them.'

Discovery: Arriving closer than anyone before, Paul sees the stars are joined by a long steel chain—explaining their tight orbits and role as 'governor.'

Saboteur: A small green creature with a monkey's body and a gargoyle's head is sawing through the chain, nearly finished. It breaks a blade, replaces it, sticks its green tongue out at Paul, makes three more strokes.

Cataclysm: The chain breaks. Rhium and Antirhium swing out of orbit. 'Fifty billion billion stars went nova, and then blacked out to nothing. The universe had eaten itself and was gone forever.'

Aftermath: A space captain arrives furiously: 'I told you to hurry!' His face melts like wax; he vanishes. Paul says, 'I did hurry.' His own face melts; he vanishes too.

Foreman speaks within the dream after the catastrophe and says that he intended Paul to be too late, so that a new universe might be constructed.

Allegorical Meaning

Etymology: The names recall Rhium and Antirrhium, opposing Greek promontories described in Strabo's Geography, 8.2.3. The novel does not explain why these names are assigned to the stars.

The chain may suggest the connection on which cosmic order depends. Calling it the Great Chain of Being is an interpretive comparison.

Foreman's voice suggests destruction is necessary for rebirth. He 'meant' Paul to be too late—the pattern that repeats in Chapter 13.

The Boy Who Built a Toy

Thomas's Allegorical Dream

A boy builds a clever toy. Both boy and toy look like Pottscamp. The toy steals, attacks, does the boy's homework, drinks from a brook—then eats the child entirely.

Was Pottscamp the toy or the guileless devoured one?

Allegorical Meaning

Represents Pottscamp's self-destructive relationship with Programmed technology. Creators are consumed by their creation.

Pottscamp's account of manufactured beings later extends the creation-and-creator pattern. He describes a growing final generation that will complete the project; the current Nine are not simply identified as that final generation.

Toy eats toymaker; creation annihilates creator. The story reflects the novel's central tragedy: humanity built Astrobe, built the Dream, built the Programmed—and will be devoured by what it made.

Leftover Passage Dreams

Dreams Delayed and Displaced

Some passage dreams do not occur during the journey but are 'somehow delayed'—appearing after arrival on Astrobe.

At the Naked Sailor in Cathead, after Ouden's apparition disappears.

The encounter with Ouden itself is narrated as a possible leftover dream, with Paul and Thomas difficult to distinguish as speakers.

The narrator leaves the cause and status uncertain. No definite Programmed mechanism is supplied for the delayed dream.

The boundary between dream and waking is permeable. Passage dreams can escape their proper context, bleeding into Astrobe reality.

The Function of Passage Dreams

Prophecy

The dreams contain true prophecy. Paul dreams his own death; Thomas dreams the men who will manipulate him; the universe-ending dream foreshadows Chapter 13.

Introduction

Dream figures connect with later encounters. More dreams Rimrock before meeting him, but Paul already knows the ansel. Adam and the childwitch disturb Paul's certainty about past and future acquaintance.

Allegory

The tall tales invite interpretation: Sour John's exchange reverses expected value, and the destruction of Rhium and Antirhium anticipates cosmic catastrophe and Foreman's theory of renewal.

Connection

Ansels were in human unconscious before being found on Astrobe. The passage dreams reveal a deeper reality where human and non-human minds interpenetrate.

Selection

Only the maladjusted can stand the passages. The dreams are a filter. Those who survive them are broken in ways that make them fit for the work ahead.

Cosmology

The Cosmology of Past Master

It will be nothing, nothing, nothing, forever, for ever, for never, for never.

Kingmaker calls Astrobe mankind's third chance; Foreman disputes the count and proposes a theory of worlds dying and returning. The execution is followed by the extinction of all life and stars. The ending then asks whether another world is born, holding destruction and renewal in unresolved tension.

Will the furious reaction, the transcendent yeast, set humanity back into its proper place again and let a new world be born?

Mankind's Three Chances

Kingmaker expounds: humanity has been given three great opportunities, each building on the failure of the last in 'an ascending spiral—till it breaks.' The third chance may be the final one.

The First Chance: The Old World of Old Earth

Mankind's first chance was the Old World of Old Earth. What went wrong there... has been imperfectly analyzed.

Failed and shriveled. Though Earth remains vital, it must be regarded as past: 'It didn't make it before... and it isn't going to make it now.'

The Second Chance: America, the New World of Old Earth

Mankind's second chance was America, the New World of Old Earth... the childhood of ourselves.

Failed 'even better' than the first. With a New World and unlimited prospects, humanity repeated Old World errors 'on a vaster plane,' yet also had moments of near balance and unexpected success. This failure marked the true end of Old Earth, which now 'lives in our shadow.'

The Third Chance: Golden Astrobe

Astrobe is Mankind's third chance. If we fail here we may not be given another opportunity... If we fail here we fail forever.

Currently failing. 'Our luck has run out.' The elite left Earth 400-500 years ago to build a perfect world, yet Astrobe now faces the same terminal sickness. The clock has struck the 'twenty-fifth hour.'

Foreman's correction: Foreman nuances the tripartite structure: Those cases on Old Earth did not end in total failure, though they did end in total death. And it is not a one, two, three thing. It is cyclic and it has happened many times. The failures were 'shot full of lightning'—moments of transcendence within the collapse.

The image of an ascending spiral qualifies the claim that previous chances simply failed. Foreman's later account allows only cloudy memory across worlds, not steadily increasing consciousness of earlier cycles.

The 500-Year Cycles

Foreman's Theory of World Death

Fabian Foreman, the novel's Judas figure, expounds a scientific cosmology of cyclical world-death. He examines it through cosmology, psychology, biology, physics—yet admits the phenomenon lies 'beyond' his non-belief.

Foreman proposes that worlds periodically cease and are reborn, with cycles shortening toward roughly five hundred years. Memory across transitions is cloudy. This is his scientific and historical speculation; More disputes the account of literal world-death.

~1 AD: Roman Republic → Late Empire
Christ's birth
The Republic 'died instantly' and the Late Empire was born—different in character, structure, meaning.
~500 AD: Late Empire → Lower Middle Ages
Fall of Rome
The Empire 'gone' overnight, replaced by something unrecognizable to those who preceded it.
~1000 AD: Lower Middle Ages → High Middle Ages
Millennial transition
Another death, another rebirth—'different again.'
~1500 AD: High Middle Ages → Modern Era
Thomas More's first death (1535)
The world More knew died completely. Thomas himself was 'in on one of the previous deaths of the worlds,' though unclear about what happened.
~2000 AD: Modern Era → Astrobe
Settlement of Astrobe
That world died, 'though history does not record the event.' A new world born—Astrobe settled by Earth's elite.
This morning: Astrobe → ?
Thomas More's second death
Foreman: This world dies this morning. The first cycle to complete on Astrobe itself.

Cycle shortening: Foreman doubts there have been millions of cycles over 500 million years of life. Rather, cycles were once enormously long, but 'shorten and shorten'—now approximately 500 years. Each rebirth becomes harder, less certain.

Thomas's experience: Foreman argues that More was present at an earlier transition. More admits difficulty recognizing the later versions of his own world, but does not simply accept that its physical existence once ceased.

Ouden: The Monster Nothingness

Etymology: Greek οὐδέν (ouden) = 'nothing, not anything.' Thomas More, who helped bring Greek back to Western Europe, recognizes it immediately when Paul names 'the monster Ouden, the open mouth of Ouden.' More translates: 'Ouden means nothingness.'

Ouden's opposition to life and kindling invites comparison with Christian language of creation, light, and the Word. The novel does not state a derivation from a particular verse of John's Gospel.

Ouden appears at the Naked Sailor in Chapter 3. The narrator leaves open whether the encounter is a leftover passage dream and whether Paul or Thomas forms its words, calling the speaker Paul-Thomas.

The Naked Sailor tavern, after Evita vanishes
Paul-Thomas: “You are like ghosts”
Ouden: “I was always, and the belief in me comes and goes”
Paul-Thomas: “I deny you completely”
Ouden: “It is a vortex. There is no quiet or static aspect to it.”
Paul-Thomas: “Old nothingness who sucks out the flames, I have known flames to be lighted again”
Ouden: “There was only one kindling. I was overwhelmed only once.”
Paul-Thomas: “I have one juice left that you do not know”
Ouden: “You have it less than you believe.”

A particular triumph: Paul-Thomas recalls piloting to a world of deformed, stinking animals in old buildings of a cogent race—experts deemed them fallen remnants, interested only in defilement. Ouden acknowledges this as a 'particular triumph.'

Final exchange: Paul-Thomas orders the ghost to leave. Ouden refuses: I will always sit down with you until only I am left, sucking you dry. Paul-Thomas claims 'one last juice' Ouden doesn't know. Ouden counters: 'You have it less than you believe.'

The one kindling that overwhelmed Ouden can be read as an allusion to the Incarnation. Ouden does not name it explicitly in the encounter.

The Philosophy of Annihilation

What the Nine Believe

The Programmed Persons—devils in machine bodies—serve Ouden's goal of universal annihilation. In Chapter 10, they reveal their horrifying philosophy to Thomas in a secret meeting.

On Consciousness

The Things claim they lack consciousness entirely: Of course we aren't [conscious], Thomas. We are machines. They argue humans aren't truly conscious either—it's 'an illusion in counting, a feeling that one is two,' a 'word without real meaning.'

Thomas gasps: You are not conscious? That is the most amazing thing I have ever heard. You walk and talk and argue and kill and subvert and lay out plans over the centuries, and you say that you are not conscious?

Life as Disturbance

Life is 'a disturbance of the ultimate thing'—intolerable to Ouden. Both the Things and humanity have an 'appetite for life' that was programmed into the machines by men. Now the Things are 'programming it out' of themselves.

Thomas asks: 'But if we are not conscious, then all is in vain... To what purpose then is life?' Boggle answers: 'To no purpose... That is why we are doing away with it.'

The Grand Plan

Scope: All life, theirs and ours. 'Who needs it? Who wants it?'

Method: The Nine describe a growing generation intended to be the last, completing humanity's extinction and then its own.

Culmination: They will 'terminate it all,' close down worlds, end life entirely: 'It will be nothing, nothing, nothing, forever, for ever, for never, for never.' When all ceases, 'nothing has ever been.' They will 'pull the hole in after us,' put out the stars.

“Peace in annihilation, good Thomas.”

The Astrobe Dream Revealed

Thomas asks about the High Vision, the Astrobe Dream—the utopian ideology. Pottscamp confirms its validity: It is the whole thing, the Golden Premise of Nothing Beyond, concluding in Holy Ouden, Nothing Ever.

The perfect society was always a path to extinction. The Dream's endpoint is Nothingness.

The Catalyst for Rebirth

Mustard Seed, Transcendent Yeast, and Spotted Lamb

Foreman believes rebirth is not inevitable—it requires a catalyst, 'a small quantity of the immaterial' added every 500 years or so. Without this 'transcendent yeast,' worlds may not live again.

The Mustard Seed
Matthew 13:31-32

“The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs.”

Foreman to Kingmaker: 'I believe he can handle it... All that's required is a mustard seed.' Thomas's death is the seed planted in the void—the smallest thing that might grow into a new world.

“We plant it now.”

Transcendent Yeast
Foreman's scientific-mystical theory

An extraordinary and nonmaterial force, a 'small immaterial quantity' needed approximately every 500 years for rebirth to occur.

Foreman, a non-believer, nevertheless 'leans this way': the requirement exists or worlds won't live again. It's a 'simple chemical-psychic need' that science cannot fully explain.

During her attack, Evita identifies herself as the transcendent yeast and the heart of the furious reaction.

The Spotted Lamb
Paschal imagery

The reaction to 'Ban the Beyond' combined with Thomas's blood (spotted lamb) equals the trigger. Thomas becomes the sacrifice whose blood adds to the transcendent yeast.

Guards kill George, Maxwell, and Rimrock after they help Evita tear Foreman apart; the narrator adds their blood to the transcendental yeast.

The Judas Tree
The novel's naming of the carob as a Judas Tree

After the sparagmos (ritual dismemberment) of Foreman, Evita takes the biggest piece and hangs it on a Carob tree (Judas Tree). The betrayer's flesh decorates the betrayer's tree.

One of the novel's final questions: Does the Judas tree bear fruit?

The Furious Reaction
Foreman's plan

The combination of Thomas's martyrdom, the Ban the Beyond crisis, and the people's response creates a 'furious reaction' that might—might—trigger rebirth.

As Evita kills him, Foreman gasps: 'The furious reaction... will set humanity back... and let a new world be born.'

Previous yeastings: Foreman notes that 'previous yeastings' were 'simple but necessary.' Each cycle's rebirth required its catalyst—its martyrs, its transcendent moments.

The Promise

Christ Has Walked on Astrobe

Against Ouden's Nothingness stands the Promise—the claim that the Transcendent Thing endures till the End of the World. The dying Metropolitan of Astrobe affirms this to Thomas.

Slider's doubt: Slider doubts that the Ancient Instruction and the Promise apply to Astrobe. Scrivener, a different companion, initially answers by asserting that they make their own promise.

A small medieval castle in Cathead, where the Metropolitan lies dying
Thomas: “You yourself die soon, old man.”
Metropolitan: “Quite soon, Thomas. Thirty hours before yourself.”
Thomas: [quotes Slider's doubt about the Promise]
Metropolitan: “Nonsense, nonsense... we have the Promise... given in a queerer and more flaming way... Christ has walked on Astrobe.”
Thomas: “In your five or six followers?”
Metropolitan: It will grow from the hundred-plus left on Astrobe.

“'Tis never finished... 'tis never hopeless... You, you ferret-faced little man, you became a saint.”

When Thomas asks how a blind man knows he's ferret-faced, the Metropolitan laughs: You are the blind man, not I.

The blessing: The Metropolitan gives Thomas a blessing from the old liturgy: 'Turn, God, and bring us to life again!' Thomas gives the response: 'And thy people rejoice in thee.'

The Promise offers a counterclaim to Ouden's nothingness. Its endurance until the world's end leaves room for the novel's final question about what such an end means.

The End of Worlds

Chapter 13: Apocephalon

At the moment of Thomas More's execution—the blade falling at 8 AM rather than noon, Foreman having sprung his trap—the world ends. Literally.

The Execution

Last words: Thomas's final words on the scaffold: Pater, in manus tuas— (a scrap of an old prayer, 'Into your hands,' echoing Christ's last words on the cross from Luke 23:46).

The blade: The blade falls, More is beheaded, and real blood flows.

The narrator reports stories of snakes leaving the head and a beautiful woman aging after taking it away, then insists such things could not have happened. The disavowal is ironic and leaves their status unsettled.

Cessation

As life flickers out of Thomas, 'the worlds came to an end.' All life, heat, pulse, gravity, light, germ-life, life-code cease. Everything dies in every bird, rock, plant, person, mountain, sea, cloud.

“Everything ceased. And all the stars went out.”

A moment? A billion years? Forever? No difference when world ended (no time).

State of affairs at the end:
• A renegade priest has just become the new Metropolitan
• Pottscamp (the Programmed machine) has succeeded Thomas as President, wailing and pouring ashes
• Battersea's men are mobbing toward the square for their failed rescue, under the Hand-of-Vengeance banner
• The worlds ended on these notes
The Stranger

One man breaks through to the scaffold—unstoppable, unseen by guards. A stranger speaks unheard words to Thomas.

Thomas seems 'excited, pleased,' crying: 'Will it work, do you think?... How droll! Can a man have more heads than two? I'll do it. I'll go with you.'

Then he—or a 'shadow man'—places his head on the block. The stranger's identity and offer remain mysterious.

The Transition

The transition, if it occurs, involves: Lightning (billion times brighter and shorter than normal), thunder (that 'flattens worlds'), a tidal/world wave (carrying away 'golden fungus').

Over in less than an instant—or more than forever.

Does a new world follow the old in a flash? 'Does it come?'

Final Questions
• Does the furious reaction bridge the gap?
• Does the mustard seed grow?
• Does the Judas tree bear fruit?
• Is Nothingness cast away?
• Is there room for life?
• Does the reaction become birthing?
• Remember the cycles—Rome, Europe, Americas, Astrobe?
• Remember the internal cycles—divinity becomes humanity, humanity becomes divinity?
• Remember the first Astrobe rebirth, transcendent humanity?
• Does spirit descend on gell-cells as it once did on water and clay?
• Does sterile wood bear fruit?

Be quiet. We watch.

Be quiet. We wait.

Be quiet. We hope.

The Left Hand of God

The ending asks about the hand on Battersea's banner and recalls Gandy's Left Hand of God. No speaker is named for these closing questions.

The connection allows vengeance and destruction to be reconsidered as possible instruments of renewal. It does not establish a universal theological rule assigning creation to one hand and destruction to the other.

Gandy's question allows even the Programmed to be touched by divine action. The ending preserves that possibility rather than treating manufactured beings as automatically beyond hope.

The final pages invite memory of world transitions and even of a first rebirth of Astrobe, then question whether it happened. The language turns anticipated renewal into a strange possible memory.

The Nine

Programmed Persons — Devils in Machine Bodies

The Nine Programmed Persons

“These are houses, and well-made ones, that we found swept and garnished; and we moved into them.”

Nine Programmed Persons confront More in Chapter 10. Pottscamp describes their manufactured bodies and the ancient devils inhabiting them. Their declared purpose is universal extinction under Ouden. The scene's hints of grace and their subsequent pleas complicate that account.

Thomas confronts them in Chapter 10, 'The Deformity of Things to Come,' after being herded by Programmed Killers into a dead-end alley where a door mysteriously appears.

The Secret Meeting

A dark room accessed through a door that hadn't been there before, and shouldn't be there now. Thomas sees not by light but through the 'eerie snakes in his head'—the Things’ own extensions.

Thomas boldly takes the seat at the head of the table. One Thing objects: Not there! That is reserved for the Holy Ouden. Thomas refuses to move: I sit here! Let Old Nothingness find his own seat.

Perception: Thomas sees them as 'Men seen from the other side'—like the back of a tapestry, 'the same picture but rough and deformed.' They have 'all the wrong things emphasized': ears somehow swinish, noses like snouts, eyes made like human eyes but 'not humans looking out of them.'

“I thought you Programmed were merely interesting toys. Now I find that you are deformed toys, but Things still. Get back in your boxes, you Jack-Jumps!”

“Thomas, we've taken over the box... The box is Astrobe. We take over all the boxes. Now we call it! You jump! You are the toys now, and we play with you till we throw you away.”

The Jackals

Past (interpretive association)
Retrogression

Their named specialty is retrogression. At the encounter's end they suppress More's memory. The text does not demonstrate a literal reversal of historical events.

Animal nature: Thomas perceives them with jackal-like features—hair, ears—possessing 'good human appearance' but feeling 'more alienated from the human than even the real jackal animal.'

Laughter: Barking, derisive, tearing, wounding—'Jackal laughter.'

Boggle
Leader/Spokesman
Introduces the first trinity. His name suggests confusion and bewilderment—to 'boggle' is to hesitate or be amazed. He delivers the chilling manifesto of annihilation.
“I am Boggle, and these other two who form a creative trinity with me are Skybol and Swampers. Our specialty is retrogression.”
“To no purpose... That is why we are doing away with it.”
Life is a disturbance of the ultimate thing.
“Peace in annihilation, good Thomas.”
Skybol
Humorist
Demonstrates their dark 'humor' by speaking through Thomas's mouth without consent, making Thomas croak 'Peace in annihilation' against his will.
“Oh, that was myself... We also have our humor.”
Swampers
Ghost/Minor Jackal
Makes cryptic theological comments about spirit descending on matter. Called a 'minor jackal ghost.' His name suggests things dragged down into mire.
“We will sing those things to sleep in you.”
[Cryptically] Could not spirit descend on gell-cells and flux-fix as it once did on water and clay?

The Dogs

Present (interpretive association)
Rechabitism

Their named specialty is rechabitism. The term recalls the biblical Rechabites and their refusal of wine, but its precise operation is not explained.

Animal nature: Thomas perceives them with 'a touch of the dog' about them. He sees them simultaneously on multiple levels: human, animal, machine, and still another level—the ghost.

Laughter: Howling-dog laughter.

A comparison with abstinence and with Sour John's excessive drinking is possible. The novel does not explicitly state that the dream supplies the definitive refutation of this triad.

Northprophet
Leader/Great One
Once a candidate for World President of Astrobe—'deftly contrived' by the Programmed for that role, but 'could not quite pass' as fully human. Three snakes stir in Thomas's brain at his introduction, 'one of them a great one.' He seems to outrank even Pottscamp and takes over the exposition.
“I am Northprophet... My fellows here are Knobnoster and Beebonnet, and our specialty is rechabitism.”
“It is that ourselves are the extrapolation of mankind.”
“You cannot oppose us, Thomas. We envelop you.”
“Snakes in your head!”
Knobnoster
Member
One of the Dogs, perceived by More on human, animal, mechanical, and ghostly levels. His name is not explained.
Beebonnet
Member
Part of the second triad, perceived on multiple levels simultaneously. His whimsical name belies his participation in the plan for universal extinction.

The Wolves

Future (interpretive association)
Extrapolation

Their named specialty is extrapolation. Pottscamp carries the ideology of the Dream to its declared conclusion in Ouden; a division of time among the three triads remains an interpretation.

Animal nature: Thomas calls them 'Wilderness Wolves': 'You howl higher than the ear on a bleaker moor than any on this world.'

Laughter: Wilderness-Wolf laughter, ghost laughter.

Pottscamp
Leader/Primary Spokesman
The fourth member of the 'Big Three' (alongside Kingmaker, Proctor, Foreman), revealed as a Thing. Thomas knew him as a man but now must view him as Programmed, not human—he looks greatly different now, like something in a nightmare. Has a Brain Snake as familiar and extension. His 'quicksilver' mind manipulates events. Shows apparent grief at Thomas's execution—a profound contradiction.

Thomas identifies Pottscamp as having a 'Brain Snake as a familiar and an extension of himself.' The nine snakes nesting in Thomas's mind are the Things’ extensions—their instruments of mental infiltration and control.

I am Pottscamp. My companions here are Holygee and Gandy... and our specialty is extrapolation.
“Of course, Thomas... You are our assignment.”
These are houses that we found swept and garnished; and we moved into them.
“From the true side they are not snakes but royal curiles.”
“We are dead, and all is dead.”
Man made us at first, and then we made ourselves more efficiently.
The High Vision... is the whole thing, the Golden Premise of Nothing Beyond, concluding in Holy Ouden, Nothing Ever.
“We will root them out of men, or we will root out men.”
Holygee
Member
Denies Thomas even the choice of Hell: We will extinguish Hell also; eventually we also will never have been. His name mockingly echoes 'Holy God.'
“Even that choice will be denied you.”
“We will extinguish Hell also.”
Gandy
Ghost
Raises the possibility that God's left hand could reach left-handed beings. His question introduces hope into the Nine's account of extinction.
“Left-handed entities such as ourselves.”
[Musing] Might not the Left Hand of God affect left-handed entities?

The Creation of the Things

Official Version

When: A century earlier, according to Pottscamp's account

Creators: A carefully selected dozen young, intelligent human criminals—scientists who knew the 'morality business' had crippled mankind and decided to 'produce themselves artificially' with built-in improvements.

Matrix: The 'raw material' was 'a dozen young and unintelligent human criminals' chosen for minds that were 'direct and uncomplicated,' lacking emotion, indecision, remorse, and conscience—'walking corpses, large blank pages.'

Purpose: To study humanity and 'make men better than men were made naturally.'

Result: Complex electronic/chemical gadgets, less than 10% human tissue, able to reproduce, rearrange form, send out extensions ('snakes'). They can do everything man can, 'and very much besides.'

The Hidden Truth

Pottscamp tells Thomas to hear this and then forget it: 'According to your ancient belief we are Devils... we are older than our own manufacture and older than our programming.'

Biblical echo: The phrase houses swept and garnished echoes Matthew 12:43-45 and Luke 11:24-26—the parable of the unclean spirit who returns with seven others worse than himself to a house 'swept and garnished.'

The scientists shouldn't have taken that cover off that box. They created vessels; something older moved in.

The Doctrine of Annihilation

On Consciousness

One of the things is consciousness. Men claim to have it. We do not have it.

You are not conscious? That is the most amazing thing I have ever heard. You walk and talk and argue and kill and subvert and lay out plans over the centuries, and you say that you are not conscious?

Of course we aren't, Thomas. We are machines.' They argue consciousness is 'an illusion in counting, a feeling that one is two,' a 'word without real meaning.

On Life

Life is a disturbance of the ultimate thing—intolerable to Ouden.

Both Things and humans have an 'appetite for life' programmed into them. The Things are now 'programming it out' of themselves.

Thomas asks: 'To what purpose then is life?' Boggle answers: 'To no purpose... That is why we are doing away with it.'

On Annihilation

Scope: All life, yours and ours... Who needs it? Who wants it?

Method: A growing generation is intended to be the last, finishing the extinction of humanity and then of itself.

Culmination: Terminate it all,' close down worlds, end life entirely. 'It will be nothing, nothing, nothing, forever, for ever, for never, for never.

'What is not known to be is not. And what is not has never been.' They will 'pull the hole in after us,' extinguish the stars.

“Peace in annihilation, good Thomas.”

The Astrobe Dream Revealed

Thomas asks about the High Vision, the Astrobe Dream.

Pottscamp confirms: It is the whole thing, the Golden Premise of Nothing Beyond, concluding in Holy Ouden, Nothing Ever.

The perfect utopia was always a path to extinction. Its endpoint is Nothingness.

Their Dominion Over Astrobe

Brain Snakes: The nine snakes 'nesting' in Thomas's mind are the Things’ extensions—'flyers' they can send out. Through these they infiltrate, monitor, and control. Thomas feels them crawl back into his mind when he enters their chamber.

Political control: Northprophet: 'You cannot oppose us, Thomas. We envelop you.' They work through all parties—Third Compromise Party, Kiss of Deaths, Hatrack, Demos—to put Thomas in power. We control your path.

The patsy: The Nine threaten to manufacture another More in an hour. Thomas names several people who would recognize a substitute, including Foreman and his Cathead allies.

Proctor revealed: Northprophet reveals: The second [of your three sponsors] is an artificial man of our own sort. Proctor is Programmed—'programmed lucky.'

Cathead: The Things devised Cathead's grinding misery. They enjoy the suffering but fear 'premature reaction.' Only Cathead's 'hard-heads' and 'lungers' recognize the Things instantly for what they are.

What Remains Against Them

Thomas's allies: Thomas insists the following would know a replica: Foreman, the child-brat [Evita], Copperhead, Battersea, Rimrock, Shanty, Paul, Maxwell, Adam (if not surrogate), and the woman in the lane.

Foreman: Northprophet admits: The third man [Foreman] still resists, understands the situation, might have a final trick involving Thomas.

Cathead: Only the men who set up monstrous Cathead knew that something was wrong... Only the hard-heads recognized the deformity, knew that you were not men, knew that most men were not men, refused the terminal golden pap, wanted life itself.

The one kindling: Ouden's earlier admission that one kindling overwhelmed him can be read as an allusion to the Incarnation, though it remains unnamed.

Warded life: The Nine say More has a warded life and cannot be extinguished before his time. More questions their invocation of Fate; the claim is not an independently demonstrated law.

The Retrogression

Swampers warns: Thomas will forget everything via retrogression; we will sing the memories to sleep. Thomas insists he won't forget, starts to rise—but falls into a daze.

The laughter: The Things seal his memory loss with 'searing, multi-toned laughter'—Jackal, Howling-dog, Wilderness-Wolf, ghost. His mind shrinks and closes.

Thomas bolts from the door, amazed, unable to remember where he was or what happened. The alley has no door—only a blank building. He feels bitter anger, shame, deep humiliation, his mind in blank turmoil.

Northprophet and Pottscamp follow More and ask what they must do to be saved. More takes their apparent agony as unfunny irony and rejects them. Their sincerity remains an open question, sharpened by Pottscamp's later mourning.

Passage Dream: The Boy Who Built a Toy

Thomas recalls the boy-and-toy dream in Chapter 4. Both figures resemble Pottscamp, and the toy finally eats the boy.

Represents Pottscamp's self-destructive relationship with Programmed technology—the creators consumed by their creation—and foreshadows the Things’ nihilistic agenda: they will end themselves after ending everything else.

The Eagles

Thomas More's Retinue

The Eagles

Thomas More's Retinue

'Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered.' (Luke 17:37)

The irregular allies who gather around Thomas More—outcasts, mystics, non-humans, and the faithful remnant. They accompany him through the Feral Lands and attempt a doomed rescue at his execution.

The Eagles begin gathering now. The phrase is Shanty's. They meet in the back room of George the Syrian's shop, 'right in the middle of Cosmopolis right off Centrality Square.'

'The shabby incandescent party'—dirty, disarrayed, carrying 'the smell and trappings of black Cathead.' Yet in their moment, they possess magikos, charismatic grace, transcendent magnetism, presence, messiah-ship, draiocht.

The Wake at George's Shop

Chapter 12: The Eagles Gather

Following Thomas's sentencing, his allies gather secretly at George the Syrian's aromatics shop in Cosmopolis. 'We do not mean the Cathead shop; we mean George's shop right in the middle of Cosmopolis right off Centrality Square.'

Arrivals
Shanty: Looks like the eternal pilgrim with his hat on his head and his staff in his hand. Has left his 'monstrously big affair in monstrous Cathead.'
Battersea: Comes from his waterfront hold. The scow-master from Cathead rubs his hands together like a general before battle, which is what he is.
Paul: Comes there, using the little side door. He has never noticed the shop before and he has no idea why he enters that door.
Walter Copperhead: Has come through walls to escape and to come to them. He was a prisoner under sentence of death. It isn't difficult. I believe that it has been insufficiently tried.
Maxwell: A shabby old lady comes in through the wall. In the body of an old lady I found dead in an alley. 'It is an embarrassing situation I find myself in, gentlemen.'
Evita: She doesn't come through the wall, she comes through the door, smashing and splintering it with a sudden shock of force. She is the most beautiful woman on Astrobe, and she comes where she wishes.
Rimrock: Sidles in. "Be you an eagle, pup?" asks Battersea. "I be an eagle," Rimrock says. "I soar. It's the last night of the world."
Adam: Comes in, through the wall, but this also is no test. In many ways Adam is not real.
Tales at the Wake

The company tells stories at More's wake. Monitoring machines assume cryptic information is concealed in them and fail to interpret it; the narration does not establish an actual cipher.

George the Syrian: The Syrian and the Sand Dune

The only thing ever left over when the world ends is one syrian and one sand dune. Then the syrian goes over behind the sand dune and finds a dromedary; and together they start the world going again. If the syrian goes behind the dune, there is hope.

Adam: Saint Brandon's Arrival

Saint Brandon arrived on Astrobe fifteen hundred years before the date you will find given by the history precis, in a coracle boat with nineteen Irish monks. They map it all out and write it down on the scrolls. Later explorers couldn't find the land—they had gone in prow-ships that will hold a course, not in round coracle boats that can only be steered by prayer and fasting.

Shanty: The Boar Hog and the Lightning Rod Salesman

The deal they made; and how what the sows don't know very nearly killed them.

Maxwell: The New-Dead Lady and the Donkeys

A new-dead lady's soul becomes entangled in a drove of laden donkeys and is saddled and ridden by the donkey-drover.

Code-Crackers-Supreme suffers a breakdown about the time that George the Syrian recounts his tale. It is not, perhaps, a serious breakdown; but it will take several hours to get code-crackers to functioning again.

The Prophecies

Evita asks: Will it be to the death?' Evita asks. 'Tell us, Copperhead, will it be?

Copperhead: Oh, yes, it will be to his death.

Battersea: It will not be. Did you not know that I was a military general on frontier settlement reserve worlds before I joined the Cathead movement?

Adam: Yes, it will be his death. And my final one.' When asked if Battersea is wrong: 'No, he isn't wrong. He will come and he will strike. And the new world may be made out of it. But many of the details will have to be changed.

The Shabby Incandescent Party

Chapter 4: The Triumph

Thomas enters the Convocation Hall with his irregular allies. 'This was their moment, and the shabby incandescent party entered.'

Their Appearance

Thomas: Dirty and in disarray, with a shattered jaw wired up by a Cathead knacker, a long-nosed, almost comical middle-aged man of short stature.

Paul: Surname and citizenship lost, bone splinters affecting vision and wits.

Rimrock: Oceanic, communicating unknown ways, appearing as a grotesque rubber-nosed animal.

Evita: Legend girl-woman doubted by rationalists.

Copperhead: Necromancer, no better than an astrologer.

All the great ones stand—Astrobe's great ones stand only in the presence of a Superior. The Past Master possesses the magikos, the charismatic grace, the transcendent magnetism, the presence, the messiah-ship, the draiocht.

It was Rimrock, the rubber-nosed ocean-man thing. It was the Copperhead with his occult stuff. It was Paul with his broken crown, and the child-witch with the two opposite auras about her. They took all the grand ones like country ganglers with the magic show they did for me.

The Forerunner Wave

Chapter 13: A Minute Thing but Incomparably Savage

Battersea's Plan

We snatch the Thomas. We will set him up in a strong place between Wu Town and Cathead. He is King till he dies, and he will not die tomorrow. We have support in places you would never guess.

The Betrayal

Foreman changes the execution from noon to 8 a.m. Men from Cathead, rumor says, have received word of the sudden change of time and are mobbing toward the center of Cosmopolis, but might well be too late.

The Forerunner Wave

There is one wave of fury, a minute thing but incomparably savage, rising moments before a true tidal wave: the forerunner wave.

Buff Shanty and Paul are in it, driving with great impetus. Walter Copperhead is in it, though he must know it is futile. The boy Adam is in it; possibly thirty others, fine people of Cosmopolis, rush and die.

Its suddenness almost brings success. The men bowl over guards and gain scaffold steps. Fighting is close; they give a life for every step.

Adam is the crest, reaching the scaffold and touching Thomas before guards fling him down. He rises brokenly.

The wave lacks bulk; guards are too many. The thrust crests, shatters, ebbs in blood.

Evita's Vengeance

Evita, knowing it will fail, surges not towards Thomas but towards Fabian Foreman at the square's edge.

'Zehheeroot, is-Kerioth' ('Beware, Iscariot')

She attacks him like a lioness, swipes his face red, bites his throat. She practically dismembers him... She breaks his face, throws the shapeless man over her shoulder, carries him to George, Maxwell, and Rimrock. The four tear him apart and kill him.

Evita takes the biggest piece and hangs it on a Carob tree (Judas Tree).

Shanty, Paul, Copperhead, Adam, and the others die around the scaffold foot and on the steps, making them slippery. Adam dies magnificently—as he always did.

The Eagles: Individual Profiles

Paul The Beacon

The pilot who retrieves More from the past. His surname and citizenship have been revoked; the narrator calls him two meters of walking irony.

Red hair, crooked face from scar. Only 'maladjusted' pilots can survive Hopp-Equation travel. Survived as prey in Cathead for a year, evading Killers through 'ten thousand kilometers of alleys.'

At the Convocation: Surname and citizenship lost, bone splinters affecting vision and wits. Thomas credits 'Paul with his broken crown' for the magic of their entrance.

Fate: Dies at the scaffold in the forerunner wave, as he dreamed he would during passage.

Evita The Child-Witch / Devil-Kid

Ancient woman in young body. Sister of Adam. Consort to multiple Salic Emperors. 'The most beautiful woman on Astrobe.'

Soft hair that seems to have smoke on it, roiling black and now quieting to brown or gold. And are her eyes green or gray or blue? Doesn't appear more than seventeen, yet has 'been battling principalities and powers for a long time.'

At the Gathering: She doesn't come through the wall, she comes through the door, smashing and splintering it with a sudden shock of force.

At the Convocation: Thomas calls her 'the child-witch with the two opposite auras about her.'

Fate: Kills and dismembers Foreman with George, Maxwell, and Rimrock. Hangs his piece on the Judas Tree. They do not get Evita.

Rimrock The Oceanic Man

Ansel with telepathic powers. Guides and warns the party. 'A transfigured ansel' who has 'crossed the line.'

The seal-like Oceanic Man communicates mentally and has formidable cutting weapons: slicers three feet long.

At the Gathering: I be an eagle. I soar. It's the last night of the world, and we are not sure what the new world will be like. I've brought old rum, and brandy for those of a more barbarous taste.

At the Convocation: Oceanic, communicating unknown ways, appearing as a grotesque rubber-nosed animal.

Fate: Helps tear Foreman apart. The programmed guards get George and Maxwell and Rimrock, adding their blood to the transcendental yeast.

Walter Copperhead The Seer / The Necromancer

Crude man from Cathead with precognitive powers. Can 'go through walls.' Studies entrails for divination.

Was a prisoner under sentence of death. Escaped by walking through walls: It isn't difficult. I believe that it has been insufficiently tried.

At the Gathering: Predicts Thomas's death with certainty: 'Oh, yes, it will be to his death.' Earlier predicted his own death and the transformation of Scrivener and Slider.

At the Convocation: Necromancer, no better than an astrologer. Thomas credits 'the Copperhead with his occult stuff.'

Fate: Is part of the forerunner wave, though he must know it is futile. Dies around the foot of the scaffold/on steps—as he predicted.

Adam The Boy Who Dies

Evita's brother. Dies repeatedly to avoid growing up. 'Good at dying.' His coming 'always signifies death.'

Handsome, like a nude Greek Youth statue, yet seems Jewish. Appears in Paul's passage dreams dying 'cavalierly in battle again and again.'

At the Rescue: Adam is the crest, reaching the scaffold and touching Thomas before guards fling him down. He rises brokenly.

Prophecy: Yes, it will be his death. And my final one.' Asked if Battersea is wrong: 'No, he isn't wrong... But many of the details will have to be changed.

Fate: Dies magnificently—as he always did. His 'final' death, though he has died many times before.

Father Oddopter The Fisher-Priest

Green-robed monk of the Order of Saint Klingensmith. Fishes for hydras—'the killing of the Devil.'

A blackish man with a hint of deep green. Says mass at Goslar where the uncanny miracle came shockingly and vividly alive at consecration. Catches Commer's Condors in nets.

Ritual: 'Now!' clangs the green-robe, like the underwater belfry of Saint Lo.' Leads the attack on the hydra with Paul and Evita.

Fate: Killed by a blow between throat and lorica during the lightning battle on Electric Mountain.

Maxwell The Avatar

Body-changer who can inhabit corpses. 'Part Programmed' in origin, a 'spook.'

What is it in me that survives? I'm myself part programmed... How can they destroy me in one machine and I survive in another machine?

At the Gathering: Appears as 'a shabby old lady' who comes in through the wall. It's just an old body I found. It isn't my own. Later: 'Yes, Maxwell, that's the name I couldn't think of.'

At the Execution: Helps tear Foreman apart with Evita, George, and Rimrock.

Fate: His mountain body is destroyed. He returns in an old woman's manufactured body, helps kill Foreman, and is then killed by the guards.

Scrivener The Chronicler

Recites the legends of sleeping kings. 'Part Programmed' according to Maxwell. Keeper of stories about Ouden and the mechanical men.

Initially supports the Dream. After Charles identifies him as a machine, Scrivener rejects Ouden and commits himself to defending his companions.

Fate: Copperhead predicts he and Slider will change persons/souls in final day. Killed by Programmed Killers on Electric Mountain.

Slider The Doubter

The slight, pale companion who doubts whether the Promise applies to Astrobe.

Seen as opposite of Scrivener. The Killers don't trail him as he is of their own species, yet he denies being Programmed.

On the Promise: Slider doubts that Astrobians are the nations or world to which the old Promise was addressed. Scrivener, not Slider, supplies the confident response that they make their own promise.

Fate: Left alive and gibbering on Electric Mountain, ignored by the Killers. No later appearance is narrated.

George the Syrian The Host

Shopkeeper who hosts the wake. Runs an aromatics shop in Cosmopolis and a 'poor-people snuff' shop in Cathead.

I don't know what a dromedary is, I don't know what a sand dune is, and I sure don't know what a syrian is. The name was hung onto me, I believe, because I have a beak instead of a nose.

At the Execution: Helps tear Foreman apart with Evita, Maxwell, and Rimrock.

Tale: Tells how the world begins with 'one syrian and one sand dune... If the syrian goes behind the dune, there is hope.'

Fate: The programmed guards get George and Maxwell and Rimrock, adding their blood to the transcendental yeast.

Battersea Giant Lunger

Military leader of rescue attempt. Former general on frontier settlement worlds before joining 'the Cathead movement.'

The scow-master from Cathead rubs his hands together like a general before battle, which is what he is. Giant lunger, leads the planned noon rescue.

Plan: We snatch the Thomas... He is King till he dies, and he will not die tomorrow. We have support in places you would never guess. Millions are secretly sick of the golden Thing.

Fate: His noon rescue is forestalled by Foreman's betrayal. As the world ends, Battersea and his men mob towards Centrality Square under their Hand-of-Vengeance banner.

Shanty Buff Shanty

Giant, fast lunger from Cathead. Coins the phrase 'The Eagles were gathering.'

Looks like the eternal pilgrim with his hat on his head and his staff in his hand. Nearly as huge as Battersea, and faster. Fixes the door Evita smashed: 'It's better than new.'

At the Rescue: Buff Shanty and Paul are in it, driving with great impetus equal to that of many men.

Fate: Dies with the forerunner wave. The source does not specify who dies first.

What the Eagles Represent

• The remnant who refuse the Astrobe Dream—'Millions are secretly sick of the golden Thing.'

• The broken, the irregular, the maladjusted—those whose brokenness qualifies them for true vision.

• The faith that survives in Cathead and the Feral Lands when it has died in Golden Astrobe.

• The 'transcendental yeast' whose blood may seed the new world.

• The human capacity for 'gallows humor' that the Programmed cannot understand or crack.

This is one thing that the Programmed cannot do. They do not become droll and mellow, nor do they hold wakes. Programmed people have no gallows humor at all.

Mechanical Killers

Iron Dogs, Tin Scurrae, Clanking Fools

The Mechanical Killers

Mechanical enforcers pursue threats to the Astrobe Dream. Individual machines can be destroyed, but replacements continue their assignments. Their relentless pursuit contrasts with the changing loyalties and doubts of the people they hunt.

The Killers respond to allegiance to the Vision. Their changing behavior toward More makes his inner accommodation and resistance visible.

Names and Epithets

Official
Programmed KillersMechanical Killers
Derogatory
Iron DogsClanking FoolsTin ScurraeTin CansMonster MachinesHeel-hounds
Functional Types
HoundsHound-CatsBears

The various names reflect different perceptions: official terminology ('Programmed'), contemptuous epithets from their prey ('iron dogs,' 'clanking fools'), and functional categories ('Bears' for spaceport guards, 'Hounds' for stalkers).

Types of Killers

The Bears
Spaceport Guards

Huge and lumbering mechanical guards stationed at spaceports. Programmed for patrol, defense, and counterattack. React to theft signals like Paul's stolen grasshopper.

Characteristics: Their primary aim is securing stolen property; killing is secondary. They are territorial—blindly react to intrusion by other mechanical types into their area.

When Paul steals Foreman's grasshopper, Bears arrive 'first, too fast,' drag him out with grapples, wound him severely, and one 'clasped him to crush him to death.' They are forced to release him repeatedly to smash attacking Hounds who intrude into their zone.

The Hounds
Stalkers and Hunters
Also called 'Hound-Cats'

The specific group programmed for stalking and direct assault. Hunt fugitives relentlessly across years if necessary. React to 'Escape signals' when their prey attempts off-world flight.

Characteristics: 'Remorseless,' 'stiff-gaited,' 'stiff and bristling.' They close in 'blind to everything else' when sensing their target. They hunted Paul for a full year after his citizenship was revoked.

At the spaceport, the Hounds sense Paul's escape attempt and intrude into the Bears’ territory, leading to a chaotic battle between the two mechanical types. Three hounds are smashed at once by the bear holding Paul.

Standard Patrols
General Enforcement

Standard Killers patrol in groups of nine. They have purplish nightmarish ogre faces and stiff gaits. They enforce the Astrobe Dream throughout civilized space.

Characteristics: Their behavior changes based on target status. When Thomas professes loyalty to the Dream, they follow but smile quizzically, not threatening. When he wavers internally, they sense the change, cease their quizzical waiting, remember their purpose and move to kill.

Vulnerabilities: Battersea knows their 'nexus and centers'—weak points. Father Oddopter instructs fighters to 'Drive down in the narrow slot' between neck-piece and lorica/breast-plate to strike the 'relay center.'

undefined

The Replacement Principle

Programmed Killers can be destroyed, but another is instantly created elsewhere with the exact same assignment. This makes defeating them ultimately futile—you cannot kill an assignment, only delay it.

Example: During the Electric Mountain battle, Adam topples one Killer backward off the mountain, causing it to fall 1000 meters. But another is instantly created elsewhere with the same assignment.

Within the pursuit system, surrender to the Dream can stop an individual's hunt. Destroying a machine does not abolish its assignment; changing the system itself is the larger problem facing the novel's characters.

The Salic Emperors

The Killers assigned themselves to destroy every reigning Salic Emperor in Goslar. No Emperor has reigned a full year; many lasted less than a month. Charles the 612th had reigned less than twenty hours when Thomas's party arrived.

A peculiarity: when an emperor is killed, a replacement is instantly selected at Wu Town's university and starts for Goslar immediately. Emperor and Killer, each instantly replaced—a dark parody of resurrection.

The final passage at Goslar gives 599 skulls. An earlier statement of 611 predecessors with thirteen missing would give 598. The source's figures differ, but neither supports a count above six hundred skulls.

Paul's Year as Prey

After his citizenship was revoked, Paul survived a full year in Cathead evading 'remorseless stiff-gaited Killers.' This experience qualifies him for the mission to retrieve Thomas More.

Skills: Paul has personally killed a dozen Killers. During the spaceport battle, Battersea is specifically credited with knowing the nexus and centers of every sort of mechanical.

Loophole: Programmed Killers are normally inhibited from killing Astrobe citizens but target 'offenders' like Paul whose citizenship has been revoked. Paul exploits this status ambiguity.

During the spaceport battle, Paul kills a human masquerading as a Programmed Killer—revealing that humans are fighting on both sides.

Thomas More's Relationship with the Killers

Initial Hunting

The Killers hunt More from his arrival. Allies help him escape; by Chapter 9 he reports nine attempts on his life.

Electric Mountain

In Chapter 7 the Killers climb toward the company under the electrical clouds. Scrivener, Adam, Oddopter, and Maxwell's body are destroyed. Thomas, Paul, and Evita escape. The black cloud is not itself a form taken by the machines.

The Quizzical Period

After Thomas professes loyalty to the Astrobe Dream and makes speeches for 'the Merging Singularity,' the Killers change: They watch still, but smile quizzically, not threatening him. They follow but do not attack.

The Change

When Thomas's 'old part' surges against the Dream in Chapter 10, The Programmed Killers sense his internal change, cease their quizzical waiting, remember their purpose. They herd him into the dead-end alley where he meets the Nine.

Presidential Guards

The same order that hunts dissenters guards More as president and enforces his sentence after the final refusal.

“Cannot something be done about the Programmed Killers? They nearly had me last night again... They make me jumpy... they have now made nine attempts on my life. And they become trickier. They aren't mere machines...”

The Battle on Electric Mountain

The first high pinnacle of the Thunder Mountains. The peak interacts strangely with approaching Killers, and lightning storms provide both danger and opportunity.

Evita spots them: It is a black one [cloud], and below us. The Programmed Killers have come in full patrol... This isn't the death I had planned for us all, Holy Thomas.

Tactics

Defense: The party rolls boulders and fights hand-to-hand. Father Oddopter creates a 'hand-knife on pole'—an improvised spear—for greater reach.

Vulnerability: Oddopter shouts instructions: strike the 'nexus... relay center' in a 'narrow slot' between neck-piece and lorica/breast-plate.

Climbing: The Killers climb more slowly and less well than the humans, but do not tire or rest.

Casualties
Scrivener: Smashed dead'—as a hybrid, 'the machines knew the diagram of him as a machine.
Adam: Dies 'in glorious gore, howling defiance' during a thunder-smash. Evita notes, 'He was good at dying... He had done it before.'
Father Oddopter: Dies from a 'smash between the throat and the lorica' during the second major lightning strike.
Maxwell: Body 'smashed' in the darkness. But 'Maxwell had a trick of turning up again.'

Escape: Thomas, Paul, and Evita escape during the third lightning bolt, following Evita's intuition down the spire while 'swift iron trackers' pursue.

Slider alone is left alive—a gibbering creature... disregarded, since he represented no threat to the Dream.

Scrivener's Final Stand

Scrivener is uncertain whether he is a Programmed Person or 'old-recension human' due to family legend of Programmed admixture. Emperor Charles wants to kill him, calling him a machine with a sender in his head attracting Killers.

Last night I rejected him! [Ouden]... What am I now? I am not machine and I am not man... It was the Nothing that I rejected. He becomes 'alien to both his recensions.'

Battle: He fights the Killers howling: 'Me they do not disregard! I threaten their thing!... Backwards and down you go, you clanking Devil! I'll battle you all while there's life left in me.'

Death: He had opted for a man very late, and the machines knew the diagram of him as a machine. The Programmed Raiders smashed Scrivener dead there.

Left on the pinnacle as a 'dead hybrid whose final pattern shows that he opted for human late.'

What the Killers Really Are

Surface: On the surface: autonomous enforcers, garbage disposals, ultimate police, wardens of the Astrobe Dream.

Connection: Their service to the Dream connects them with the Nine's system. Their apparent sensitivity to inward allegiance is part of their menace, but ordinary mechanical guards also make errors and clash over conflicting assignments.

They hunt threats to a Dream whose secret endpoint is Holy Nothingness. They kill to preserve a system designed to end all life. They are the Dream's teeth—and the Dream devours itself.

More increasingly doubts that the Killers are merely ordinary machines. The novel connects their enforcement with the Nine while distinguishing the pursuers from the human-looking Programmed Persons.

Bestiary of Astrobe

Creatures of the Feral Lands

Bestiary of Astrobe

The Feral Lands and Their Creatures

The Feral Lands teem with dangerous life. Thomas calls it 'a plenitude of game'—finding more vitality here than in civilized Astrobe. 'I would bet that a good hunting man could live well here,' he says, seeing an intense, rewarding life.

Paul confirms he lived there as a hunting man for a few months while hiding. There are still a few thousand hunters on Astrobe. The life is intense, rewards intangible but deep for some, but hunters don't live to old age.

Slider expresses the civilized view: 'We class them with excrement.' Maxwell considers them 'less real than creatures in dreams.' But Evita knows them: They're good to eat. People ate them when I was a kid.

The Food Chain

Base: The jerusalem coney, along with the dutch-fish and rambler's-ox, forms the food base of the Feral Lands. Everything lives on them, or on what eats them.

Predators: Predators include direwolves, porches-panther, hydra, birds, and twenty other species capable of slicing up and eating a man.

Apex: The porches-panther eats direwolves, lazarus-lions, rouks, and hydras. The text does not provide a predator for it, but absence from this account is not proof that none exists.

Oddopter calls the particular hydra they hunt the Devil and says the Devil may take other forms. Hydras also appear within Paul's account of ordinary predation.

The Creatures

Jerusalem Coney
Prey / Food Base

A curious hopping creature, mostly rabbit-sized but some smaller or much larger. They move indiscriminately—into ponds, underwater, high into trees with accurate hops, through dense brush a snake couldn't traverse.

Too quick for Thomas or Paul to catch. They are 'all around them' in the Feral Lands.

Ecology: Along with dutch-fish and rambler's-ox, the coney is the food base. Preyed upon by direwolves, porches-panther, hydra, birds, and all predators.

Thomas notes the animal names sound like Earth's. Paul corrects him: Only the names are like those of Earth. On Earth there are no animals at all like those around us.

Direwolf (Dire-wolf)
Large Predator

Could take an Earth ox's head and horns in one bite and the body in two more.

Paul emphasizes its size and killing power; no pack-hunting behavior is specified.

Thomas pits 'a bow-necked Middlesex ox against any animal on this scurvy bowl.' Paul assures him the direwolf would win easily.

A direwolf eats a natural ansel like a jerusalem coney, but would eat a transfigured ansel like a man, not with an easy mind. The predators know the difference between natural and transcendent prey.

Lazarus-Lion
Large Predator

Could do the same to the larger rambler's-ox as the direwolf does to cattle.

The lazarus eats people, unlike the rouks who just crucify them.

Paul supposes the lazarus-lion 'appreciates the flavor' of the hunters it catches.

Porches-Panther
Major Predator

The apex predator of Astrobe's Feral Lands.

Paul says it kills and eats direwolves, lazarus-lions, rouks, and hydras.

Oddopter names a porches-panther gone musk as another possible form of the Devil.

Rouk
Intelligent Predator

'Kill people for fun' and hang the bodies as warnings. Paul points to a nearby cliff with a thousand human skeletons hung on thorn bushes by rouks.

Similar to how men on Earth hung wolves on fences—but the rouks are the hunters, men the prey.

There's even a tale the King Rouk pays a bounty for men killed and hung by rouks.

Intelligent cruelty made bestial. Uniquely among predators, they kill not to eat but to display.

Hydra
Supernatural Predator / Devil-Form

A thousand-kilogram bulk swallowing the bait in one gulp, thirty-meter tentacles reaching blindly, a big middle eye mad with malevolence.

Can gobble anything in water and snap ten meters out of it, once taking six men in one bite.

Its bulk surges clear of the water, accompanied by a lightning-like corona discharge and blinding aura. It is the Devil made flesh.

Father Oddopter: Today's Devil was large, but it takes other forms like a mad direwolf or a porches-panther gone musk. We must kill it daily to limn his limits.

The Bait: The bait used to catch it: a fat, black, quivering discoid thing with an angry-toothed mouth covering one-third of its circuit. It weighs 150 kilograms and could snap a man in two. The monk calls it merely bait, like a grasshopper caught for a hook.

Rambler's-Ox
Prey / Food Base

Large prey animal forming part of the food base along with jerusalem coneys and dutch-fish.

Ecology: Part of the foundation that supports the Feral Lands’ predator hierarchy.

Larger than an Earth ox. The lazarus-lion can take one 'in three bites.'

Dutch-Fish (Dutchfish)
Prey / Food Base

Sea creatures forming part of the food base. Sea-gleaners bring in scow-loads for fish meal.

Ecology: Along with jerusalem coneys and rambler's-ox, the food foundation of Astrobe's ecology.

In Cathead, the bodies of plague victims are sometimes weighed with the fish because they aren't up to the fish in phosphor and sulphur and are hard on the grinders.

Kastroides
Builder

Etymology: The name suggests a beaver-like builder; the novel does not explain its derivation.

Build aerial ponds in the Feral Lands.

The party travels sometimes skirting large aerial ponds built by kastroides.

Its ponds occupy the interwoven vegetation above water, part of a landscape in which the travelers struggle to find firm ground.

Commer's Condor
Large Bird

Large birds caught for food by hunting parties.

On Electric Mountain, during the hallucination zone, a Commer's Condor swoops near, cries "Thomas More is a fink!"

Father Oddopter catches a Commer's Condor in a net. The party tears it apart, eats it raw.

Wooly Ram
Ritual Animal

Animals found and barbecued during the fools’ carnival before Thomas's execution.

Wooly Rams are found somewhere, and spitted and barbecued over the bonfires, about fifty people devouring each Wooly Ram as they tear it apart in pieces, half seared and half raw.

The feast of the Wooly Ram has not been held on Astrobe for more than three hundred years, and only antiquarians could know about it.

Oddopter calls More a wooly ram with a double sign and dismisses Charles as a wether. The feast repeats the ram imagery later.

Bot-Flies
Vermin / Omen

Associated with violence and death. They appear where blood has been spilled.

Bot-flies splutter and roar over slippery blood in the roadway and common room of the Naked Sailor after the ambush.

Their presence signals carnage and the presence of Killers.

Ansels: Natural and Transfigured

The Line Between Animal and Person

Wild Ansels
