Natural ansels inhabit Astrobe's waters. Rimrock's account of ascent from the physical ocean is linked metaphorically with an interior ocean of dreams.

Their votes were disallowed in Astrobe elections after ansel leaders registered millions of wild ocean ansels.

Hunters kill them. A direwolf eats a natural ansel like a jerusalem coney.

Transfiguration

An ansel that crossed the line becomes entirely different from a natural ansel. Paul doesn't know how the new species is acquired, but all species know the difference.

A direwolf eats a natural ansel like a jerusalem coney, but would eat a transfigured ansel like a man, not with an easy mind. There's a difference between natural and transcendent prey known to meat-eaters.

The green-robe calls it 'impossible theology': A creature already alive shouldn't receive a soul and intelligence, yet this seems the case with exceptional ansels.

Animals are disturbed after eating humans, and Rimrock would be human by this test.

Paul confirms Rimrock would eat ansel meat and has, but doesn't care for it—overrated. An ansel 'feels no repugnance' at eating natural ansels.

Sprites and Ghosts

The Spirit Ecology

Sprites

Sextus Empiricus wrote that every environment has its sprite.

Father Oddopter appears and tells Thomas: Sextus Empiricus wrote of both of us. You are a sprite too, who just thinks himself a man because he was raised by humans.

Taibhse

Meaning: 'Ghosts' or 'revenants' in Gaelic.

Emperor Charles calls Maxwell and Thomas 'Taibhse'—having intuition as Emperor.

Father Oddopter explains ghosts are the same as Taibhse—those who leave bodies and heads behind them. Evita is called 'black-hearted kid' who is Taibhse.

Thomas asks if superstition is rampant. The green-robe supposes so, noting 'psychic force/libido' is strong—as once on Old Earth (Africas, Haitis). Astrobe's nature was tamed recently.

The Feral Ecology

This is a salt that has not lost its savor! Thomas contrasts the Feral Lands with 'insipid civilized Astrobe,' seeing potential for 'a better blending.'

Astrobe cannot be more exposed to its backlands. These things are worse than death and need to be hidden away forever.

The Hunter's Life

The life is intense, rewards intangible but deep for some.

Hunters don't live to old age.

There are still a few thousand hunters on Astrobe.

Twenty other species around them are capable of slicing up and eating a man.

Political Parties

The Party Jungle of Astrobe

Political Parties of Astrobe

The Party Jungle

Chapter 9 lists many overlapping political factions. Their names mix recognizable political positions with wordplay. The Nine claim broad influence across them, while the novel also shows opposition beyond the official public consensus.

In Chapter 10 the Nine claim to control More's path through several parties and threaten to make a replacement in one hour. More names people who would recognize the substitute.

The Evolution of Astrobe Elections

One Person One Vote

Old Earth idea

The original democratic system, imported from Earth.

The Weighted Vote

Additional votes awarded for distinguished service. Most ranks carry votes; entertainers might get accolades. Wealth is complex: Kingmaker might have a thousand votes, while another rich man had only a quarter vote due to unpopularity.

• Cathead and Barrio citizens get only a quarter vote each under blanket penalty.

• Ansels and other intelligent non-humans get one-eighth vote.

A scandal occurred when ansel leaders registered millions of wild ocean ansels; their votes were disallowed, restricting voting to land-living Astrobe creatures.

Sensing Machines

Current system (Vote abolished)

The Vote itself is done away with, replaced by sensing machines that work on everyone's auras, keeping a running record. They assess and compile the total weight of opinion and choice on Astrobe.

'The Weighted Vote carried out with honesty and justice.' Fine intellect and judgment have more effect than notions; strong personality weighs more than lesser persons, while frustration subtracts. They cannot be tampered with.

Cathead and the Barrio exert unexpectedly strong influence. The claim that their concentration of intellect is impossible is ironic. A modification to discount anti-Dream judgments is being planned but will not be ready for this election.

Establishment Coalition

Parties associated with the governing order. These groupings organize the guide's discussion; they are not official classifications given in the novel.

Center Party

More's party, supported by the three Masters. Foreman says they are unsure whether Pottscamp belongs to it, or even whether he is a man.

The Center Party is satirical—there is no middle in the cosmic conflict between Being and Nothing.

Compromise Parties First, Second, and Third Compromise

The Third Compromise Party is one the Nine work through to control Thomas. Certain parties they don't want joining them, as they swing to clear winners and cause trouble.

Programmed Liberal Party

One of the establishment factions. The name itself is an oxymoron—the Programmed have no liberty.

Opposition Factions

Parties with names suggesting resistance or refusal. Their full platforms and degree of independence are not supplied.

Intransigents Also: Reformed Intransigents

The name suggests a form of opposition. The text does not establish a complete platform or prove that every act of opposition is theatrical.

Obstructionists Also: New Obstructionists

The name suggests a form of opposition. The text does not establish a complete platform or prove that every act of opposition is theatrical.

Ideological Parties

Parties organized around specific beliefs or constituencies.

Demos

One of the parties the Nine work through. Greek for 'the people'—another ironic name in a society where individuality is being erased.

Solidarity Labor Party

Labor faction—though meaningful labor has largely vanished in golden Astrobe.

Mechanicus

Party presumably aligned with Programmed interests.

Unreconstructeds

'Humans only.' A resistance faction rejecting human-Programmed synthesis.

Ochlos

'Blessed by Ouden.' Greek for 'mob' or 'rabble.' A party explicitly aligned with Nothingness.

The name and association with Ouden connect this faction to the novel's politics of nothingness.

Eccentric and Opportunist

Parties defined by opportunism, wordplay, or obscure purposes.

Hatrack Party Also called Conglomerate Party

One of the parties the Nine work through. Swings to clear winners and causes trouble—'We want our hands unbound when we go to work after we have won.'

Kiss of Death Party

Another party the Nine use. The name is grimly literal—their support is fatal to genuine reform.

Hive / Golden Drones

Insect imagery—the collective over the individual.

Penultimate / Ultimate Parties

Named for eschatological positions—next-to-last and last things.

Censor / Pyramid / New Salt

Various minor factions with obscure platforms.

Wordplay Parties

Party names built around a sequence of puns. Their exact platforms should not be inferred solely from their names.

Esthetics

Its name suggests aesthetics and beauty; the novel does not develop a full platform.

Anesthetics

Its name turns the previous party's word toward numbness, inviting a comparison with the Dream's lethargy.

Local Anesthetics

'Jokesters, disregarded.' Their opinions count for nothing. Politics reduced to puns.

The progression Esthetics → Anesthetics → Local Anesthetics mirrors Astrobe's decay from beauty to numbness to irrelevance.

The Crank Party

A Party of One

The Man

Not wild-eyed, but dull-eyed, speaks in singsong.

Rudely calls Thomas 'Thomas Momus, the Big Boys’ Toy.' Claims leadership of a certified party and demands fair hearing by law.

The Party

The Crank: 'Only myself, doubting Thomas.' Certified via bureaucratic quirk allowing a one-man party.

“I organized it and named it. I am the Crank and I make myself heard.”

Platform

Against all false things.' Battles 'Humanism which has no meat, and Materialism which has no bones.

Thomas likes the phrase—'doesn't mean anything'—and plans to use it himself.

I see the parties at an end. All are dying. Soon only my own party will remain.

Grievances Against Astrobe

• Compulsory pornography and ethics equal time in schools

• Perversion and normalcy given equal space (though normalcy gained then)

• Evaluators allowed to terminate marriages

• Schools teaching only things in accord with the Golden Dream

• Law denying offspring to private persons

• Psychologs made a privileged class with tampering powers

• Mechanical brain tampering permitted

The human person should be inviolate. Adjustability charts shouldn't be everything. Man should choose his own occupation and unhappiness.

Thomas's Response: 'No, I do not, Crank, on no point whatsoever.' Thomas rejects every grievance, affirms the Dream.

The Misidentification

The Crank thinks Thomas is 'doubting Thomas the Apostle'—a hero who betrayed an old mountebank.

No I am not. You are badly confused.

The Crank claims Thomas owes his popularity to this false identification.

Thomas orders his 'contrivances' (Programmed Persons) to throw the Crank out. 'I hate it!' the Crank roars. 'Damn all mechanicals to the reclamation heap!'

The Crank exposes coercion that More currently accepts. His confused identifications and refusal to endure Cathead make him an awkward witness, but the expulsion shows More's intolerance of dissent.

How the Nine Control the Parties

Northprophet reveals in Chapter 10 how political control actually works:

Multi-Party Infiltration

The Nine claim to work through several parties. Their assertion of complete control is challenged by Foreman, Cathead, and the larger opposition Battersea describes.

Path Control

They control his path. Thomas's political rise is orchestrated, not organic.

Brain Snakes

'Snakes in your head!' The Nine's extensions nest in Thomas's mind, speaking through his mouth. Paul warns: You've been saying many things... that don't sound like you. It's only a mechanical trick.

The Patsy

The Nine threaten to manufacture a replacement More in one hour. More disputes how successfully that substitute could deceive his acquaintances.

Proctor Revealed

Proctor is their own artificial man... programmed lucky. One of the Big Three is himself a Programmed Person.

The political system channels choices toward the Dream. Its designers propose discounting dissenting judgments, but the change is not yet implemented at More's election. This distinction leaves room for the unexpected strength of Cathead and other opponents.

Thomas on the Campaign Trail

Thomas campaigns and enjoys it. He excels at rhetoric—the noblest rhetor, with a clear touch and intricate lash to his tongue.

I cannot move mountains but can move the world ahead, implementing the Astrobe dream. Perfection is in stages; obstacles will be removed, unhealthy growth excised. He preaches sanity, perfect human-Programmed symbiosis, all minds and bodies merging into one.

Paul's Warning: You were talking nonsense, you know. I wonder if you were even listening to yourself.

Thomas's Admission: “Paul, I said words... but there were other words that I did not say... Somebody else spoke some of those words out of my mouth.”

Paul's Explanation: It's one of the oldest tricks of the Programmed. They crawl into your mind and take control. It's only a mechanical trick.

Thomas cannot kick the snakes out. His will isn't what it used to be. He begins to sound like one of them: 'We should all strive for the synthesis, part man and part Programmed... submerge ourselves in our mechanical brothers for the good of all.' Paul warns: 'They'll eat us alive if we do, Thomas.'

Embedded Tales

Embedded Tales and Passage Dreams

Psychic Space Debris

Past Master is suffused with tales within tales—passage dreams experienced during Hopp-Equation travel, stories told at the wake on the night before the execution, legends recited on the mountain climb, and allegories whose 'cryptic meaning' even Code-Crackers-Supreme cannot break.

Hopp-Equation space contains 'psychic space debris'—fragments of billions of minds, poignant, comic, horrifying, exalting episodes. The dreams compress approximately five years of psychic experience into one month. Only the 'maladjusted' can stand the passages; well-adjusted pilots crack up.

Passage Dreams

Twenty Thousand Dreams in Ninety-Second Intervals

During Hopp-Equation travel, passengers experience vivid, self-contained dream episodes lasting approximately 90 seconds each. Paul experiences approximately 20,000 such dreams. Thomas, traveling with him, dreams as well—his visions sinking into his mind's cellar, to resurface when he meets those persons.

Recurring Dream Figures

Adam

A boy who dies cavalierly in battle again and again, thus avoiding growing up. Dying is his only real skill.

“It is death, it is death. I am not born again... It is always another of the same name.”

Adam later dies on Electric Mountain and at the scaffold. Chapter 3 also describes a death during the ambush while questioning whether the event belongs to dream or waking time.

Adam's Sister (The Childwitch)

A 'childwitch who decided to go to Hell before she died.' Paul is unsure if he knew her previously, knows her only in dreams, or will know her later.

The childwitch anticipates Evita, identified as Adam's sister in Chapter 5. Her age and willingness to enter Hell recur in Evita's account of herself.

The Oceanic Man

Thomas meets 'an oceanic man named Rimrock' in his passage dreams—not odd in dream.

The ansel Rimrock, who will guide and warn Thomas throughout the novel. Ansels were in human unconscious before being found on Astrobe.

The Composite Female

Thomas encounters a female creature who is simultaneously Succubus, Eve, Lilith, Judith, Mary, Valkyrie.

Evita again—ancient woman in young body, consort to emperors, killer of Foreman, torn between damnation and holiness.

The Spider with a Lion's Head

One of three quick dreams Thomas has of 'three unknown men.' This one represents Kingmaker.

Kingmaker's dual nature: the spider's web of power, the lion's heraldic nobility. 'The Lion' is his epithet; the spider suggests manipulation.

The Peculiar Fox

Second of Thomas's three dream-men. Represents Proctor.

Proctor is 'The Sleek Fox'—cunning, lucky, ultimately revealed as a Programmed Person himself.

The Hawk Shuffling Shells

Third dream-man: a hawk shuffling shells at a table, and one shell was different. Represents Foreman.

Foreman is 'Hawk-Face'—the shell game suggests his manipulations, the 'different shell' perhaps Thomas himself or the transcendent yeast.

Tall Tales in the Space Debris

Not all dreams are heavy. Light vital stuff and tall tales drift there too—every tall tale ever told, still drifting in Hopp-Equation space.

Sour John's Emerald Kidney

Tall Tale / Allegorical Dream

Dreamer: Paul (who 'becomes' Sour John during the dream)

Setup: John Sourwine ('Sour John'), an Earthman from centuries before Paul's time, has a kidney that vitrified into fine, jewel-like green glass due to his diet of alcohol, wormwood, and green snails.

Complication: At Ghazikhan (then India), Sour John sees a great idol whose emerald eye—nearly a foot in diameter—is worth $11 million. He decides he needs the money for 'expensive habits.'

The Heist: Sour John has the ship's boy help surgically remove his vitrified kidney, then trims, lathes, and buffs it to perfection—'the most beautiful kidney in the world.' At midnight, he climbs the 500-foot sheer idol, pries out the emerald, substitutes his kidney (a perfect fit), and climbs down. He sells the emerald in Karachi for $11 million and lives high—but can no longer drink water with only one kidney.

Twist: Three years later he learns that the substituted kidney is now valued at thirteen million dollars.

Punchline: 'I figure I lost two million dollars on the deal,' Paul says, waking up.

Paul interrupts his own dream, correcting that Ghazikhan isn't a seaport (information from a psychteacher machine). His Sour John persona retorts: 'I say it is a sea-port.'

Allegorical meaning: One possible reading contrasts a product of bodily excess with an apparently priceless sacred object. The exchange complicates ordinary judgments about purity, value, and loss. The reversal of expected value can be compared with Cathead's preference for costly human life over sterile perfection. The novel does not explicitly identify each element of the story with a Programmed faction.

Rhium and Antirhium

Apocalyptic Dream

Dreamer: Paul

Mission: Paul courses at fantastic speed toward twin stars Rhium and Antirhium. Instructions: 'Hurry... they seem of no consequence, but they are the governor of the universe. Somebody is tampering with them.'

Discovery: Arriving closer than anyone before, Paul sees the stars revolve joined by a long steel chain—explaining their tight orbits and their role as 'governor.'

Saboteur: A small green creature with a monkey's body and a gargoyle's head is sawing through the chain, nearly finished. It breaks a blade, replaces it, sticks its green tongue out at Paul, and makes three more strokes.

Cataclysm: The chain breaks. Rhium and Antirhium swing out of orbit. 'Fifty billion billion stars went nova, and then blacked out to nothing. The universe had eaten itself and was gone forever.'

Aftermath: A space captain arrives furiously: 'I told you to hurry!' His face melts like wax and vanishes. Paul says, 'I did hurry.' His own face melts; he vanishes too.

Coda: Foreman's voice: Is it quite finished? If it is quite finished, then perhaps we can begin to construct a new universe. It's all right. It worked out well. I meant you to be too late.

Allegorical meaning: The names recall Rhium and Antirrhium, opposing Greek promontories described in Strabo's Geography, 8.2.3. The novel does not explain why these names are assigned to the stars. The broken chain anticipates cosmic destruction, while Foreman's speech within the dream anticipates his theory of renewal.

The Sleeping Kings

Scrivener's Legends

Scrivener recounts versions of sleeping-king legends. They suggest a pattern for More's mission, but his versions need not coincide with every historical tradition.

“Every Old-Earth Nation, my grandmother told me, had its mythos of a sleeping king who would one day awaken and rule again in a new golden age.”

Alaric (The Goths)

Buried underneath the Busento River—its course changed for the burial and changed back to flow over him.

He was to arise again one day and lead the Gothic element, 'that shaggy thing that is the basis of a dozen peoples.'

Arthur of Britain (The British)

In kingly sleep in an ensorceled room at the bottom of a lake.

Awaiting Britain's need.

Brian Boru (The Irish)

Buried on horseback in a pit with great stones heaped around him.

When he wakens he will scatter the stones and ride again.

El Cid (The Spanish)

Not buried at all but riding forever a horse in death-sleep over dark moors in Estremadura.

Still riding.

Barbarossa (The Germanies)

Asleep at a table in a cave in a mountain, his beard grown through the table.

Waiting.

Henry VIII (England)

Thomas jests: immured with six wives in a peculiar arrangement.

(Thomas's dark humor.)

Kennedy (America)

Riding in a car.

Added by Scrivener.

Roadstorm (Astrobe)

Marooned in Star King.

An Astrobian sleeping king.

The Mechanical Men's Sleeping King

Early mechanical men wished for a mythos—a mystique, a god, a hero, a sleeping king—like humans had. They searched Old Earth backward. Found a small broken gear train in an Egyptian tomb: hard wood cogs, bronze bearings, unknown use. Clumsy, earliest true mechanical spirit. They brought it to Astrobe as their sleeping king.

Humans snickered.

Then the Celestial Nothingness came. Ouden dismissed the toy king: Tut away such toys... I am your god and your king. Ouden became god and king for the Programmed Persons since—and soon for all beings. 'He grows and grows, and all the other kings die.'

More is brought alive from his past by Chronometanastasis. Symbolically, this recalls the return of a sleeping ruler, without making the technology a literal resurrection of a corpse.

Tales at the Wake

The Night Before the Execution

The Eagles gather in George's shop before the execution. Their tales defeat the monitoring machines’ attempts to interpret them as code.

Automatic monitors pick up the tales but cannot make anything of them. They tie into Code-Crackers, then Code-Crackers-Supreme. Neither can crack the code—they cannot at all figure what cryptic information is concealed in the tales. This isn't code like you meet every night.

Adam's Tale: Saint Brandon and the Nineteen Monks

Teller: The boy Adam

The first human people came to Astrobe fifteen hundred years before official history records. 'By the holies, it had been Saint Brandon himself in a coracle boat that was round as a tub.' He sloshed and bounded over the Stoimenof Sea, having started in the North Atlantic on Old Earth—supposing he was still sailing the same water. He piles out when it runs onto land, and nineteen Irish monks with twinkling pates follow him out. On first arrival they find only jerusalem conies, which will not answer their questions. But Saint Brandon and his monks map out the new land with exact description. Then they get back into the coracle boat and in ninety-nine days are back in Dingle Bay where they started.

But later explorers, going out into the North Atlantic Ocean of Old Earth, don't find any such land; and they say that Saint Brandon has lied. He has not. Those later explorers had gone in prow-ships that will hold a course, not in round coracle boats that can only be steered by prayer and fasting and are likely to wander clear off the Earth.

Code-Crackers Supreme labors mightily to break the code and arrive at the cryptic meaning behind it, and they cannot do it.

'Blessed be this rum,' says Rimrock the ansel.

George's Tale: The Syrian and the Sand Dune

Teller: George the Syrian

The only thing ever left over when the world ends is one syrian and one sand dune, all other features of the world being blotted out by the terminal catastrophes. There is that terrible second or million years when nothing moves—for a second and a million years are the same when there is no movement in anything. Then the syrian goes over behind the sand dune and finds a dromedary; and together they start the world going again.

That is the way it was in the earliest version of Genesis. That is the way the world begins every time. You will hear stories about a man and a woman, or about a turtle raising the sky up from off the earth. Do not believe them. Every time the world begins it begins with a syrian and a dromedary.

“Now, I don't know what a dromedary is, I don't know what a sand dune is, and I sure don't know what a syrian is. The name was hung onto me, I believe, because I have a beak instead of a nose.”

The world will end again tomorrow. Watch then for a syrian and a sand dune. If the syrian goes behind the dune, there is hope; if he does not, or if there is neither syrian nor sand dune, then the world is done forever.

Code-Crackers-Supreme suffers a breakdown about the time George recounts this. It is not, perhaps, a serious breakdown; but it will take several hours to get code-crackers to functioning again. So the monitoring is dropped. No point in setting down what even the code-crackers cannot crack.

'Blessed be this rum,' says Evita.

The Boy Who Built a Toy

Thomas's Passage Dream / Allegory

A boy builds a clever toy. Both the boy and the toy look like Pottscamp. The toy steals, attacks, does the boy's homework, drinks from the brook—then eats the child entirely.

Was Pottscamp the toy or the guileless devoured one?

The toy consuming its maker can be read as an image of manufactured beings turning against humanity. Pottscamp's account describes a growing final generation, rather than identifying the present Nine as the final generation themselves.

The story also reflects the novel's central tragedy: humanity built Astrobe, built the Dream, built the Programmed—and will be devoured by what it made.

The Function of Embedded Tales

• They resist decoding—even Code-Crackers-Supreme cannot crack them. Truth lives in forms that mechanical analysis cannot penetrate.

• They preserve and transmit meaning through catastrophe. George's story of the syrian and the sand dune is about how stories themselves survive the end of worlds.

• They prophesy. The passage dreams show Paul his own death; Thomas dreams the men who will manipulate him; Adam's tale of Saint Brandon maps a land that 'later explorers' cannot find.

• They disturb the separation of dream and waking life. Recurring figures link the travelers’ dreams with their later encounters, leaving questions about time and identity open.

• They embody Lafferty's method. Past Master itself is a tall tale drifting in psychic space debris—a story whose 'cryptic meaning' resists easy analysis, told at the wake of a world.

The Promise

Christ Has Walked on Astrobe

The Promise

We Last Till the End of the World

In Cathead, More meets the dying Metropolitan and hears that Christ walked on Astrobe and renewed the Promise. More leaves unconvinced, but the encounter supplies a claim that challenges the Dream and remains central to the ending.

The theological question at the heart of Past Master: Does the Promise—that the Church will last till the end of the world—apply to Astrobe? Is Astrobe 'the world'? Are its inhabitants 'the nations'?

Slider's Argument Against the Promise

We Are Not the Nations

The Instruction: The Ancient Instruction was Go to All Nations. But 'we are not the Nations'—something different.

The Promise: The Promise (that the Transcendent Thing endures till the End of the World) wasn't given to 'us'—a different world.

The Mutation: Can't assume they are human. How deep is the Astrobe mutation? How many are Programmed Persons? How much programmed descent in 'old-line humans'?

Slider fears that the old Promise may not cover Astrobe and questions the depth of its human mutation.

Scrivener responds with confidence in the Dream: they are beyond the old nations and world, and make their own promise. His attitude differs from Slider's anxious doubt.

The Metropolitan of Astrobe

The Pope of Astrobe

Setting

A small medieval castle dwarfed by tenements in Cathead.

A coughing man tells Thomas: 'Nobody lives there... The Metropolitan of Astrobe dies there.' Thomas remarks on the long dying time.

Thomas knocks, hears only a low moan or rale, and enters. After passing through empty rooms, he finds a room with an old battered bed under a faded royal canopy.

The Man

A very old, thin black man, skeletal, emitting a fetid odor. Thomas thinks him dead.

Identification: He wears the fisherman's ring—identifying him as the Metropolitan, the Pope of Astrobe.

'Eaten up.' He has food and drink but 'no stomach left.' Blind, though he can make the effort to open his eyes.

Attendants

'I have five or six followers left.' Someone checks on him every few hours.

A young, filthy, coughing man enters to attend him, telling Thomas the old man was sometimes crazy, sometimes not and urging patience.

Prophecy: I will die thirty hours before yourself.

After this Metropolitan dies, a different man succeeds him and places Astrobe under interdict. The successor, formerly a renegade priest for thirty years, appears in Chapter 12.

The Recognition

Saints John and Thomas

Liturgy: The Metropolitan, eyes still closed, begins speaking in liturgical canto, reciting the Latin prayer for the feast day of Saints Joannem et Thomam.

Thomas's Question: Thomas recognizes his own name and asks about Joannem.

Answer: Saint John Fisher. You have saints’ day jointly.

Memory: Thomas recalls Fisher died fourteen days before him—and had never heard his own collect.

Reply: The Metropolitan: Few have. Save from the other side.

The Metropolitan identifies Thomas More by the liturgical calendar of the Church—not by politics or history, but by sanctity. He knows who has come because he knows the communion of saints.

The Promise Itself

Is this the end? Are you the last?

“No, I am not the last, Thomas.”

“We have the promise. We last till the end of the world.”

Slider's Objection Dismissed

Thomas quotes Slider's argument: 'We are not the world... no promise was ever given to us.'

Nonsense, nonsense. We have the Promise.

The Revelation

The Promise was given on Astrobe in latter days, in a queerer and more flaming way.

Christ has walked on Astrobe in human form with Saint Klingensmith and others.

The burning promise was given, and the flame is beginning to rise, starting with my five or six followers.

Growth

There are over a hundred followers left on Astrobe.

It will grow.

If you are of the Faith, Astrobe's stones and clods will sing of the Promise. If you regard it as legend, learn the legends—they are richer than Old Earth's.

The Blind Man

The Metropolitan tells Thomas he is a living witness to the unseen, a ferret-faced little man who became a saint.

“How can you know I'm ferret-faced, blind man?”

The Metropolitan laughs: You are the blind man, not I.

Thomas, with his golden rhetoric and political compromises, cannot see what the dying, blind Metropolitan sees: the Promise, the presence of Christ, the flame beginning to rise. Spiritual sight belongs to the skeletal man in the ruined castle, not to the Past Master who will be king.

The Blessing

“Turn, God, and bring us to life again!”

“And thy people rejoice in thee.”

The versicle and response draw on Psalm 85 (84 in the Vulgate), asking God to restore life so that his people may rejoice.

Thomas rises to leave. Outside, he thinks: 'The last of them... This is the way it ends here.'

The Order of Saint Klingensmith

The Green-Robed Monks

Founder: Saint Klingensmith walked with Christ on Astrobe when the burning promise was given.

The Order

Dress: The monks wear green robes. The blackish complexion with a hint of green describes Father Oddopter individually.

Location: They dwell in the Feral Lands, fishing for hydras and keeping true faith far from the Golden Cities.

Sworn rule against staying in the same place two nights running. They have no permanent home.

Father Oddopter

He is a green-robed monk of the order of Saint Klingensmith... a blackish man with a hint of deep green, who winks and grins at the startled party.

He blesses the party, praying for preservation from dire-wolves, panthers, and programmed things.

He identifies each member of Thomas's party, knowing them by report and dream: Maxwell (avatar who burns bodies), Evita (archetype in monks’ dreams), Paul (who will suffer stark death), Thomas (revenant with a double sign, strange instrument of the Holy Ghost), Slider (the nothing man), Scrivener (less-than-nothing).

'What in particular are you fishing for, Father Oddopter?' 'You'll see.' He is fishing for the Devil—the hydra.

The Devil-Kill

The killing of the Devil must be done afresh daily, or our days be at an end.

The monks bait the hydra with a smaller creature, then attack when it surfaces—'cutting and hacking' through the giant eye into the brain.

Today's Devil was large, but it takes other forms like a mad direwolf or a porches-panther gone musk. We must kill it daily to limn his limits.

Father Oddopter says mass for over a hundred people in Goslar. An 'uncanny miracle came shockingly and vividly alive at the consecration'—heavens opening, Spirit descending.

The Church on Astrobe

History

Most churches have been razed three hundred years ago.

The feast of the Wooly Ram has not been held for more than three hundred years—only antiquarians could know about it.

The Church survives in Cathead, in the Feral Lands, in the hundred-plus followers scattered across Astrobe.

Revival

A slight revival... in Cathead' and 'non-burlesque rites.

On the night before Thomas's execution, the newly-appointed (or self-appointed) Metropolitan of Astrobe has put that whole world under interdict, until penance be done. Groups make up and sing ballads about it.

Then the tolling begins—on five hundred great bells of churches mostly razed three hundred years ago. That sound has not been heard within living memory on Astrobe. But five hundred great bells toll, and the people remember the names of them. The Archangel Gabriel, the Giant, Saint Peter, Mephistopheles, the Black Virgin, Saint Hilary—and 'one more, high and powerful and clear, the July Bell.'

The bells toll for Thomas More. The whole great golden unbelieving city of Cosmopolis does homage to Thomas More who will die tomorrow.

Cathead and the Golden Cities

Immediately after leaving the Metropolitan, Thomas sees sea-gleaners bringing in Dutchfish. It is plague day. Three men have died. The scow-master strips their boots and rolls the bodies into the fish cargo. The buyer docks pay for each body—they just aren't up to the fish in phosphor and sulphur and are hard on the grinders.

The Promise is given in the midst of death. The Church survives where the Golden Dream has failed—in Cathead, where bodies are weighed with fish, where the Metropolitan dies in a ruined castle, where Father Oddopter fishes for the Devil in the green darkness.

The Carnival and Execution

Chapters 12-13

The Carnival and Execution

Chapters 12-13: The Ultimate People and Apocephalon

Etymology: From Greek apo- ('away from,' 'separation') and kephalē ('head'). Literally: separation of the head.

The wake, carnival, and bells precede the execution. Foreman advances it from noon to eight, frustrating Battersea's rescue. More refuses Pottscamp's offer. The forerunner wave dies trying to reach him; Evita and three companions kill Foreman. The Stranger speaks with More before the beheading. The worlds end, and the final questions ask whether renewal follows.

The Wake at George's Shop

The Eagles Gather

Setting

The back room of George the Syrian's aromatics shop in Cosmopolis, 'right off Centrality Square.'

'The Eagles were gathering.' The phrase is Shanty's.

Paul enters through a side door. Copperhead has escaped through walls; Maxwell appears in a manufactured old woman's body. Evita tries the barred door and then smashes through it.

Tales at the Wake

The Eagles tell stories that the monitoring machines cannot interpret. The machines assume concealed information, but the narrative does not confirm a cipher.

Automatic monitors record and interpret but fail to understand. This isn't code like you meet every night.

• George's tale of the Syrian and the sand dune: The only thing ever left over when the world ends is one syrian and one sand dune... If the syrian goes behind the dune, there is hope.

• Adam's tale of Saint Brandon arriving on Astrobe 1500 years before official history, with 19 Irish monks in a coracle boat.

• Shanty's tale of the boar hog and lightning rod salesman.

Adam's Prophecy

Question: Evita asks: 'My brother, you know these things also. Will it be his death?'

“Yes, it will be his death. And my final one.”

Adam says Battersea is not wrong: he will strike, and a new world may be made, although many details must change. This does not withdraw Adam's prediction of More's death.

The Fools’ Carnival

A Fools’ Holiday Such as They Have Not Had for a Hundred Years

The night before the execution, Cosmopolis erupts in unprecedented revelry. It is a fools’ carnival indeed, all split into high-spirited warring factions spilling over into masquerade.

Activities

'Happy fighting.' Not lungers or hard-heads from Cathead, but civilized Cosmopolitans. Heads are broken, and people laugh, as if it had been a thousand years before.

'Ban and Beyond' banners flown and pulled down in glorious melee. 'Sackcloth and Ashes' faction marches and jokes.

The newly-appointed Metropolitan has put the whole world under interdict; groups make up and sing ballads about it.

High Ladies of Astrobe dress as crones and hawk candy heads and skulls for the beheading. Wooly Rams found and barbecued—the feast of the Wooly Ram has not been held on Astrobe for more than three hundred years.

Drinking and shouting, looting and arson, all carried out in pretty good spirits.

New Emotions

A whole barrelful of new emotions spilled into the streets around Centrality Square.

Anger (and who of the Citizens has been angry in their whole lives?), wonder, truculence, battle-joy, revelry, serpents’ tooth remorse, utter penitence, pinnacled hope, joy-in-murder, joy-in-humility.

All the detectable Programmed Persons are in hiding. They feel fear, an emotion that is not even programmed into them. They cannot reason this thing out at all, and reason is the only thing that the Programmed Persons have.

The Five Hundred Bells

The Old Old World Funeral Toll

Then the tolling begins. On the great bells of a forgotten or museumized church, then on another and another, then on five hundred.

Most of these Churches have been razed three hundred years ago. How are their giant bells sounding the Old Old World Funeral Toll now? That sound has not been heard within living memory on Astrobe.

But five hundred great bells toll, and the people remember the names of them.

Archangel GabrielThe GiantThe White OgreThe Shepherd KingSaint PeterKing of BavariaYellow DwarfSaint SimeonThe DutchmanArchbishop TurpinRhinelanderDanielJew BellMephistophelesThe Black VirginShip BellThe MountainSaint Hilary

And one more, high and powerful and clear, the July Bell.

The whole great golden unbelieving city of Cosmopolis does homage to Thomas More who will die tomorrow.

Foreman's Theory of World Death

The Mustard Seed and Transcendent Yeast

The Visit

Foreman visits Thomas at dawn. He is 'High Civilian in Charge of Execution.'

He finds Thomas unusually placid for a man scheduled to die. The two weigh each other with cautious eyes.

The Theory

Worlds die periodically—instantly ceasing all life, heat, gravity, meaning. Foreman believes he will witness it today.

Foreman proposes transitions around Christ's birth, 500, 1000, 1500, and 2000, followed by the current Astrobian crisis. He places More's first death near the transition from the High Middle Ages to the modern world, not near the year 1000. This remains his theory.

A transcendent yeast, a small quantity of the immaterial, must be added every 500 years or so for rebirth. Thomas's death and the reaction to the 'Ban the Beyond' push will be the trigger.

“The mustard seed, we plant it now.”

Thomas's death is absolutely required. Foreman insists: 'All other hopes are vain.'

The Betrayal

Foreman Changes the Time

A mechanical voice pings 'Ten minute call!' Foreman declares: 'All right, Thomas... We go now to your end. Come, come.'

Thomas protests—it is not yet 8 a.m., he dies at noon, nothing is ready.

I changed it, Thomas. I changed it to eight o'clock... There was no other way.

Foreman admits he knew about Battersea's rescue plan—being his former commander—and picked up the details easily.

Thomas accuses him of murder despite friendship. Foreman affirms: This is the only way to bring off the reaction—humanity's rediscovery.

“I don't consent.”

You are the only ultimately honest man I can think of, who has shown stubborn honesty before and has a curious magnetism, becoming a symbol once and needing to become one again. We had almost run out of symbols on Astrobe.

Thomas moans: 'I die for it, and I don't even know what it's about.'

Pottscamp's Offer

Thomas is brought to a standstill before Pottscamp at the foot of the scaffold, 'as required by ritual.'

Offer: Will you reconsider? Sign now, and live happily. Or die meanly. If Thomas dies, Pottscamp becomes Surrogate President and will sign the bill himself.

'Snake-in-my-brain... I will not have died for the Oudennothing!' Thomas sees now that the Thing they try to kill is the only Thing that matters.

Off with my head if only to close my ears to this babble! Out of my way, you damnable jump-jack!

Pottscamp flees as though stricken, then sits on the ground, moaning and howling like an old Hebrew, pouring dust and ashes over his head.

The Forerunner Wave

A Minute Thing but Incomparably Savage

Context

Thomas More has been World President, King, for nine days. And now he will die.

The early-morning rain has stopped, and now there is a rush to complete the act.

The men from Cathead, rumor says, have received word of the sudden change of time and are mobbing toward the center of Cosmopolis, but might well be too late.

The Attack

There is one wave of fury, a minute thing but incomparably savage, rising moments before a true tidal wave: the forerunner wave.

Buff Shanty and Paul are in it, driving with great impetus. Walter Copperhead is in it, though he must know it is futile. The boy Adam is in it. Possibly thirty others, fine people of Cosmopolis.

Its suddenness almost brings success. The men bowl over guards and gain scaffold steps. Fighting is close; they give a life for every step.

Adam

Adam is the crest, reaching the scaffold and touching Thomas before guards fling him down.

He rises brokenly.

Adam dies magnificently—as he always did.

Failure

The wave lacks bulk; guards are too many. The thrust crests, shatters, ebbs in blood.

Shanty, Paul, Copperhead, Adam, and the others die around the scaffold foot and on the steps, 'making them slippery.'

Evita's Vengeance

Sparagmos Enacted

Evita, knowing it will fail, surges not towards Thomas but towards Fabian Foreman at the square's edge.

The Attack

'Zehheeroot, is-Kerioth,' she howls ('Beware, Iscariot').

She attacks him like a lioness, swipes his face red, bites his throat. Foreman screams in terror.

I be a cold fury and not a witch. Woe to him by whom it comes... Certain primitives were wont to kill a dog to be company to the hero... You are such a dog.

Foreman's Last Words: Foreman gasps: No, no, woman! I'm the master of it all... The furious reaction... will set humanity back... and let a new world be born.

Evita sings she is the heart of that reaction, reveling in it, calling Foreman a 'dog puppeteer.'

She practically dismembers him. She breaks his face, throws the shapeless man over her shoulder, carries him to George, Maxwell, and Rimrock. The four tear him apart and kill him.

Evita takes the biggest piece and hangs it on a Carob tree (Judas Tree).

Foreman has done his part well, planned it all except his own death; everything was meant well.

The guards kill George, Maxwell, and Rimrock, adding their blood to the transcendental yeast. They do not catch Evita.

The Stranger

Can a Man Have More Heads Than Two?

One man breaks through, unstoppable, unseen by guards. This stranger goes to Thomas on the scaffold, speaks unheard words.

Thomas seems excited, pleased. He cries loudly: 'Will it work, do you think?... How droll! Can a man have more heads than two? I'll do it. I'll go with you.'

But apparently Thomas doesn't go, anywhere but to his death. The stranger disappears into the crowd or charged air; guesses remain about his identity.

Some say something disappears from Thomas then—his essence—leaving a shadow man. A weird old woman cries she can see through him.

Unidentified. Possibly Christ.

Last Words

Pater, in Manus Tuas—

The rest is legend: quips Thomas supposedly said (some good, some cute, most in books of quotations), but he didn't say them, not this time or the first.

His only last words on the scaffold are "Pater, in manus tuas—" (a scrap of old prayer).

The prayer begins Father, into your hands, echoing Christ's words in Luke 23:46. It breaks off before the blade falls.

The blade falls and More is beheaded. The narrative insists on the reality of the blood and death.

The narrator reports the snakes and the woman carrying the head, then disavows them with an insistence that such things could not happen. The tone preserves uncertainty rather than settling every prodigy as fact or falsehood.

The World Ends

Everything Ceases. And All the Stars Go Out.

But one thing does really happen. At the moment life flickers out of the beheaded corpus, the worlds come to an end.

All life and heat and pulse go out of the world. It dies in every bird, rock, plant, person, mountain, sea, cloud. It dies in gravity, light, heat, germ-life, life-code. Everything ceases. And all the stars go out.

Is it for a moment? Or a billion years? Or forever? There is no difference when the world ends, no time to measure time by.

Remember how it had been? A priest renegade just becomes Metropolitan; a programmed machine succeeds to president but wails, pouring ashes. Battersea and his men mob towards Centrality Square under their Hand-of-Vengeance banner. On such notes the worlds end.

The Questions

And is a new world born? Yeasted? Does the furious reaction bridge the gap? Does the mustard seed grow? The Judas tree bear fruit?

Does lightning lace things together or sunder forever? Thunder flattens worlds; a tidal wave carries away golden fungus.

In less than an instant, more than forever, it is over. But has it sequence? Does a new world follow?

The narrator asks whether the hand on the banner is misunderstood and recalls Gandy's Left Hand of God. The question is not spoken by Northprophet.

Remember cycles (Rome, Europe, Americas, Astrobe)? Cycles internal, electrifying? Divinity becomes humanity? Humanity becomes divinity?

Can spirit come down on gell-cells, flux-fix? Shall sterile wood fruit? Is Avid Nothingness cast away? Room for life? Return to real life? Does reaction become birthing?

Be quiet. We watch.

Be quiet. We wait.

Be quiet. We hope.

Time Travel

Chronometanastasis and Hopp-Equation Space

Time Travel in Past Master

Past Master employs two distinct modes of temporal/spatial displacement: Chronometanastasis (retrieving persons from the past) and Hopp-Equation Travel (interstellar transit). Both involve profound dislocations of reality, identity, and consciousness.

Both forms of travel disturb identity. More's retrieval resembles resurrection symbolically, but the machine takes him while alive in his own past. The later visit to his grave makes his simultaneous relation to life and death visible.

Chronometanastasis

Travel into the Past

Etymology: A Greek-derived name for travel through time. Its function is shown by the tuned loop and its calibrated attachments.

“Find a dead man who once led well. Let him lead again.”

Chronometanastasis has been a working thing for a dozen years.

The Apparatus

Location: Kingmaker's London office on Earth

Device: A 'tuned antenna-like loop'—the 'basic machine' with attachments for calibration.

To the observer, the traveler vanishes into 'crackling air.' To the traveler: 'unholy gray confusion that is deeper than darkness.' All time travelers experience sickness.

Requirements

Coins: Brooks supplies coins of the required period. Paul jokes about the problem of spending Tomorrow Coins in the wrong day.

Calibration: Paul brings a calibrated attachment. He says Brooks need not know its exact calibration, not that calibration is unnecessary.

The Paradox of Two

Question: “Will there be two of me, then, Paul?”

More's Answer: “Every man is a multitude.”

History records More's death 'on a certain date in an extreme manner, and in this realm.' The retrieved More exists simultaneously—his bones remain in his grave at St. Peter in Chains while he walks on Astrobe.

Candidates Considered

Plato: 'Too cold, too placid.' Foreman calls him essentially 'a programmed person himself'—a just man who believed he could never be unhappy.

King Yu, Mung K'o, Chandragupta, Stilicho, Charles the Great, Cosimo I, Macchiavelli, Edward Coke, Gustavas Vasa, Lincoln, Inigo Jones: Almost good enough... a little something lacking in each.

I want a man who can be unhappy over an unjust situation.' More's 'showy act of honesty' that costs his head makes him uniquely qualified—or his 'one honest moment.

The Time Men

Previous Visitors to Thomas More

One of the great mysteries of the book. Who are these travelers?

More has been visited by time travelers before due to his historical significance. He has 'a number of past and future things in my head.'

He asked questions of his visitors and knows 'a little of several futures.'

What the Time Men Revealed

• Paul lives approximately 1000 years hence, during the 'First Astrobian Time of Troubles.'

• Astrobe is 'wobbly' then, and will still be wobbly 1000 years after Paul's death—just a different wobble. Astrobe survives the current crisis.

• The man who saves Astrobe was 'shamefully treated,' his name unknown, identified only as 'the Past Master.'

The Utopia Irony: Time travelers told More his 'angry humor piece' Utopia was always misunderstood as depicting an ideal world. He wrote it in 'bitter and laughing irony' about the 'sickest of all possible worlds.' He finds the future 'slack' for mistaking satire for a 'vapid dream.'

Hopp-Equation Space

The Medium of Interstellar Travel

Hopp-Equation Space travel breaks reality. Not like ordinary space—persons and things 'aren't the same' during traversal.

Physics

Distance: The novel gives the distance as 1.5 parsecs and describes an ordinary light-speed journey as over five years. Its stated figures are approximate and do not align exactly.

Duration: Hopp-Equation Travel takes about one Astrobe month (approximately 700 standard hours).

Speed: Approximately 64× light speed.

No sense of motion. The universe disappears. No worlds, stars, or duration perceived.

The Fundamental Reversal

'Absolutely fundamental reversal' or 'total reversal of polarity'—a common private joke among pilots.

• Paul becomes left-handed during passage.

• He jokes it's the only way he could sing soprano, which he often does in this state.

• Thomas experiences it as inexpressible fury: He seethes with inexpressible fury. He asks Paul if it happens to all Hopp-Equation travelers.

“What's time to a revenant? I've been dead a thousand years, that I should live to such shame.”

Hopp-Equation travel is very new.

Passage Dreams

Twenty Thousand Dreams in Ninety-Second Intervals

Mechanism

Sleep is restricted to 90-second intervals by instrumentation. Paul becomes adept, experiencing intricate dreams.

He calculates having at least 20,000 memorable, gemlike, self-contained, widely different dreams during passage—each a short life.

Attributed to compressing 4.5 years of psychic awareness (Law of Conservation of Psychic Totality) into one month. Nearly 5 years of psychic experience crowded into a month; psychic mass isn't foreshortened.

Nature

Debris: 'Psychic space debris'—fragments of billions of minds, poignant, comic, horrifying episodes.

Ansels: The ansel appears in many dreams; ansels were in human unconscious before being found on Astrobe.

Paul knew some dream monsters were real creatures living in Hopp-Equation space—some encountered only by him, others by multiple pilots in the same way and place.

Only the maladjusted can stand passages; well-adjusted pilots crack up. Hopp-Equation pilots are a peculiar breed.

This is why Paul—irregular, citizenship revoked, hunted by Killers—can make the journey. His very brokenness qualifies him.

Paul's Journey to Retrieve More

Outbound

Paul leaves in Foreman's spacecraft with permission keyed for it. The grasshopper he steals to reach the spaceport is a different vehicle.

Paul travels from Golden Astrobe to Blue Earth. Earth appears bluish from Astrobe; Astrobe golden from Earth—due to their suns’ different white light.

Paul makes Earth-fall on the morning side, 'a beautiful experience that never gets old.' He lands in London, stables his craft.

In London

Kingmaker has extensive Earth interests; Paul knows his way around. Brooks manages the London office, immediately flustered by an Astrobe visitor—Earthmen feel inferior since the elite left for Astrobe 400-500 years ago.

Paul presents forged credentials (he could have gotten real ones but prefers doing things himself). Brooks accepts them, respecting 'the buccaneer in a man.'

The Time Jump

Paul steps through the tuned antenna-like loop, disappearing to Brooks into crackling air.

Materializes ankle-deep in mud on the edge of a large, sprawling wooden town—16th-century London.

In a ramshackle public house, Paul eats wood-cock, 'very high beef,' barley bread, and an onion 'the size of a child's head.'

The proprietor warns: 'The King's men are everywhere, friend. Walk in Christ.'

Chelsea

After an hour or two of walking, Paul reaches Chelsea. He is pleased the English haven't yet become 'that most unhandsome of people.'

He spots Thomas More walking in his frozen garden, 'wrapped up like a sheep.' Paul recognizes him instantly, though he only slightly resembles Holbein's portrait (which looks more like Holbein).

More Visits His Own Grave

After returning through the tunnel loop to modern London, Thomas insists on visiting St. Peter in Chains church.

The priest confirms the bones and ring found in the grave. He assumes the ring worn by the living More is a replica, failing to recognize his visitor.

The priest assumes More is an antiquarian. More corrects: 'No, I'm an antiquary... I have a special interest in this man.'

What other man, Paul, looks down on his own grave and he in it? All except my head.' His head is buried at Canterbury—'Parboiled it, did they not?

More expresses desire to see his head but deems the 70-mile journey 'too long'—despite preparing for a 1.5 parsec trip to Astrobe.

The Return to Astrobe

Thomas brings mystery novels, revels, bonanzas, science fiction (all new to him), plus newly discovered tobacco (stogie declared most wonderful thing since Evangels). He plans to smoke and read the whole trip.

All goes well until the first cosmic disappearance. Thomas tries to bellow, but his voice won't—the fundamental reversal has occurred.

More experiences thousands of dreams in sleeps of at most ninety seconds. Figures include Rimrock, a composite female, a lion-headed spider, a fox, and a hawk shuffling shells. Their relation to the people he meets becomes apparent later.

Annotations

The twenty-fifth hour

Kingmaker imagines a crisis continuing beyond the last possible hour. The title also invites comparison with C. Virgil Gheorghiu’s novel about a person trapped in the classifications and machinery of modern society. The resemblance is especially apt while Astrobe’s mechanical Killers batter down the building.

C. Virgil Gheorghiu, The Twenty-Fifth Hour (1949; English translation, 1950).

The lion, the fox, and the hawk

Kingmaker’s lion and Proctor’s fox recall Machiavelli’s advice that a prince needs both strength and cunning. Foreman’s hawk adds a third figure to the pair. Their competing claims to control one another make government a contest among these different kinds of power.

Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chap. 18.

Kingmaker and Fabian

Kingmaker’s name recalls Warwick, the magnate who made and unmade English kings. Fabian can suggest Fabius Cunctator, the Roman commander famous for delay, and the society named after him. Foreman’s waiting and carefully timed intervention suit that association, although the novel does not explain his name.

Shakespeare, 3 Henry VI, 3.3; the historical epithets Warwick the Kingmaker and Fabius Cunctator.

The crack of doom

The phrase belongs to Macbeth’s vision of a seemingly endless succession of kings. Here the Masters argue over postponing judgment while the Killers provide the thunder outside. A familiar expression becomes a physical event in the scene.

Shakespeare, Macbeth, 4.1.

The doom clock

Foreman’s mechanical man belongs to the clock that threatens Astrobe. The image recalls the Doomsday Clock of Cold War public life. A manufactured president cannot save the world if he is another part of the machinery bringing about its end.

The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ Doomsday Clock, introduced in 1947.

Deaths and failures

Foreman distinguishes the death of a historical world from its failure. His account develops into the five-hundred-year sequence in Chapter 13. Toynbee offers a useful comparison for the language of civilizational breakdown, especially the later phrase Time of Troubles; Foreman’s particular chronology is his own.

Arnold J. Toynbee, A Study of History; Past Master, chap. 13.

Byerly and the manufactured candidate

Byerly’s name appears amid doubts about whether a candidate is human and a proposal to manufacture the ideal president. This makes Asimov’s Stephen Byerley, the politician suspected of being a robot, a plausible allusion. The spelling differs, and Lafferty leaves the connection unstated.

Isaac Asimov, “Evidence” (1946) and “The Evitable Conflict” (1950).

Chronometanastasis

The name combines Greek words for time and migration. It makes travel into the past sound like a change of dwelling. The embedded resemblance to anastasis, resurrection, also suits the project of bringing a long-dead man back into public life.

Greek chronos, time; metanastasis, migration; anastasis, rising or resurrection.

Why Plato is rejected

Foreman objects to Plato’s claim that justice makes a man happy. He wants someone who can be unhappy over an unjust situation. The discussion tests the difference between designing an ideal commonwealth and suffering with the people who inhabit an actual one.

Plato, Republic 1.354a; Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

A great man from the past

The candidates include rulers, counselors, a jurist, and an architect. Foreman reduces his own list to More and to one decisive act of honesty. This resembles the great-man theory of history, but the choice also makes the supposedly exemplary man dependent on those who recruit him.

Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841).

The honest moment and the lost head

The exchange anticipates More’s execution on Tower Hill in 1535 and his second execution on Astrobe. Roper records More speaking plainly against the statute after his conviction. That episode helps illuminate Foreman’s interest in a final honest act; Lafferty’s More is a fictional reworking of the historical martyr.

William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, account of the trial and execution.

The mustard seed

Foreman needs only a very small beginning. The Gospel seed that grows into a great plant gives his political experiment a religious scale. Chapter 13 returns to the image when he explains what he expects More’s death to accomplish.

Matthew 13:31–32; Mark 4:30–32; Luke 13:18–19.

Paul the traveler

More explicitly connects the pilot with his name-saint, the apostle whose journeys fill Acts. The comparison gives Paul’s mission a spiritual possibility that its organizers do not explain to him. His confession before his own birth adds a comic reversal to that connection.

Acts 13–28.

The guards and the hounds

Paul’s escape depends on bringing the mechanical guards and Killers together like bears and hounds in a baiting. The image anticipates the journey to More’s England, where bear-baiting was a familiar public spectacle. Paul and his allies arrange the encounter and exploit the confusion.

The English bear-baiting tradition.

Reversal in Hopp-Equation space

Paul’s change of handedness recalls the mirror-reversed traveler in Wells’s “The Plattner Story.” Lafferty extends the joke to sex and voice. This bodily reversal also begins the novel’s larger pattern of left-handed actions and unexpected means of rescue.

H. G. Wells, “The Plattner Story” (1896).

Dreams and the human unconscious

The statement that ansels existed in the human unconscious before people discovered them on Astrobe invites comparison with Jung’s archetypes. The novel lets an image encountered in dreams become a creature met in waking life. It does not require that every passage dream be decoded into a single fixed meaning.

C. G. Jung, writings on the collective unconscious and archetypes.

Adam

The first man’s name belongs to a boy who repeatedly appears in scenes of battle and death. His insistence that each death belongs to another bearer of the name complicates any simple account of resurrection. The biblical association brings the deaths of individual men into the story of mankind.

Genesis 2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45.

Sour John and the stolen emerald

Sour John is also a storyteller in Lafferty’s “The Ugly Sea.” His theft of an idol’s green eye recalls J. Milton Hayes’s music-hall monologue, but the replacement kidney turns the adventure into a joke about mistaken value. Paul’s objection to the port’s geography is overruled by the teller.

R. A. Lafferty, “The Ugly Sea” (1960); J. Milton Hayes, “The Green Eye of the Little Yellow God” (1911).

Rhium and Antirhium

The paired stars borrow the names of the opposing headlands at the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth. Their linked rotation resembles a centrifugal governor regulating a machine. When the chain breaks, the dream makes a cosmic catastrophe out of a mechanical failure.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.86; Strabo, Geography 8.2.3.

More’s Utopia

More calls his book a bitter joke that later readers have mistaken for a blueprint. This is the fictional More’s account of his intention. It establishes the central predicament: the author must live in, and eventually govern, a world that has taken his imagined commonwealth seriously.

Thomas More, Utopia (1516).

The sickest possible world

More’s description of Utopia reverses the familiar formula of the best of all possible worlds. The later history of that formula, especially Voltaire’s Pangloss, makes the line another deliberate-looking anachronism in the speech of a man who already knows several futures.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Theodicy (1710); Voltaire, Candide (1759).

The meeting at Chelsea

Paul finds More free in his garden before the decision that will lead to his death. Historically, More refused the oath in April 1534 and was imprisoned until his execution in July 1535. The novel combines that situation with a journey about a thousand years back from 2535; its calendar does not resolve into an exact historical date.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More; More’s imprisonment, 1534–35.

Holbein’s portrait

Paul recognizes More partly from Holbein’s portrait. The contrast between the short, familiar-looking man and the tall Astrobian pilot makes the historical figure physically unheroic before the narrative tests what kind of hero he can become.

Hans Holbein the Younger, Sir Thomas More (1527), Frick Collection.

Past Master

The title joins a master from the past with the ordinary meaning of an expert. It also recalls an office formerly held in a guild or lodge. The later language of masters, a station, and an inner circle extends those institutional associations.

The guild and Masonic office of past master; Past Master, chap. 4.

Mercy and the old things

More’s Latin plea for mercy belongs to the language of prayer. The publican’s farewell and lament for the old things likewise draw on scriptural idiom. In this scene the promise of things made new is heard by someone who fears what the religious changes will destroy.

Miserere mihi, Domine, Roman Missal, Introit for the Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Colossians 2:6; Revelation 21:4–5.

Looking into his own grave

The chapter title comes from More’s visit to the grave that already contains his bones. The historical More prepared a tomb and epitaph at Chelsea, but his body was buried at St. Peter ad Vincula in the Tower. Lafferty’s scene makes the traveler confront the fact of his first death before he goes to meet a second.

More’s Chelsea epitaph (1532); Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More.

The head and the signet ring

The burial tradition separates More’s body in the Tower from his head at Canterbury. The future priest’s discovery of identifiable bones and a signet ring belongs to Lafferty’s fiction. Its purpose is to make More’s presence and his completed death equally tangible.

Thomas Stapleton, Tres Thomae (1588), account of Margaret Roper and More’s head.

Enskied and sainted

The rare verb enskied recalls Lucio’s description of Isabella in Measure for Measure. Paul has just reminded More of his canonization; the flight then sends the sainted man literally into the sky. More’s enthusiasm for a newly discovered cigar keeps the ascent comic.

Shakespeare, Measure for Measure, 1.4.

The woman in More’s dream

Succubus, Eve, Lilith, Judith, Mary, and Valkyrie bring demonic, maternal, holy, and martial figures into one image. Judith’s beheading of Holofernes is especially pointed in a novel about More’s head. The composite anticipates Evita without reducing her to one of its names.

Genesis 2–3; Judith 13; the traditions of Lilith and the Valkyries.

The Naked Sailor and the seven hells

More places the inn in a numbered division of Hell and consoles Paul that three worse divisions remain. The Qur’an supplies seven gates, while later commentaries arrange the inhabitants differently. The joke’s exact assignment of Christians to a fourth division should be read as More’s statement within the scene.

Qur’an 15:44; George Sale, Preliminary Discourse to The Koran (1734).

Poverty and Utopia

More’s outrage at starvation and punishing labor recalls Hythloday’s indictment of England in Utopia. Cathead confronts him with a further difficulty: its inhabitants have chosen to leave material abundance. His familiar political explanations cannot yet account for that choice.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

Holy poverty

More accepts voluntary religious poverty but recoils from deprivation that degrades its sufferers. The distinction matters throughout the Cathead chapters. His admiration for a modest life does not make him an advocate of the conditions he sees here.

The Franciscan tradition of holy poverty; More’s account of common life in Utopia.

The oceanic man

Rimrock’s seal-like body and ability to move on land recall the seal-people of northern folklore. His shifting between no legs, four, and two can also suggest the Sphinx’s riddle about man. More’s decisive test, however, is intellect and spirit rather than an animal’s outward shape.

The selkie tradition; Apollodorus, Library 3.5.8.

Ouden and the Greek joke-names

Ouden means nothing. The name extends the learned naming games of Utopia, whose island, city, and river carry teasing Greek meanings. Here the word becomes a speaker who describes his nothingness as active, hungry, and destructive.

Greek ouden, nothing; More, Utopia.

Nothingness and evil

More’s denial that Ouden has being can be read alongside Augustine and Aquinas on evil as a privation of good. Ouden answers that his nothingness is a vortex. The exchange tests what that destructive claim means; it does not by itself settle the novel’s metaphysics in Ouden’s favor.

Augustine, Confessions 7.12; Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 48.

The one kindling

Ouden remembers a single kindling that overcame him and claims that he is extinguishing it. John’s light shining in darkness supplies a strong biblical comparison. Paul-Thomas answers with the possibility of rekindling and with a resource that Ouden does not know.

John 1:4–5.

Every man a king

The golden inhabitants appear to fulfill the promise associated with Huey Long’s slogan. Their magnificence makes More eager to join them. Later encounters ask whether this universal royalty has left its beneficiaries capable of thought, refusal, or spiritual life.

Huey P. Long, Every Man a King (1933) and the Share Our Wealth slogan.

A catalogue of paradises

More praises Astrobe through a mixture of Gospel language, classical myth, and Irish otherworld geography. The pearl of great price stands beside Iris, Great Brasil, and the Hesperides. This abundance of names reveals how much hope he brings to what he is seeing.

Matthew 13:45–46; the myths of Iris and the Hesperides; the Irish Hy-Brasil tradition.

The whited sepulcher

Evita’s answer comes from Christ’s denunciation of tombs beautiful outside and full of death within. She supplies the diagnosis while More is still admiring the surface. The contrast governs both this chapter and the later discovery of Astrobe’s deformed reverse.

Matthew 23:27.

Fawney men and false gold

A fawney man practices a ring swindle, passing a worthless ring off as valuable. More’s compliment to Rimrock therefore associates enchantment with deceptive gold. It belongs beside the repeated question of what Golden Astrobe’s apparent wealth is worth.

The thieves’ cant terms fawney and fawney rig.

The Greek and Jewish mechanical man

More explicitly recalls older dreams of artificial servants. Greek examples include Hephaestus’s golden attendants and the bronze Talos; the Jewish tradition supplies the golem. Pottscamp’s dream of the toy that consumes its maker gives that admiration a frightening sequel.

Homer, Iliad 18.417–20; Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 4; the golem tradition.

The president as a masked performer

The former presidents’ extravagant names sound to More like gladiators or American wrestlers. His sponsors likewise plan to present a recognizable persona to the public. The joke makes political office resemble a staged performance whose billing matters more than its holder’s freedom to act.

The novel’s explicit comparison with gladiators and masked professional wrestlers.

Washing one’s hands

Proctor’s description of Kingmaker and Foreman’s refusal to wash his hands recall Pilate. The gesture concerns responsibility for a death already being planned. Foreman’s willingness to own his part does not remove the moral question of what he is doing to his friend.

Matthew 27:24.

Termination and the satisfied guest

Proctor compares the man ready to die with a guest who has eaten enough. Lucretius and Horace use the satisfied guest as an image of leaving life without complaint. Astrobe turns that consolation into an argument for readily available termination.

Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 3.938; Horace, Satires 1.1.117–19.

Termination and More’s own book

Utopia allows priests and magistrates to urge a voluntary death upon someone suffering from incurable, painful illness. Astrobe makes termination a common response to weariness. The altered conditions are essential to the comparison: Lafferty’s institution is much broader than the practice described by More.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Slaves, and of Their Marriages.”

False dawn

Foreman spoils the consoling proverb about darkness before dawn by inserting a false dawn. He later claims responsibility for making a particular sun rise, borrowing language ordinarily applied to God. His confidence invites scrutiny as the cost of his promised renewal becomes clear.

Matthew 5:45; the proverb about darkness before dawn.

The thirty shells

Foreman’s counting and weeping make the shells a strong counterpart to Judas’s thirty pieces of silver. The scene anticipates the betrayal named openly in Chapter 13. The warning about Mother Carey’s chicken adds the storm petrel’s maritime associations to the threatened victim.

Matthew 26:15; 27:3–5; the sailors’ name Mother Carey’s chicken.

Camiroi and Puca

The school assignments in Pottscamp’s dream contain names from Lafferty’s other fiction. Treating those peoples and languages as ordinary school subjects gives the invented worlds a shared background while the toy’s effortless learning exposes the child’s dependence on it.

Lafferty, “Primary Education of the Camiroi” (1966), “Polity and Custom of the Camiroi” (1967), and The Reefs of Earth (1968).

The Shape of Things to Come

The title names Wells’s future history, in which a world administration reorganizes civilization and suppresses religion. Astrobe’s managed happiness and its treatment of worship as an antiquity give the allusion particular force. Chapter 10 answers this title with The Deformity of Things to Come.

H. G. Wells, The Shape of Things to Come (1933), especially book 4.

The same everywhere

Kingmaker’s praise of Astrobe’s uniformity recalls Utopia’s closely similar towns. More’s wish to travel puts the author in opposition to the commonwealth associated with his name. He insists on seeing what an account of the whole planet leaves out.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Towns, Particularly of Amaurot.”

The Dream as a version of Utopia

The precis machine describes common access to goods, freedom from poverty, and a simplified legal order. These recall institutions in Utopia, although the golden world gives them a different purpose. More’s recognition is also a crisis of authorship: his joke has become a place people must inhabit.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2.

The Big O and the Omega Point

Astrobe’s account of humanity converging into a single organism invites comparison with Teilhard de Chardin’s Omega Point. The novel’s Omega becomes Ouden and the Big O, a destination described as nothingness. This is a satirical resemblance; Teilhard’s own account gives convergence a transcendent and Christian end.

Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, The Phenomenon of Man (1955; English translation, 1959).

Holy Nothingness

The Dream’s religious vocabulary makes the abolition of transcendence sound like an act of worship. It can be read against the death-of-God debates contemporary with the novel. The phrase also occurs in Richard Rubenstein’s theology, but the shared wording alone does not establish a direct source.

Richard L. Rubenstein, After Auschwitz (1966); Thomas J. J. Altizer, The Gospel of Christian Atheism (1966).

Travel beyond the booths

Utopia regulates travel with official permission; Astrobe’s instantaneous transport serves the civilized regions. The comparison helps explain why a walk matters here. Leaving the convenient network lets More encounter places and people that the official description does not adequately explain.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of the Travelling of the Utopians.”

Hunting and the author of Utopia

More’s delight in either end of a hunt contrasts with the Utopians’ contempt for hunting. The contrast separates the character’s appetites from the rules of the society in his book. His attraction to the wild draws him further from Astrobe’s claim that civilized life is complete.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, discussion of pleasure and hunting.

The tree and its fruit

More imagines his joke as a tree unexpectedly bearing fruit, then judges a failing religious institution by the image of a barren tree. The Gospel language makes him apply to the Church a test that also bears on his own political invention.

Matthew 7:17–20; Luke 13:6–9.

The replica Mass

The museum rite combines guitar, drugs, theatrical dress, and commercial sponsorship. Its details turn a religious service into a degraded exhibit. The scene can be read in relation to the liturgical and popular culture of the 1960s, but its grotesque composite is Lafferty’s fictional projection.

The novel’s account of the museumized Mass; mid-twentieth-century liturgical and popular culture.

Dante’s infernal instruments

More himself invokes Dante when he hears the instruments. Relevant passages include Barbariccia’s obscene trumpet, Master Adam’s lute-shaped body and drum-like belly, and Nimrod’s horn. The reference is comic and composite: Dante does not describe an orchestra of guitars in the lowest circle.

Dante, Inferno 21.139; 30.49–54, 103; 31.12–18.

What he will be given to see

Pottscamp’s assurance about what will be given in the hour recalls Christ’s promise of words to disciples brought before hostile authorities. The change from speaking to seeing suits More’s journey. The question is whether he can recognize what the encounters disclose.

Matthew 10:19–20.

Rimrock’s sky

The ansels’ ancestors climbed through what they had taken for the sky and found land above the sea. Plato imagines a sea-dweller making a similar discovery in the Phaedo. The parallel makes Rimrock’s account a challenge to the belief that one’s familiar world exhausts reality.

Plato, Phaedo 109c–110a.

Evita, Eve, and Lilith

More calls Evita Lilith rather than Eve; she claims both names. The exchange brings the first mother and the rebellious first wife of later Jewish legend into the same woman. It continues the composite female figure of More’s passage dream.

Genesis 2–3; Alphabet of Ben Sira, the Lilith story.

All nations and the end of the world

Slider questions whether Christ’s commission and promise apply beyond Earth. His argument depends on taking nations and world in a narrowly terrestrial sense. Chapter 8 gives the Metropolitan’s direct answer, making this a dispute within the novel rather than an established limit on the Promise.

Matthew 28:19–20; Past Master, chap. 8.

The sting in the tail

The closing image of a fair face and a dangerous tail recalls Dante’s Geryon, the embodiment of fraud. It also belongs to the proverbial poison reserved for the tail or end. Astrobe’s pleasing appearance has concealed what More discovers behind it.

Dante, Inferno 17.1–27; the proverb in cauda venenum.

Old animal names on a new planet

Kastroides recalls the extinct giant beaver Castoroides, and the direwolves likewise borrow a prehistoric name. Paul warns that the resemblance lies in the names. The earthly vocabulary helps the travelers begin to describe creatures whose behavior and proportions remain unfamiliar.

The names Castoroides and dire wolf; the novel’s explanation of borrowed animal names.

Rouks and the roc

The enormous predatory bird recalls the roc of travel legend. Its habit of displaying human bodies on thorns also resembles a shrike’s impaled prey, enlarged to a human scale. More’s comparison with men hanging dead wolves reverses the ordinary relation between hunter and hunted.

The roc in the Sindbad voyages and Marco Polo; the natural history of shrikes.

Sextus and the sprite

More names Sextus Empiricus in support of a being suited to every environment. Father Oddopter then appears as an answer to the speculation. Sextus reports arguments about living beings in different cosmic regions; the scene turns that philosophical material into a joke about the observers themselves.

Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists, book 1; compare Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.42.

Babes in the woods

Oddopter’s grand title for a familiar story mocks the travelers’ innocence. Like the abandoned children of the ballad, they do not fully understand the danger surrounding them. His greeting is protective advice delivered as teasing.

The ballad “The Babes in the Wood” and its later theatrical versions.

Doubting Thomas

The apostle asks for evidence before believing; More sees the Devil-kill and then tries to exclude what he has seen from his account of reality. Oddopter challenges the rule by which More has decided in advance that only one order of things can exist.

John 20:24–29.

Fishing for the Devil

The bait and hook invite comparison with the Christian interpretation of Leviathan: the Devil takes what he desires and is caught through it. Gregory the Great reads the hook as Christ’s humanity concealing divinity. Evita’s bait and Oddopter’s fishing give that theological image a violent comic form.

Job 41:1, or 40:20 in the Douay-Rheims numbering; Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job, book 33.

The hydra and the daily killing
