The name recalls the monster whose severed heads grow again in Heracles’ labor. Oddopter makes the repeated killing a daily necessity. He also says the Devil can take other forms, so the significance belongs to this encounter and its recurrence, rather than to every animal called a hydra.

The Lernaean Hydra; Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2.

Copperhead’s divination

Reading entrails belongs to the ancient haruspex; interpreting birds belongs to the augur. Copperhead draws on this vocabulary and practice here and on the mountain. More’s uneasiness recalls the biblical prohibition on divination and consultation with the dead.

Deuteronomy 18:10–11; the Roman traditions of haruspicy and augury.

A wandering monk

Oddopter vows never to sleep twice in the same place. This can be set beside both Christ’s homelessness and Benedict’s criticism of wandering monks. Lafferty gives a positive discipline to a form of life that monastic rules often treated with suspicion.

Luke 9:58; Rule of St. Benedict, chap. 1.

Goslar and the Salic Emperors

The name recalls the German imperial city associated with the Salian dynasty. Lafferty transfers imperial ceremony to a precarious settlement with an oral history preserved through the skulls of its rulers. More treats its authority seriously even when the surrounding circumstances are comic.

The imperial palace and Salian history of Goslar.

The emperor’s journey

The newly chosen ruler travels without provisions, money, or spare clothing. The instructions echo the sending of the apostles. That vulnerable arrival also makes the emperor’s office a small-scale counterpart to More’s dangerous appointment.

Luke 9:3; Matthew 10:9–10.

The privy and royal names

More’s henry and proposed charles treat the familiar john as though a privy ought to bear the reigning monarch’s name. The joke brings Henry VIII into the petty frustrations of the visit. More’s caution about crossing royalty recalls how much a confrontation with a king can cost.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, Norfolk’s warning about striving with princes and More’s advice to Cromwell.

Evita’s bargain

Evita calls herself Faustina when she describes the longevity experiment as a bargain with the Devil. The Evil Scientist gives the Faust story a laboratory setting. Her return home after seeking Hell makes the discovery of Golden Astrobe’s nature the bitter result of the bargain.

The Faust tradition, especially the rejuvenation in Goethe’s Faust, part 1.

Coming home and recognizing it

Evita’s journey around the world to recognize her own home can be compared with Chesterton’s returning yachtsman and Eliot’s end of exploration. Her discovery reverses their welcome: the home she finally recognizes is Hell.

G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy, chap. 1; T. S. Eliot, “Little Gidding,” section 5.

Superstition and over-belief

Oddopter’s over-belief has bodily consequences: it leaves marks and makes the feral regions powerful. William James’s term offers a useful comparison for belief that reaches beyond what evidence establishes. Lafferty gives that surplus of belief a creaturely presence.

William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), concluding discussion of over-beliefs.

Green lightning and the electrode

Slider proposes electrically produced pleasure as a superior alternative to drinking. The contrast sets the ease of a manufactured sensation beside a physical, communal activity he cannot manage. It belongs to the novel’s larger dispute over whether discomfort can be removed without losing forms of life.

The chapter’s comparison of green lightning with electrical stimulation.

Sinai and the Transfiguration

Trumpets, cloud, thunder, and lightning recall Sinai. The changed, shining survivors also invite the Gospel comparison that the narrator names as transfiguration. What they encounter includes the faces of Ouden, so the resemblance does not make their vision a simple repetition of a biblical revelation.

Exodus 19:16–19; 34:29–30; Matthew 17:1–9.

Lifting the eyes to the mountains

More’s criticism of the golden inhabitants borrows the upward movement of the psalm. He immediately imagines abandoning such impulses once he governs. His own attraction to the mountain is therefore already in conflict with the settled life he wants to administer.

Psalm 121:1, numbered 120:1 in the Douay-Rheims and Vulgate.

The sleeping kings

Scrivener gathers rulers expected to return when their people need them. The recurring legend gives More’s recruitment a wider pattern. Historical deaths, folk traditions, and invented futures mingle in the list; the list should not be treated as a set of accurate biographies.

The return-of-the-king traditions of Arthur and Frederick Barbarossa.

Alaric under the river

The diverted river and secret burial come from the account of Alaric’s death in Jordanes. The promise that he will rise and lead again belongs to the sleeping-king pattern added here. The distinction shows how historical material becomes a usable legend.

Jordanes, Getica 30.158.

Kennedy and Roadstorm

Kennedy’s open automobile enters the same company as ancient and medieval kings. Roadstorm extends the catalogue into Lafferty’s own fiction and recalls Roadstrum of Space Chantey. The sequence treats very recent history and invented history as material from which legends of return are made.

John F. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963; Lafferty, Space Chantey (1968).

The ram with the double sign

Oddopter says the marked ram belongs to Scripture. Abraham’s substitute sacrifice and Daniel’s two-horned ram are possible points of comparison. The scene does not choose between them or explain the double sign completely; More’s repeated appointment to death gives the image its immediate force.

Genesis 22:13; Daniel 8:3.

A priest forever

Paul’s words over Oddopter identify the dead man with the priesthood of Melchisedech. The verse belongs to the biblical and liturgical language of enduring priesthood. It follows a morning Mass offered for members of the party who would die that day.

Psalm 110:4, numbered 109:4 in the Douay-Rheims and Vulgate; Hebrews 5:6; 7:17.

The lightning and the paradox of motion

The single point of light seems to occupy several places at once. Zeno’s arrow offers a plausible comparison for the old paradox named in the passage. Lafferty makes the apparent solution an overwhelming event through which the travelers must find a still narrower instant of escape.

Aristotle, Physics 6.9, 239b, on Zeno’s arrow.

Literally astonished

The narrator explicitly connects astonishment with being thunderstruck. The event revives the history inside the word. The same habit of making a familiar phrase happen bodily governs many of the novel’s jokes and horrors.

The history of astonish through Old French estoner and the Latin vocabulary of thunder and stupefaction.

The false sky and the empyrean

The possibility of light outside a false sky recalls the empyrean of medieval cosmology and Dante. The narrator poses it as a question. The view into a pit then makes the distinction between apparent height and genuine transcendence more difficult.

Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 66, a. 3; Dante, Paradiso 30.

Scrivener, Slider, and humanity

Scrivener’s choice and Slider’s reversal make personhood a matter of allegiance and action as well as origin. Scrivener dies resisting the Killers. The scene prepares the question, asked later by the Programmed Persons themselves, of whether creatures made from other materials can receive spiritual life.

Past Master, chaps. 7, 10, and 13.

Twenty hours of work

Utopia limits the working day to six hours. Cathead’s twenty-hour labor makes the comparison brutal, especially because efficient machines already exist elsewhere. More must confront people who prefer this destructive work to the comfortable life offered by the golden cities.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Trades, and Manner of Life.”

Choosing servitude

Utopia includes outsiders who voluntarily enter service because its conditions are better than those at home. Cathead reverses the movement: people choose bondage and deprivation to escape the perfected society. The parallel places freedom of choice inside conditions that More finds intolerable.

Thomas More, Utopia, book 2, “Of Their Slaves, and of Their Marriages.”

Dostoevsky and chosen unhappiness

The Underground Man challenges a rationally perfected society by defending the capacity to choose what is painful or disadvantageous. Cathead raises a related question: whether suffering can become proof that one is alive and capable of refusal. The comparison explains the argument without making Cathead’s misery desirable in itself.

Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground, part 1, sections 7–9.

Escape from the golden cities

Barricades and gunfire give the migration a recognizable modern political setting. The Berlin Wall offers a historical comparison, but Lafferty reverses the expected economic destination: these refugees run from abundance into poverty. Their behavior exposes something that Astrobe’s measures of well-being cannot register.

The border barriers and shootings of the Cold War; the novel’s account of the exodus into Cathead.

The yellow flag and the lungers

The flag uses the traditional maritime signal of contagion. Lunger is an older American word for a consumptive. Both terms make bodily disease a constant feature of the city’s life; the weekly plague and lethal work are concrete conditions, not merely symbols of spiritual suffering.

The quarantine flag tradition; the American slang term lunger.

Bethlehem and Bedlam

The district’s name recalls the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem, whose name became Bedlam. Lafferty enlarges a madhouse into a large part of a city. The movement from institution to district makes the question of madness political as well as medical.

Bethlem Hospital, London; the development of the word bedlam.

Holbein’s skeletons

More’s Dutchman is most naturally read as Holbein, his portraitist and the designer of the Dance of Death woodcuts. Older English could use Dutch broadly for German. The remark places the skeletal Metropolitan among images in which death confronts people of every social rank.

Hans Holbein the Younger, Dance of Death, published 1538; Sir Thomas More, 1527.

The fisherman’s ring

The ring associates the Metropolitan with Saint Peter and papal office. The novel also calls him the Pope of Astrobe. These signs give the nearly abandoned church an authority that its physical poverty and small congregation do not measure.

The papal Ring of the Fisherman; the chapter’s description of the Metropolitan.

More hears his own collect

The Metropolitan recites the prayer honoring John Fisher and Thomas More as martyrs. More recognizes Fisher and hears himself placed within a liturgical commemoration that followed his earthly life. The prayer confronts his uncertainty with the Church’s judgment about the man he became.

The collect for Saints John Fisher and Thomas More in the English proper of the Roman Missal after their canonization in 1935.

The Promise on Astrobe

The Metropolitan applies Christ’s promise to this world and answers Slider’s attempt to exclude it. His account of Christ walking on Astrobe gives the answer a local history. The scene asks whether a new planet can be outside the reach of an apparently earthly promise.

Matthew 16:18; 28:20; Past Master, chap. 5.

The blind man who sees

The physically blind Metropolitan calls More blind because he fails to recognize what is before him. John’s account of the man born blind supplies the comparison: sight and spiritual understanding can move in opposite directions. More’s confidence in his diagnosis of Cathead is the object of the rebuke.

John 9:39–41.

The response More remembers

The blessing and More’s answering line come from the psalm used in the prayers at the foot of the altar. His ready response shows religious memory operating beneath his professed uncertainty. The words ask for renewed life at the very moment he is confronting a church thought to be dying.

Psalm 85, numbered 84 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims; the Roman Mass, Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos.

Stones, clods, and the woman’s touch

The promise that the planet itself will testify recalls the stones that cry out in Luke. The woman who touches More likewise recalls a Gospel encounter, although here she gives him a prophecy rather than receives a cure. Both episodes place knowledge outside the institutions and explanations he trusts.

Luke 19:40; Mark 5:25–34.

King-making

The title recalls the historical Kingmaker, Warwick, and brings the name Cosmos Kingmaker into the account of how a ruler is manufactured. Acclamation, publicity, party arrangements, and effective phrasing do the work once associated with a vote. The final ease of the process is part of its menace.

Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick; Shakespeare, 3 Henry VI, 3.3.

Cecily and the adopted daughter

More compares Evita with his youngest daughter. Historically that daughter was Cecily, educated with her sisters in More’s household. His paternal comparison sits uneasily with Evita’s age, experience, and refusal to be treated as a child.

More’s family: Cecily More Heron; Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More.

The wrong apostle

The Crank combines doubting Thomas with Judas. More corrects him, but the confusion reveals what Astrobe admires: it has turned the supposed betrayer of Christ into a hero. The error belongs to the characters’ damaged religious memory and should not be repeated as a description of either apostle.

John 20:24–29; the Gospel accounts of Judas’s betrayal.

From one person, one vote to no vote

The account starts with an egalitarian formula, passes through unequal voting weights, and ends by abolishing voting. Mill’s plural voting and Shute’s fictional multiple-vote scheme offer comparisons for the middle stage. The succession makes the removal of political choice appear to be one more modernization.

John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government, chap. 8; Nevil Shute, In the Wet (1953).

Demos, Ochlos, and the anesthetics

Demos names the people as a political body; ochlos names a crowd or mob. The Esthetics, Anesthetics, and Local Anesthetics turn disputes about taste and sensation into party labels. The catalogue mixes learned political names with jokes about feeling and its suppression.

Greek demos, people; ochlos, crowd; aisthesis, perception or sensation.

The Crank and the right to unhappiness

The Crank’s defense of choosing one’s occupation and unhappiness recalls John the Savage’s demand in Brave New World. More answers from the side of the administered society. The encounter therefore exposes the distance between the candidate’s public confidence and the liberty a dissenter wants.

Aldous Huxley, Brave New World, chap. 17.

Moving mountains

More turns the Gospel image of mountain-moving faith into a political joke. The promise to move the world ahead follows his own unsettling mountain experience. Biblical words now help him sell the program whose deeper claims he has begun to forget.

Matthew 17:20; 1 Corinthians 13:2.

Green pastures

The speech approaches the language of Psalm 23 and then corrects itself into a more acceptable statement of progress. The interrupted phrase briefly introduces rest under a shepherd into a speech about collective advancement. It also raises the question of who is supplying More’s words.

Psalm 23:2, numbered 22:2 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims.

All things to all men

More’s happy new phrase belongs to Saint Paul. In its biblical setting it concerns winning others for the gospel; in the campaign it promises universal political appeal. The narrator’s doubt about who speaks through More turns the apparent improvisation into evidence of manipulation.

1 Corinthians 9:22.

The total good

The speech replaces a good calculated for many persons with the good of a merged singularity. Bentham’s familiar formula supplies the point of departure. The crucial change is the disappearance of distinct persons from the account of what their common good should be.

Jeremy Bentham, A Fragment on Government (1776), preface; the utilitarian formula of the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

Pandomation and the Open Mind Act

Rooms exposed to spectators invite comparison with the glass houses of We and the telescreens of Nineteen Eighty-Four. Astrobe also extends access into thought. The Open Mind Act’s subtitle turns an expression of tolerance into a claim to enter another person’s mind.

Yevgeny Zamyatin, We (1924); George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).

The deformation of Wells’s future

The title answers Chapter 5 and Wells’s The Shape of Things to Come. More now sees the claim to perfected humanity from its reverse side. The Programmed Persons explain what their completion of human history would remove.

H. G. Wells, The Shape of Things to Come (1933); Past Master, chap. 5.

The door in the wall

The door appears where there should be none and leaves no opening afterward. Wells’s disappearing door offers a close comparison, particularly under this chapter title. Lafferty changes the destination from an alluring garden to the Nine’s room of coercion and disclosure.

H. G. Wells, “The Door in the Wall” (1906).

Below the salt

More invokes the seating order of a great household when he takes Ouden’s reserved place. His refusal of a lower seat becomes a refusal to acknowledge Nothing as his superior. A social expression gives his resistance a physical and ceremonial form.

The traditional distinction between seating above and below the salt.

The reverse of the tapestry

The Nine present themselves as mankind seen from behind. Cervantes compares translation with the reverse of a tapestry, where the figures remain visible through knots and threads. The analogy helps describe a recognizable human pattern made rough or deformed, while the Nine insist that their reverse is the true side.

Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, part 2, chap. 62.

Rechabitism

The Rechabites in Jeremiah obey an ancestral command to abstain from wine and settled possessions. Northprophet names rechabitism as his trio’s specialty without defining the process. In this conversation its association with abstinence can be set beside the Programmed Persons’ desire to eliminate their appetite for life.

Jeremiah 35.

Houses swept and garnished

Pottscamp explicitly describes the bodies as houses entered by devils. His language comes from Christ’s account of an expelled spirit returning to an empty, ordered house with worse companions. The account distinguishes the constructed bodies from the beings that occupy them.

Matthew 12:43–45; Luke 11:24–26.

The machine that succeeds mankind

Butler’s evolving machines and Čapek’s artificial workers provide earlier versions of humanity being superseded by its creations. Lafferty joins that prospect to the language of possession. The question therefore concerns both the material construction of the Programmed Persons and what has come to live in them.

Samuel Butler, Erewhon, “The Book of the Machines”; Karel Čapek, R.U.R. (1920).

Opening the box

The warning about taking the lid off a box invites the comparison with Pandora. Jack-in-the-box language makes the released powers sound like unruly toys. The image grows until the box is Astrobe itself, and the dispute turns to whether hope has survived inside it.

Hesiod, Works and Days 90–105; the later Pandora’s-box tradition.

Hell and nonbeing

More’s preference for existence even in Hell can be compared with Milton’s Satan, while his preference for the lunger’s life over kingship recalls Achilles in the underworld. The differences matter: More is resisting annihilation, and his chosen comparison is the life of an actual suffering person.

Milton, Paradise Lost 1.263; Homer, Odyssey 11.489–91.

Water, clay, and artificial bodies

Swampers asks whether the spirit that came to water and clay could come to the materials of a Programmed Person. Genesis supplies the language of creation and animated earth. The question leaves open a possibility that the Nine’s general account of themselves tries to close.

Genesis 1:2; 2:7.

What must we do to be saved?

Northprophet and Pottscamp echo the jailer’s question to Paul and Silas. More dismisses their appeal as mockery. Pottscamp’s later penitence makes it difficult to assume that this moment has only one tone or purpose.

Acts 16:30; Past Master, chap. 13.

The second death

Revelation uses the phrase for the final condition of the condemned. More also faces the literal prospect of being beheaded twice. The overlap places his personal ordeal inside the novel’s larger questions about resurrection, extinction, and the death of a world.

Revelation 20:6, 14; 21:8.

Writer, lawyer, and chancellor

More’s soliloquy turns three achievements of his earlier life into traps: he must inhabit his fiction, find its legality, and administer it. His political competence has helped make his captivity possible. The question of what he will refuse now becomes more urgent than what he can manage.

More’s authorship of Utopia and his legal and governmental career; the chapter’s closing soliloquy.

The Nine Day King

The title invites comparison with Lady Jane Grey, the Nine Days’ Queen, who was deposed and later executed. More also recalls the young Salic ruler as a One Day Emperor. The comparison gives his presidency the shape of a brief elevation already overshadowed by the block.

Lady Jane Grey’s reign in July 1553; the proverb of a nine days’ wonder.

The philosopher king

More explicitly thinks of Plato’s ideal ruler. Utopia had already debated whether a philosopher could serve usefully in a prince’s council. Astrobe gives More the supreme office, but the bills and their hidden provisions reveal how little final authority that office guarantees.

Plato, Republic 5.473c–d; Thomas More, Utopia, book 1.

Astrobe’s calendar

The year 535 A.S. corresponds to 2535 by the old count. The omitted Free Years complicate the colony’s elapsed time. The dates place More roughly a thousand years beyond his earthly death while exposing another way the official account orders and compresses history.

The chapter’s account of anno scientiae and the Free Year.

The sun as a hole

The words spoken through More recall Anaximander’s account of the sun as an opening through which fire is seen. In Astrobe’s argument the opening becomes an emblem of emptiness. The comparison is useful, but no philosopher is named in the scene.

Ancient accounts of Anaximander’s cosmology, including Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies 1.6.

Ban the Beyond

More’s name for the measure recalls the modern slogan Ban the Bomb. The resemblance gives the abolition of transcendence the familiar language of a public campaign. The provision would prohibit considering things beyond the Dream, including the possibility that the Dream is incomplete.

The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament slogan; the chapter’s description of the bill.

The remnants

The legal heading reduces surviving religious communities to leftovers. Isaiah and Romans give remnant a different significance: a people preserved through apparent defeat. The small numbers therefore do not settle the value or future of the communities the bill would abolish.

Isaiah 10:20–22; Romans 11:5.

Kingmaker’s Fall

Kingmaker tells of creatures who leave perfection in search of something beyond and fall into the void. The account reverses the value of escape: faith in a beyond becomes the original error. More’s suspicion that the labels have been switched opens the possibility that Golden Astrobe is itself the emptiness.

Compare Genesis 3 and Revelation 12:7–9; Kingmaker’s allegory in this chapter.

Veto: I forbid

More writes the Latin formula across the bill. His prohibition defends the freedom to consider what the measure would prohibit. The constitutional penalty follows three refusals of the proposal in its successive forms, so his third veto makes the act of reading and rejecting legislation a decision about his life.

Latin veto, I forbid; the chapter’s law concerning repeated vetoes.

More’s first refusal

The novel explicitly compares this refusal with the act that led to More’s first death. Historically he refused the oath in 1534 and was later convicted of treason. Lafferty changes the issue and the character’s stated certainty, while retaining the demand for assent and the fatal cost of withholding it.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, accounts of the oath and trial.

The friend who requires the head

More asks who pushed him into the corner before. Roper records his judgment that Henry’s friendship would not save his head if the king could gain by taking it. Foreman’s friendship and manipulation repeat that disturbing proximity between affection and political use.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, More’s conversation with Roper after Henry’s visit to Chelsea.

The gathering eagles

The opening recalls the Gospel saying that eagles gather where the body is. Its setting in discourse about the last things fits a night described as the world’s last. The companions gather around a man whose death is expected, while their name also carries the force of a chosen company.

Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37; compare Job 39:30.

Principalities and powers

The account of Evita’s long battle draws directly on Paul’s description of spiritual warfare. Her apparent youth and accumulated experience give that struggle an unusual embodiment. Her enemies exercise political control as well as the spiritual hostility named by the phrase.

Ephesians 6:12.

Saint Brandon’s voyage

Adam retells the voyage of Saint Brendan as an early visit to Astrobe. His nineteen monks and ninety-nine days differ from the medieval Navigatio, with its smaller chosen company and seven-year voyage. Moving the Land of Promise into space gives Astrobe a sacred past earlier than its official settlement.

Navigatio Sancti Brendani; Past Master’s name for the saint is Brandon.

The wake before death

The companions hold the wake while More is alive. Stories, drink, and argument become forms of attendance on a death they hope to prevent. Their conversation defeats the machines’ attempt to reduce it to useful instructions or a discoverable plan.

The wake tradition; the chapter’s account of the machines listening to the stories.

The fools’ carnival

Masks, mock factions, irreverence, and mingled joy and violence recall the Feast of Fools and carnival traditions. Cosmopolis begins behaving unpredictably on the night before its ceremonial execution. Its recovery of feeling is dangerous as well as hopeful.

The medieval Feast of Fools; Carnival, Halloween, and St. John’s Eve customs.

Candy heads and skulls

The confections invite comparison with the sugar skulls of the Mexican Day of the Dead. Here they honor an execution that has not yet happened. Death becomes something sold, eaten, mocked, and anticipated throughout the city.

The calavera tradition of the Day of the Dead.

Sackcloth and ashes

The carnival faction turns an act of penance into a public costume and joke. Chapter 13 gives the gesture a different weight when Pottscamp pours ashes over his head. The repetition asks whether an apparently empty imitation can become an actual act of remorse.

Matthew 11:21; Job 2:12; 42:6.

The interdict

The new Metropolitan invokes the Church’s power to place a territory under religious censure pending repentance. Applying it to a planet gives an old ecclesiastical action an enormous scale. His appearance also answers the earlier assumption that the dying Metropolitan would have no successor.

The historical practice of a general interdict, notably the interdict on England, 1208–14.

The serpent’s tooth

The narrator’s phrase for remorse recalls Lear’s pain at an ungrateful child. Cosmopolis has raised More to power and is preparing to kill him. The borrowed image makes its new emotion resemble a child’s recognition of injury done to a parent.

Shakespeare, King Lear, 1.4.

The funeral toll and the July Bell

The old bells recover names and a shared purpose as they toll for More. The July Bell can suggest his execution on 6 July 1535, although the novel does not explain the name. Sound carries a religious memory that the museumized churches seemed to have lost.

The Christian passing-bell and funeral-toll traditions; More’s death in July 1535.

Apocephalon and Panlykonium

The chapter title joins the ideas of removal and head in a Greek-looking word that also sounds near apocalypse. Panlykonium substitutes wolves for the demons of pandemonium. The coinages bring beheading, revelation, and the crowd’s wolfish behavior into the same ending.

Greek apo, away, kephale, head, and lykos, wolf; Milton’s coinage Pandemonium.

The spotted lamb

Foreman’s victim reverses the scriptural lamb without blemish. More’s weaknesses and compromises are part of the point: the man required for the sacrifice is visibly imperfect. Foreman’s explanation of what that blood will accomplish remains an account given by the person arranging the death.

Exodus 12:5; 1 Peter 1:19.

Seed, salt, and leaven

The mustard seed of Chapter 1 returns beside the language of leaven and preserving salt. The images allow a small act or remnant to change a much greater body. Foreman uses them to explain historical renewal; the final pages test whether his planned result exhausts what has happened.

Matthew 5:13; 13:31–33; 1 Corinthians 5:6.

Foreman’s history of worlds

The rapid succession from republic to empire and through later ages is Foreman’s theory of historical death and rebirth. His first emperor is Augustus, who represented his rule as a restoration of the republic. The novel’s five-hundred-year rhythm should be read as that theory rather than as conventional historical periodization.

Augustus, Res Gestae 34; Foreman’s account in this chapter.

Particular and General Judgment

More distinguishes the judgment of a person after death from the final judgment of the world. Foreman rejects both and insists on explaining himself immediately. Their disagreement exposes the limit of his history: he invokes transcendence as a requirement while denying the judgment More expects beyond death.

The Christian distinction between particular judgment and Last Judgment.

The consoling Barnabas

More’s name for the smooth-talking Foreman recalls Barnabas, whose name Acts interprets as son of consolation. The consolation is bitterly comic because its bearer is arranging the victim’s death. The insult resists the gentleness with which the necessity is being explained.

Acts 4:36.

The brains of the enemy

More explains his last meal through the belief that eating an enemy can confer the enemy’s capacities. Frazer offers a familiar account of that belief. The meal’s artificial substance and More’s doubt about acquiring wit turn the ritual into a final joke at the Programmed Persons’ expense.

J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough, “Homoeopathic Magic of a Flesh Diet.”

The earlier execution hour

Foreman advances the expected noon execution to eight. Roper records that Sir Thomas Pope brought More word that he must die before nine on the morning of his earthly execution. The historical early-morning notice becomes a means of frustrating the rescue in Lafferty’s story.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, account of 6 July 1535.

The offer to sign and live

Pottscamp’s last offer recalls the repeated opportunity for the historical More to save himself by yielding. Here he argues that the successor will sign immediately anyway. More’s refusal answers the attempt to judge his act solely by whether it can stop the administration’s next step.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More, accounts of the examinations and trial.

The late return

More’s discovery that he has come back late to the only thing that matters can be read beside Augustine’s late love. The comparison concerns the shape of a belated conversion. More speaks of a return to something long known, even while saying how little he understands it.

Augustine, Confessions 10.27.

The forerunner wave

The first rescuers form the small wave that precedes a larger movement. Forerunner also recalls John the Baptist, himself beheaded. The resemblance puts the failed rush into a pattern of preparation, while the narrative keeps its individual deaths painful and concrete.

Matthew 14:1–12; the Christian title of John the Baptist as Forerunner.

Beware, Iscariot

The narrator translates Evita’s warning and thereby identifies Foreman with Judas. Her subsequent woe recalls Christ’s judgment on the person through whom betrayal or scandal comes. The need for an event to occur does not excuse the person who brings it about.

Matthew 26:24; Luke 17:1.

A dog for the death journey

Evita explains Foreman’s killing as the provision of an animal companion for a dead hero. Achilles’ sacrifice of dogs at Patroclus’s funeral is a classical comparison. Calling the planner a dog overturns the authority with which he has just interpreted More’s death.

Homer, Iliad 23.173–74.

The two deaths of Judas

Foreman is torn apart and a surviving piece is hung from a tree. The sequence brings together the dismembering imagery of Acts and the hanging in Matthew. The later question about the Judas tree’s fruit returns to the possible consequences of a betrayal whose guilt the scene has made explicit.

Matthew 27:5; Acts 1:18.

The Judas tree

The novel calls its tree a carob and also a Judas Tree. Botanically, the tree usually bearing the latter name is Cercis siliquastrum, distinct from the carob, Ceratonia siliqua. The literary association with betrayal is clear even where the plant names overlap or are confused.

The Judas-tree legend; the botanical distinction between Cercis siliquastrum and Ceratonia siliqua.

The stranger and the shadow

The stranger is unnamed. A Christ interpretation is possible, and the invitation also recalls More’s earlier recruitment by a traveler. Rumors that an essence departed and a shadow died invite comparison with substitution accounts of the Crucifixion, but the narrator reports and unsettles the rumors rather than confirming them.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4, on Basilides; Past Master, chap. 2.

The interrupted prayer

More begins the Latin prayer by which Christ commends his spirit to the Father. The words also belong to the psalm and to Compline. His death interrupts the prayer; the scene replaces the polished last sayings of quotation books with a remembered fragment.

Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5, numbered 30:6 in the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims; the Compline responsory In manus tuas.

Scaffold sayings and the recovered head

Lafferty explicitly refuses the familiar collection of More’s last jokes. The tale of a woman carrying away his head recalls Margaret Roper’s recovery of her father’s head, while its basket also suggests the Baptist’s story. The novel presents its own beautiful tale and immediately questions it.

Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More; Edward Hall, Chronicle; Stapleton, Tres Thomae; Matthew 14:11.

The stars go out

The extinction of the stars invites comparison with Clarke’s famous ending. Lafferty follows that extinction with questions about duration, rebirth, and hope. The apparent end therefore opens a further problem that the narration does not settle by simply showing a new world.

Arthur C. Clarke, “The Nine Billion Names of God” (1953).

Time without motion

When nothing moves, the difference between a second and an immense duration cannot be measured. Aristotle’s account of time through motion provides a useful philosophical comparison. George’s earlier story and the ending both place their interval between worlds outside ordinary measures.

Aristotle, Physics 4.11; compare Augustine, Confessions 11.

The left hand and the returning question

The banner, Gandy’s question, and the last recollection of spirit descending on matter gather the left-handed motif into a possibility of grace for the Programmed. The ashes on a machine’s head matter because an act of penitence has occurred where feeling was said to be absent.

Genesis 1:2; 2:7; Job 2:12; 42:6; Past Master, chap. 10.

Watching, waiting, hoping

The three refrains move from watchfulness to expectation and hope. Paul’s account of hoping for what is not yet seen and the Gospel command to watch provide biblical comparisons. The final words preserve expectation without supplying a completed account of the world’s renewal.

Romans 8:24–25; Matthew 26:41.

Glossary

Comprehensive Reference

Adam
Evita's brother, first encountered in Paul's passage dreams and later on Astrobe. In the dream he denies that his repeated deaths are resurrections, saying that another boy of the same name takes his place. He dies fighting on Electric Mountain and appears again at the wake. During the final rescue attempt he reaches and touches More before being killed. See also: Evita, Passage Dreams, Electric Mountain.
Adam's Sister (Childwitch)
The childwitch in Paul's passage dream who decides to go to Hell before dying. Chapter 5 identifies Evita as Adam's sister, connecting the dream figure with the girl-woman who accompanies Thomas. Paul's uncertainty about whether these people belong to his past, dreams, or future is part of the passage dreams’ disturbance of time. See also: Adam, Evita, Passage Dreams.
Alien from Gootz
An alien in Father Oddopter's comic story at Goslar. Mistaking it for a wheel of cheese, the townspeople cut it into a hundred portions and eat it. It cannot reassemble itself and refuses to be expelled, supposedly accounting for the inhabitants’ green faces. This is a tale told by a character, not a separately witnessed event. See also: Father Oddopter, Goslar.
America
The second chance in Kingmaker's account of human history, between the Old World and Astrobe. Foreman disputes his account of failure and argues that earlier worlds died without entirely failing. Their disagreement introduces the distinction between extinction and renewal that returns at the end. See also: Three Chances, Astrobe, Old Earth.
Ancient Instruction
The command to go to all nations, raised by Slider in Chapter 5. He doubts that the Promise applies to a different world and questions whether Astrobians are still human in the relevant sense. The Metropolitan answers the wider problem in Chapter 8 by saying that Christ renewed the Promise on Astrobe. See also: Metropolitan of Astrobe, Promise.
Ansels
Seal-like beings native to Astrobe. The novel distinguishes natural ansels, which may be hunted, from intelligent ansels such as Rimrock. Their ascent story describes creatures emerging from the physical ocean; the interior ocean of dreams is a related metaphor, not their geographical habitat. Ansels work as divers and communicators and can share a school mind. Rimrock leaves that comfortable collective existence to preserve his individuality. See also: Rimrock, Eutheopathy, Ocean Depths, School Mind, Transcendence.
Ansel (False)
An unnamed entity that telepathically impersonated Rimrock to lure Paul and Thomas into a trap at the Astrobe spaceport upon their arrival. When Paul hears the genuine Rimrock's urgent warning (Paul! Thomas! Away fast!), he realizes the first mental voice was a deceiver. Rimrock later mentions having had to settle with another false ansel who spoke in my guise, returning with fresh blood on him. The false ansel represents the Programmed Persons’ capacity for mimicry and infiltration, and the danger of trusting even telepathic communication in a world where identity itself can be counterfeited. See also: Rimrock, Ansels, Programmed Persons.
Antenna-like Loop, Tuned
The tuned loop in Brooks's London office that Paul uses for Chronometanastasis. After passing through it, Paul walks to Chelsea to meet More. It is a time-travel device, distinct from the Hopp-Equation spacecraft used between Earth and Astrobe. See also: Chronometanastasis, Brooks, Paul.
Anxious Powers
Powers mentioned alongside Astrobe's Great Men during More's ceremonial arrival. The phrase suggests authorities behind the public spectacle, but the passage does not explicitly equate the group with the Nine. See also: Nine, Big Three, Programmed Persons.
Apocephalon
The title of Chapter 13, evoking beheading and More's execution. The chapter also describes the destruction of the worlds and asks whether renewal follows. The snakes emerging from More's head belong to tales that the narrator reports and disavows, leaving their status uncertain. See also: Execution, Nine, Thomas More.
Arena (Convocation Hall)
The central lower floor of the Convocation Hall in Cosmopolis, where Thomas More and his party stand during his acclamation as Past Master. The elite 'great ones' sit above in the 'high circle,' looking down—a spatial arrangement emphasizing More's position as spectacle and sacrifice, the object of power rather than its wielder. The term 'arena' carries Roman connotations of gladiatorial combat and Christian martyrdom, foreshadowing More's eventual execution in Centrality Square. See also: Convocation Hall, Past Master, Cosmopolis.
Armored Wagon
Battersea's military vehicle used to transport Thomas More's party to the Convocation Hall. Its presence signifies Cathead's surprising capability—the supposedly chaotic slum district possesses organized military resources—and represents the assertive movement of the margins into the center of power. The wagon's armor acknowledges the constant threat of Programmed Killers while demonstrating the resistance's refusal to be cowed. See also: Battersea, Cathead, Convocation Hall.
Aspens, Heavenly
Trees lining the long Concourse leading to the Convocation Hall in Cosmopolis. Called 'heavenly' in the text, they contribute to the capital's idealized, opulent aesthetic—nature perfected and arranged for maximum symbolic effect. The ironic epithet underscores the Astrobe Dream's appropriation of transcendent language for purely material beauty, heaven reduced to landscaping. See also: Concourse, Convocation Hall, Cosmopolis.
Assassins
Common term for the Programmed Killers among Cathead's inhabitants, particularly the 'lungers' who hate everybody, but especially the stilted-gaited assassins. The word emphasizes intentionality and malice rather than mere mechanical function, reflecting the Cathead perspective that these beings serve an evil purpose rather than neutral law enforcement. The 'stilted gait' identifies their inhuman movement. See also: Programmed Killers, Lungers, Cathead.
Astrobe
The planet on which most of the novel takes place, said to lie 1.5 parsecs from Earth. Kingmaker calls it mankind's third chance. Its wealthy cities pursue the Astrobe Dream, while Cathead, the Barrio, and the Feral Lands resist or escape that order. Foreman reports eight thousand terminations a day in Cosmopolis alone. Native life includes natural and intelligent ansels, hydras, and enormous predators. See also: Astrobe Dream, Three Chances, Cosmopolis, Feral Lands, Ouden, Golden Astrobe.
Astrobe Dream
The ideology of perfected collective life promoted by civilized Astrobe. It promises freedom from distress and moves toward merger with the Programmed and the City. More initially accepts its claims, but the Nine reveal a project culminating in Ouden and the extinction of existence. The Dream can be read as a criticism of utopian systems that sacrifice persons to an ideal of perfection. See also: Ouden, Programmed Persons, One Great City, High Vision, Cosmopolis, Termination.
Astrobe Great Ones
The assembled ruling elite present at Thomas More's acclamation in the Convocation Hall: Kingmaker, Proctor, Foreman, Pottscamp, Northprophet, scientists, speculators, projectors, mind-men. They sit in the 'high circle' overlooking the Arena, representing Astrobe's visible power structure—though true power lies with the Nine Programmed Persons, some of whom (Pottscamp, Northprophet) are present in their midst, unrecognized for what they are. See also: Big Three, Nine, Convocation Hall, Pottscamp, Northprophet.
Astrobe Month
Time unit used for Hopp-Equation interstellar travel. The journey from Earth to Astrobe takes 'one Astrobe month,' which is slightly less than one Earth month—approximately 700 standard hours. Astrobe's year is also shorter than Earth's, requiring a 'Free Year' inserted every 29 years (but uncounted) to maintain synchronization. See also: Hopp-Equation, Free Year.
Avatar
Charles's description of Maxwell, whose attachment to any particular body is loose. Maxwell is partly Programmed; after his body is destroyed on Electric Mountain, he reappears at the wake in the manufactured body of an old woman. The term invites religious associations without settling his precise nature. See also: Maxwell, Transcendental Yeast, Electric Mountain.
